bashkurdistan.t: An autonomous Bashkir state proclaimed during the Russian Civil War, which switched from the Whites to the Bolsheviks to win recognition.
bashkurdistan.o: After the [[e:february-revolution|February Revolution]] of 1917 [[e:bashkirs|Bashkir]] nationalists led by [[e:zeki-velidi-togan|Ahmet-Zaki Validi]] (Zeki Velidi Togan) held congresses in [[e:orenburg|Orenburg]] and Ufa. In November 1917 they proclaimed the territorial autonomy of Bashkurdistan, in rivalry with [[e:tatars|Tatar]] plans for the [[s:idel-ural-state|Idel-Ural State]].
bashkurdistan.r: The [[e:bashkirs|Bashkir]] government formed its own army and initially sided with the anti-Bolshevik forces, including the [[e:komuch|Komuch]] government and [[e:alexander-kolchak|Admiral Kolchak]]. Disappointed by the [[e:white-movement|Whites]]' refusal of autonomy, Validi negotiated with [[e:moscow|Moscow]], and in February 1919 the Bashkir army went over to the Red side.
bashkurdistan.e: In March 1919 the Soviet government recognised the [[e:bashkir-autonomous-soviet-socialist-republic|Bashkir Autonomous Soviet Republic]], the first autonomous republic in [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]]. Validi soon broke with the Bolsheviks over their limits on autonomy and fled to [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]]. The republic is the ancestor of today's [[e:bashkortostan|Republic of Bashkortostan]].

banu-ammar-of-tripoli.t: A family of Shi'i judges who made Tripoli an independent city-state, famed for its library, until the Crusaders took it in 1109.
banu-ammar-of-tripoli.o: The Banu Ammar were a family of [[e:qadi|qadis]] in [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] under the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]]. Around 1070, as Fatimid control of the coast collapsed, the qadi Amin al-Dawla Abu Talib al-Hasan ibn Ammar made the city independent.
banu-ammar-of-tripoli.r: The city prospered from trade, [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], paper and olive groves, and the Banu Ammar founded a Dar al-Ilm, a house of learning with a famous library. They kept their independence by diplomacy with the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]] and [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]]. [[e:jalal-al-mulk-ali|Jalal al-Mulk Ali]] extended their rule along the coast, and in 1099 the emir of [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] paid the passing [[e:crusader-states|Crusaders]] to spare the city.
banu-ammar-of-tripoli.e: From 1102 [[e:raymond-iv-of-toulouse|Raymond of Saint-Gilles]] besieged [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] from a castle he built on [[e:mount-pilgrim|Mount Pilgrim]]. [[e:fakhr-al-mulk-ibn-ammar|Fakhr al-Mulk]] went to [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] in 1108 to seek aid in vain, and in July 1109 the city fell to the [[e:crusader-states|Crusaders]] and became the capital of the County of Tripoli. Later chroniclers claimed the library was burned.

banat-republic.t: Short-lived multi-ethnic republic proclaimed in Temesvár in 1918, an attempt to keep the mixed Banat region together as Austria-Hungary collapsed.
banat-republic.o: As [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] dissolved at the end of October 1918, Social Democrats and local leaders in [[e:timisoara|Temesvár]], led by the lawyer [[e:otto-roth|Otto Roth]], proclaimed the [[e:banat|Banat]] Republic on 1 November 1918. They hoped to preserve the unity of the Banat, home to [[e:romanians|Romanians]], [[e:serbs|Serbs]], Germans, Hungarians and others, within a democratic [[e:hungary|Hungary]].
banat-republic.r: A people's council with representatives of the different nationalities tried to keep order, organise a civic guard and supply the towns. The republic had little military force and was not recognised by any state; Romanian and Serbian national councils in the region rejected it.
banat-republic.e: Serbian troops entered [[e:timisoara|Temesvár]] on 15 November 1918 and ended the republic within about two weeks of its proclamation. The [[e:banat|Banat]] was later divided between [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]], the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]] and [[e:hungary|Hungary]] by the post-war treaties of 1919 to 1920.

banate-of-macso.t: Hungarian banate south of the Sava around Mačva and Belgrade, a frontier province contested with Serbia for over two centuries.
banate-of-macso.o: Around 1254 [[e:bela-iv-of-hungary|Béla IV of Hungary]] created a banate in the [[e:macva|Mačva]] region south of the [[e:sava|Sava]] and gave it to his son-in-law, the Rus prince [[e:rostislav-mikhailovich|Rostislav Mikhailovich]], who also held Bosnian lands.
banate-of-macso.r: The ban governed a mixed Serbian and Hungarian population from Macsó and [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]], guarding the southern frontier and the trade route to the [[e:balkans|Balkans]]. From 1284 it passed to the deposed Serbian king [[e:stefan-dragutin|Stefan Dragutin]] as part of the [[s:kingdom-of-syrmia|Kingdom of Syrmia]]. Later bans were Hungarian [[e:magnates|magnates]], notably the Garai family in the 14th and 15th centuries.
banate-of-macso.e: With the Ottoman advance, the banate lost its strategic role; the office lapsed in the late 15th century, and the region fell to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], with [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]] itself taken in 1521.

baku-khanate.t: A small Caspian khanate centred on the walled city of Baku, known for its oil and salt trade and its resistance to the Russian advance.
baku-khanate.o: After the assassination of [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] in 1747, Mirza Muhammad Khan I, of a local family of governors, made [[e:baku|Baku]] and the [[e:absheron-peninsula|Absheron]] peninsula an independent khanate within the walls of the old [[e:shirvanshah|Shirvanshah]] city. The town, with its [[e:maiden-tower|Maiden Tower]] and palace, was small but well fortified and had a busy harbour.
baku-khanate.r: The khans controlled [[e:baku|Baku's]] harbour and the oil [[e:well|wells]] and salt pans of [[e:absheron-peninsula|Absheron]], whose products were exported across the Caspian to [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[e:russia|Russia]]; oil revenues were a key source of income. The khanate was too small to stand alone and between 1768 and 1789 depended on [[e:fatali-khan-of-quba|Fatali Khan]] of the [[s:quba-khanate|Quba Khanate]].
baku-khanate.e: In 1806 the Russian commander [[e:pavel-tsitsianov|Pavel Tsitsianov]] was killed at the gates of [[e:baku|Baku]] while accepting its surrender from [[e:huseyngulu-khan|Huseyngulu Khan]]. Russian troops occupied the city later that year, and the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] annexed the khanate, laying the ground for Baku's later oil boom.

bartians.t: Prussian people of the land of Barta in the upper Łyna valley, conquered by the Teutonic Order after long resistance in the 13th century.
bartians.o: The Bartians inhabited Barta, an inland Prussian territory around modern [[e:bartoszyce|Bartoszyce]] in north-eastern [[e:poland|Poland]], divided into Greater and Lesser Barta. They are known mainly from the chronicle of [[e:peter-of-dusburg|Peter of Dusburg]], written in the 14th century.
bartians.r: They lived in farming communities ruled by local nobles with fortified places, and shared the religion and language of the other [[e:old-prussians|Prussians]]. Their territory lay between [[s:prince-bishopric-of-warmia|Warmia]], [[s:natangians|Natangia]] and the Galindian wilderness.
bartians.e: The [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]] subdued Barta around 1240 and built [[e:bartoszyce|Bartenstein]]. The Bartians rose in the [[e:great-prussian-uprising|Great Prussian Uprising]] from 1260 under their leader [[e:diwanus|Diwanus]], besieging Order castles, but by 1274 they were defeated. Their land became part of the Order's state, and the people merged into the Prussian peasantry.

bihat-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Bundelkhand Agency, known mainly from British lists of the small states of central India.
bihat-state.o: Bihat was confirmed as a separate holding by a British sanad in 1807, one of the small estates recognised after the British gained control of [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]].
bihat-state.r: It consisted of a handful of villages under a hereditary chief. Little else is recorded.
bihat-state.e: After independence Bihat was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

balsan-state.t: A small Rajput hill state east of Shimla, one of the Simla Hill States until 1948.
balsan-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500 and links it to the Sirmur royal house, but little is reliably known of its origins.
balsan-state.r: Balsan was a small mountain state on the Giri river. It was occupied by [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Little else of its history is recorded.
balsan-state.e: Balsan merged into [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948 and is now part of [[e:shimla|Shimla]] district.

bukey-horde.t: A Kazakh khanate between the Volga and the Ural rivers, created with Russian permission in 1801 and ruled by Jangir Khan.
bukey-horde.o: In 1801 the Russian emperor Paul I allowed the sultan [[e:bukey-khan|Bukey]], a son of [[e:nurali-khan|Nurali Khan]] of the [[s:junior-juz|Junior Juz]], to lead some 5,000 families across the [[e:ural-river|Ural River]] into the steppe between the Ural and the [[e:volga|Volga]] left empty by the [[e:kalmyks|Kalmyk]] departure of 1771. Bukey was recognised as khan in 1812.
bukey-horde.r: The Inner Horde was a Russian-protected khanate under its own [[e:genghisid-principle|Chinggisid]] rulers. [[e:bukey-khan|Bukey]]'s son [[e:jangir-khan|Jangir Khan]], who ruled from 1823, built a capital at Khan Ordasy, opened a school, encouraged trade fairs and gave land to his supporters, which provoked resentment. The revolt led by [[e:isatay-taimanuly|Isatay Taimanuly]] and the poet [[e:makhambet-otemisuly|Makhambet Otemisuly]] in 1836 to 1838 was suppressed with Russian help.
bukey-horde.e: After [[e:jangir-khan|Jangir Khan]] died in 1845, [[e:russia|Russia]] did not appoint a successor and placed the horde under a provisional council and Russian administration. Its lands are now in western [[s:kazakhstan|Kazakhstan]].

british-raj.t: Direct British Crown rule over the Indian subcontinent from 1858 to 1947, ending with independence and partition.
british-raj.o: After the rebellion of 1857, the [[e:government-of-india-act-1858|Government of India Act of 1858]] transferred the territories of [[s:company-rule-in-india|Company rule in India]] to the British Crown. A [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] governed from [[e:kolkata|Calcutta]], and [[e:queen-victoria|Queen Victoria]] was proclaimed Empress of [[e:india|India]] in 1877. The capital moved to [[e:new-delhi|New Delhi]], announced in 1911 and inaugurated in 1931.
british-raj.r: [[e:british-india|British India]] comprised directly ruled provinces and more than five hundred [[e:princely-state|princely states]]. The Raj built railways, canals and an [[e:indian-civil-service|Indian Civil Service]], but famines in 1876 to 1878 and 1943 killed millions. The [[e:indian-national-congress|Indian National Congress]], founded in 1885, and later the [[e:all-india-muslim-league|Muslim League]] pressed for self-rule; [[e:mahatma-gandhi|Gandhi's]] mass campaigns of non-cooperation, the [[e:salt-march|Salt March]] and [[e:quit-india-movement|Quit India]] challenged British authority.
british-raj.e: Weakened by the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] agreed to withdraw. The [[e:indian-independence-act-1947|Indian Independence Act]] of 1947 partitioned [[e:british-india|British India]] into the [[s:dominion-of-india|Dominion of India]] and the [[s:dominion-of-pakistan|Dominion of Pakistan]], amid mass migration and violence; [[s:myanmar|Burma]] had been separated in 1937.

cr.a: Edinburgh Geographical Institute; J. G. Bartholomew and Sons.

bailundo-kingdom.t: The largest Ovimbundu kingdom of the central Angolan highlands, whose caravans carried trade deep into the interior until its defeat in 1903.
bailundo-kingdom.o: Bailundo (Mbalundu) was founded by the 18th century, tradition says by the warrior Katyavala, on the [[e:benguela|Benguela]] highlands. It was one of several [[e:ovimbundu|Ovimbundu]] kingdoms, alongside the [[s:viye-kingdom|Viye Kingdom]] and the [[s:wambu-kingdom|Wambu Kingdom]], which formed as raiding states supplying captives to Benguela.
bailundo-kingdom.r: The king ruled from a fortified capital through titled officials and village chiefs. [[e:ovimbundu|Ovimbundu]] traders organised long-distance caravans reaching the [[e:lunda-empire|Lunda]] lands and the upper [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]], dealing in slaves, then [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], beeswax and, in the late 19th century, wild [[e:rubber|rubber]]. American missionaries settled in Bailundo from 1881 under King Ekuikui II.
bailundo-kingdom.e: Falling [[e:rubber|rubber]] prices, debt and Portuguese abuses provoked the Bailundo revolt of 1902 under King Mutu-ya-Kevela. Portuguese forces crushed it in 1902–03, ending the kingdom's independence within [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]].

british-virgin-islands.t: British island territory east of Puerto Rico, taken from the Dutch in 1672, once home to Quaker planters and now a major centre of offshore companies.
british-virgin-islands.o: [[e:dutch|Dutch]] buccaneers and settlers had a foothold on [[e:tortola|Tortola]] when English forces from the [[e:leeward-islands|Leeward Islands]] seized it in 1672. Over the following decades English settlers spread to [[e:virgin-gorda|Virgin Gorda]], [[e:jost-van-dyke|Jost Van Dyke]] and [[e:anegada|Anegada]], and the islands were formally attached to the Leeward Islands government.
british-virgin-islands.r: A small planter society grew [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and [[e:cotton|cotton]] with enslaved labour; an 18th-century [[e:quakers|Quaker]] community on [[e:tortola|Tortola]] and [[e:jost-van-dyke|Jost Van Dyke]] produced [[e:john-coakley-lettsom|John Coakley Lettsom]] and [[e:william-thornton|William Thornton]], architect of the [[e:united-states-capitol|United States Capitol]]. An elected assembly existed from 1773 but lapsed in 1902 as the economy declined after emancipation. Many islanders turned to fishing, smallholding and work in the neighbouring Danish and [[e:united-states-virgin-islands|American Virgin Islands]].
british-virgin-islands.e: After the [[e:leeward-islands|Leeward Islands]] federation ended, the BVI became a separate colony in 1960 and gained ministerial government in 1967. They did not seek independence. Tourism, yachting and, from 1984, the [[e:international-business-companies-act-british-virgin-islands|International Business Companies Act]] made them prosperous, and they remain a [[e:british-overseas-territories|British Overseas Territory]].

banate-of-jajce.t: Hungarian frontier province built around the Bosnian royal fortress of Jajce, which held back the Ottomans for more than sixty years after the fall of Bosnia.
banate-of-jajce.o: When [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] conquered the [[s:kingdom-of-bosnia|Kingdom of Bosnia]] in 1463, King [[e:matthias-corvinus|Matthias Corvinus]] of [[e:hungary|Hungary]] counter-attacked and retook the fortress town of [[e:jajce|Jajce]] after a siege in December 1463. In 1464 he organised the recovered strongholds of central and northern [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] as a banate, a military province under a ban, to shield [[e:croatia|Croatia]] and southern Hungary.
banate-of-jajce.r: The banate was essentially a chain of garrisoned castles along the [[e:vrbas|Vrbas]] and [[e:pliva|Pliva]] valleys, financed by the Hungarian crown and commanded by bans such as [[e:imre-szapolyai|Emeric Szapolyai]]. It survived an Ottoman siege led by [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] himself in 1464 and later attacks, relieved in 1525 by [[e:krsto-frankopan|Krsto Frankopan]]. Its Catholic population shrank as war emptied the countryside.
banate-of-jajce.e: After the Hungarian defeat at [[e:battle-of-mohacs|Mohács]] in 1526, the crown could no longer supply its Bosnian outposts, and [[e:jajce|Jajce]] surrendered to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1527. The town became part of the Ottoman sanjak of [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]], and the frontier moved north into [[e:croatia|Croatia]].

bashahr-state.t: The largest of the Simla Hill States, stretching up the Sutlej to the Tibetan border, whose Rajas grew rich on trade in wool and salt with Tibet.
bashahr-state.o: The ruling family claimed descent from Pradyumna, son of [[e:krishna|Krishna]], and has a long traditional pedigree; the register's date marks a traditional point in its history. The early capital was at Kamru in [[e:kinnaur|Kinnaur]], and later rulers moved between [[e:sarahan|Sarahan]] and [[s:rampur-state|Rampur]] on the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]].
bashahr-state.r: Bashahr controlled the upper [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]], including [[e:kinnaur|Kinnaur]], and its Rajas profited from trade with [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] through [[s:rampur-state|Rampur]], where the annual Lavi fair exchanged wool, horses and salt. The Bhimakali temple at [[e:sarahan|Sarahan]] was the family shrine. [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] occupied the state in the early 19th century before the British restored the Raja by sanad in 1815.
bashahr-state.e: Bashahr merged into [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948. Its last Raja, [[e:virbhadra-singh|Virbhadra Singh]], later served six terms as Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh. The area is now in [[e:shimla|Shimla]] and [[e:kinnaur|Kinnaur districts]].

berones.t: A Celtic people of the upper Ebro in La Rioja, whose towns Vareia, Tritium and Libia lay on the routes into the Meseta.
berones.o: The Berones lived in the upper [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] valley, in modern [[e:la-rioja-spain|La Rioja]], from about the 4th century BCE. [[e:strabo|Strabo]] described them as [[e:celts|Celts]], and their neighbours were the [[s:autrigones|Autrigones]], [[s:pellendones|Pellendones]] and [[s:vascones|Vascones]].
berones.r: Little is known of their government. Their towns included [[e:vareia|Vareia]] near [[e:logrono|Logroño]], [[e:tritium-magallum|Tritium]] and Libia, and they lived from farming the fertile [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] valley and herding. They reportedly served as [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] in conflicts of the 2nd century BCE.
berones.e: They came under Roman control in the 2nd century BCE during the Celtiberian wars. In 76 BCE [[e:quintus-sertorius|Sertorius]] captured [[e:vareia|Vareia]] during his war against [[e:rome|Rome]]. The Berones were absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]], and [[e:tritium-magallum|Tritium Magallum]] became a major Roman pottery centre.

bit-agusi.t: Bit Agusi, the Aramaean kingdom of Arpad, a leader of north Syrian resistance to Assyria, known from the Sefire treaties.
bit-agusi.o: [[e:gusi|Gusi]], an Aramaean chief, founded the kingdom in the early 9th century BCE in the plains north of [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]]. It took the name House of Gusi, and its capital became Arpad, at [[e:tell-rifaat|Tell Rifaat]].
bit-agusi.r: Its kings, such as [[e:attar-shumki-i|Attarshumki]] and [[e:matiilu|Mati'ilu]], led coalitions of Syrian states. [[e:mat-river|Mati]]'ilu signed a treaty with [[e:ashur-nirari-v|Ashur-nirari V]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] and another, preserved on the [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] [[e:sefire-steles|Sefire steles]], with Bar-Ga'yah of KTK, giving rare insight into Aramaean treaty language and curses.
bit-agusi.e: [[e:matiilu|Mati'ilu]] joined an alliance led by the [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Kingdom of Urartu]]. Tiglath-Pileser III besieged Arpad from 743 to 740 BCE, captured it and made Bit Agusi an Assyrian province.

bombay-presidency.t: The British province of western India governed from Bombay, which grew from a set of marshy islands into India's commercial capital.
bombay-presidency.o: Portugal ceded [[e:mumbai|Bombay]] to [[e:england|England]] in 1661 as part of [[e:catherine-of-braganza|Catherine of Braganza's]] dowry, and [[e:charles-ii-of-england|Charles II]] leased it to the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] in 1668. The Company's western presidency moved from [[e:surat|Surat]] to Bombay in 1687. The presidency expanded greatly after the defeat of the [[e:maratha-confederacy|Maratha Confederacy]] in 1818 and the conquest of [[e:sindh|Sindh]] in 1843.
bombay-presidency.r: A governor in council ruled from [[e:mumbai|Bombay]], under the Governor-General from 1773. Land reclamation joined the islands, and Bombay became a hub of the [[e:cotton|cotton]] trade, especially during the [[e:american-civil-war|American Civil War]], and of textile mills, shipping and banking dominated by [[e:parsis|Parsi]], Gujarati and [[e:baghdadi-jews|Baghdadi Jewish]] merchants. [[e:mountstuart-elphinstone|Mountstuart Elphinstone]] organised the [[e:deccan|Deccan]] conquests. [[e:sindh|Sindh]] was administered as part of the presidency until 1936.
bombay-presidency.e: [[e:mumbai|Bombay]] became a province of the [[s:british-raj|British Raj]], and the [[e:indian-national-congress|Indian National Congress]] was founded in the city in 1885. In 1947 Bombay Province joined the [[s:dominion-of-india|Dominion of India]]; in 1960 it was divided into [[e:maharashtra|Maharashtra]] and [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

bulungan-sultanate.t: Sultanate of north-eastern Borneo on the Kayan river, whose palace was destroyed by the Indonesian army in 1964.
bulungan-sultanate.o: Bulungan grew from a [[e:kayan-people-borneo|Kayan Dayak]] chiefdom on the Kayan river of north-east [[e:borneo|Borneo]]. Around 1731 its ruler Wira Amir converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] and took the title [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Amiril Mukminin, founding the sultanate at [[e:tanjung-palas|Tanjung Palas]]. Its early rulers were often under the influence of the [[s:sulu-sultanate|Sulu Sultanate]] and [[e:berau-sultanate|Berau]].
bulungan-sultanate.r: The sultans governed a mixed Kayan, [[e:tidung-people|Tidung]] and Malay population, exporting forest products, birds nests and rattan. [[e:dutch|Dutch]] contracts in the 19th century made Bulungan a self-governing domain of the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]], and the discovery of oil on Tarakan island early in the 20th century gave the region new importance.
bulungan-sultanate.e: Bulungan joined [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]] after independence. In 1964, during the Confrontation with [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]], the army accused the court of links with Malaysia, burned the palace and killed members of the royal family, ending the sultanate. The area now forms part of North Kalimantan province.

bengal-presidency.t: Britain's largest province in India, governed from Fort William at Calcutta, which was the capital of British India until 1911.
bengal-presidency.o: The [[e:east-india-company|English East India Company]] built [[e:fort-william-kolkata|Fort William]] at [[e:kolkata|Calcutta]] around 1700 and made it the seat of a presidency. After [[e:battle-of-plassey|Plassey]] in 1757 and the grant of the diwani of [[e:bengal|Bengal]], [[e:bihar|Bihar]] and [[e:odisha|Odisha]] in 1765, the Bengal Presidency became a territorial government; from 1773 its governor was also Governor-General over the other presidencies.
bengal-presidency.r: The presidency once stretched from [[e:assam|Assam]] to the [[e:punjab|Punjab]] and governed vast populations through district collectors. The Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixed land revenue with zamindars. [[e:kolkata|Calcutta]] became the commercial and intellectual capital of [[s:british-raj|British India]], the centre of the [[e:bengal|Bengal]] [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] associated with [[e:ram-mohan-roy|Ram Mohan Roy]] and [[e:rabindranath-tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]]. The famine of 1770 and that of 1943 killed millions.
bengal-presidency.e: [[e:george-curzon|Lord Curzon]] partitioned [[e:bengal|Bengal]] in 1905; protests forced reunion in 1911, when the capital moved to [[e:delhi|Delhi]]. In 1947 Bengal was partitioned again, [[e:west-bengal|West Bengal]] joining the [[s:dominion-of-india|Dominion of India]] and [[s:bangladesh|East Bengal]] the [[s:dominion-of-pakistan|Dominion of Pakistan]], later becoming Bangladesh.

british-west-africa.t: The administrative grouping that placed Britain's scattered West African posts under one governor at Freetown for much of the 19th century.
british-west-africa.o: In 1821, after the dissolution of the [[e:company-of-merchants-trading-to-africa|Company of Merchants]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] placed its forts on the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]] and its post on the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] under the governor of [[e:sierra-leone|Sierra Leone]], [[e:charles-maccarthy|Charles MacCarthy]], as the British West African Settlements. The arrangement was meant to save money and to coordinate the campaign against the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]].
british-west-africa.r: The grouping was never stable. The [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]] was returned to merchant rule in 1828. In 1843 the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] became a separate colony and the crown resumed control of the [[e:gold-coast|Gold Coast]] forts, which received their own governor in 1850. In 1866 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] revived the scheme as the [[e:west-africa|West Africa]] Settlements, with a governor-in-chief at [[e:freetown|Freetown]] over [[e:sierra-leone|Sierra Leone]], the Gambia, the Gold Coast and [[s:kingdom-of-lagos|Lagos]], each with an administrator. Distances, disease and poor communications made central control difficult.
british-west-africa.e: The [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]] and [[s:kingdom-of-lagos|Lagos]] were separated in 1874 as the [[e:gold-coast|Gold Coast]] Colony, and the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] regained its own governor in 1888, ending the arrangement. [[e:sierra-leone|Sierra Leone]] continued as the [[s:sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate|Sierra Leone Colony and Protectorate]].

banjar-sultanate.t: The Muslim sultanate of southern Borneo, a major pepper exporter, abolished by the Dutch in 1860 after the Banjarmasin War began.
banjar-sultanate.o: In 1526 [[e:sultan-suriansyah|Raden Samudra]], a prince of [[s:negara-daha|Negara Daha]], won a civil war with help from [[s:demak-sultanate|Demak]], accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] and took the name [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Suriansyah. He founded his capital at [[e:banjarmasin|Banjarmasin]] near the mouth of the [[e:barito-river|Barito River]]. The royal chronicle, the [[e:hikayat-banjar|Hikayat Banjar]], tells the story.
banjar-sultanate.r: Banjar grew rich on [[e:pepper|pepper]], exported to Chinese, English and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] traders in the 17th century, as well as gold and diamonds. After a Dutch attack in 1612 the court moved upriver to [[e:martapura|Martapura]]. Islamic scholarship flourished, notably under [[e:muhammad-arsyad-al-banjari|Muhammad Arsyad al-Banjari]] in the 18th century, and [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Adam issued a law code in 1835.
banjar-sultanate.e: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] gained increasing control through treaties. A succession dispute after [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Adam's death led to the [[e:banjarmasin-war|Banjarmasin War]] from 1859, led by [[e:pangeran-antasari|Pangeran Antasari]], and the Dutch abolished the sultanate in 1860, though resistance continued until 1905.

bamana-empire.t: A powerful Bambara kingdom ruled from Segou on the Niger, built by slave soldiers and destroyed by the jihad of Umar Tall in 1861.
bamana-empire.o: Around 1712 [[e:biton-coulibaly|Mamari Kulibali]], known as Biton, turned a young men's association of [[e:bambara-people|Bambara]] hunters and farmers into a standing army and made himself king at [[e:segou|Segou]]. He defeated rivals, raided the [[e:niger-river|Niger]] valley and created a kingdom that dominated the middle Niger from Djenne towards [[e:timbuktu|Timbuktu]].
bamana-empire.r: The army, the tonjon, was made up largely of war captives bound to the king, and in 1766 its commander [[e:ngolo-diarra|Ngolo Diarra]] seized the throne and founded a new dynasty. Under [[e:da-monzon-diarra|Da Monzon Diarra]] in the early 19th century [[e:segou|Segou]] reached its height. Most [[e:bambara-people|Bambara]] followed traditional religion, while Muslim [[e:marka|Marka]] and Somono traders and boatmen handled commerce. [[e:mungo-park|Mungo Park]] passed through Segou in 1796.
bamana-empire.e: [[e:segou|Segou]] fought the [[s:massina-empire|Massina Empire]] for decades but fell to [[e:el-hadj-umar-tall|Umar Tall]], who took the city in March 1861 and made it the capital of the [[s:toucouleur-empire|Toucouleur Empire]]. [[e:bambara-people|Bambara]] memory of [[e:biton-coulibaly|Biton]] and [[e:da-monzon-diarra|Da Monzon]] lives on in epic poetry.
bamana-empire.re: Bambara traditional religion, Sunni Islam among traders

banu-jami-emirate-of-gabes.t: A Hilalian Arab dynasty that ruled the port of Gabès in southern Tunisia during the breakup of Zirid Ifriqiya.
banu-jami-emirate-of-gabes.o: After the [[e:banu-hilal|Banu Hilal]] invasions of the 1050s shattered the [[s:zirid-emirate|Zirid emirate]], local lords took control of the cities of [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]]. Around 1097 the Banu [[e:jami|Jami]], a family of the Riyah, an Arab tribe of the Banu Hilal, established themselves as rulers of [[e:gabes|Gabès]] on the gulf of the same name.
banu-jami-emirate-of-gabes.r: Little is known in detail. The Banu [[e:jami|Jami]] ruled the town and its coastal oasis, with its date palms and irrigated gardens, relying on Arab tribal support. Around 1117 the emir [[e:rafi-ibn-makkan|Rafi ibn Makkan]] quarrelled with the [[e:zirid-dynasty|Zirids of Mahdia]] over his merchant ship and sought help from [[e:roger-ii-of-sicily|Roger II of Sicily]], an early step in Norman intervention in [[e:africa|Africa]].
banu-jami-emirate-of-gabes.e: [[e:gabes|Gabès]] came under Norman influence in the 1140s, and in 1160 the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] under [[e:abd-al-mumin|Abd al-Mu'min]] conquered it along with the rest of [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]], ending the Banu Jami dynasty.

british-cameroons.t: Two strips of former German Kamerun ruled by Britain from Nigeria, whose 1961 plebiscites split them between Nigeria and Cameroon.
british-cameroons.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] took a narrow western portion of [[s:kamerun|Kamerun]] in the division of 1916, confirmed as a [[e:league-of-nations-mandate|League of Nations mandate]] in 1922 and a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory after 1946. It consisted of two separate areas: the [[e:northern-cameroons|Northern Cameroons]], bordering [[e:bornu|Bornu]] and [[e:adamawa-emirate|Adamawa]], and the [[e:southern-cameroons|Southern Cameroons]], with [[e:buea|Buea]] as its centre.
british-cameroons.r: Both parts were administered as part of [[s:colonial-nigeria|Colonial Nigeria]], the north with the [[e:northern-region-nigeria|Northern Region]] and the south with the Eastern Region, an arrangement many southern Cameroonians resented. Former German plantations around [[e:mount-cameroon|Mount Cameroon]] became the [[e:cameroon|Cameroons]] Development Corporation. In 1954 the [[e:southern-cameroons|Southern Cameroons]] gained its own legislature, with [[e:emmanuel-endeley|Emmanuel Endeley]] and later [[e:john-ngu-foncha|John Ngu Foncha]] as premier.
british-cameroons.e: In UN plebiscites in February 1961 the [[e:northern-cameroons|Northern Cameroons]] voted to join [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]], and the [[e:southern-cameroons|Southern Cameroons]] voted to join [[e:cameroon|Cameroon]], which it did on 1 October 1961. The English-speaking legacy of the south remains a source of tension in Cameroon.

betsimisaraka-confederation.t: An east Malagasy confederation forged by Ratsimilaho, son of an English pirate, which controlled trade with the French islands.
betsimisaraka-confederation.o: Early 18th-century east [[e:madagascar|Madagascar]] was dominated by Tsikoa clans from the south and by the descendants of [[e:piracy|pirates]] who had settled at [[s:ile-sainte-marie|Ile Sainte-Marie]] and the coast. Around 1712 [[e:ratsimilaho|Ratsimilaho]], son of the English pirate [[e:thomas-white-pirate|Thomas White]] and a Malagasy princess, united the northern clans against the Tsikoa and was chosen king, ruling from [[e:fenoarivo-atsinanana|Fenoarivo]].
betsimisaraka-confederation.r: [[e:ratsimilaho|Ratsimilaho]] governed through alliances and assemblies of clan chiefs, and the mixed-descent [[e:zana-malata|Zana-malata]] formed an elite. The confederation supplied [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:cattle|cattle]] and slaves to French [[s:ile-bourbon|Ile Bourbon]] and [[s:isle-de-france|Isle de France]] through [[e:toamasina|Toamasina]] and [[e:foulpointe|Foulpointe]]. He married a [[e:sakalava|Sakalava]] princess of [[s:boina|Boina]] to secure alliances.
betsimisaraka-confederation.e: After [[e:ratsimilaho|Ratsimilaho's]] death in 1750 the confederation fragmented among rival chiefs, and French traders gained influence. In 1817 [[e:radama-i|Radama I]] of the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]] took [[e:toamasina|Toamasina]], bringing the east coast under Merina rule.

british-bechuanaland.t: The British Crown colony south of the Molopo River, created in 1885 to secure the road to the interior.
british-bechuanaland.o: After the [[e:warren-expedition|Warren Expedition]] dispersed the freebooter republics of [[s:stellaland|Stellaland]] and [[s:goshen|Goshen]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] proclaimed southern [[s:bechuanaland-protectorate|Bechuanaland]], between the [[e:molopo-river|Molopo River]] and the Cape border, a [[e:crown-colony|Crown colony]] on 30 September 1885, with [[e:vryburg|Vryburg]] as its capital.
british-bechuanaland.r: An administrator, Sir [[e:sidney-shippard|Sidney Shippard]], governed the colony, which included the lands of the [[s:batlhaping-chiefdom|Tlhaping]] and [[e:barolong|Barolong]]. Much land was allocated to white farmers, while reserves were set aside for [[e:tswana-people|Tswana]] chiefs such as [[e:montshiwa|Montshiwa]]. The colony secured the route along which the railway to [[e:mahikeng|Mafeking]] was later built.
british-bechuanaland.e: British [[s:bechuanaland-protectorate|Bechuanaland]] was annexed to the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]] in 1895 and later became part of [[s:republic-of-south-africa|South Africa]]. The territory north of the [[e:molopo-river|Molopo]] remained the Bechuanaland [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]], which became independent [[e:botswana|Botswana]].

cr.a: Original: Acts of Union 1800 Vector: Yaddah

boii.t: A powerful Celtic people of central Europe whose name survives in 'Bohemia', builders of large fortified towns before Dacian and Germanic pressure broke them.
boii.o: The [[s:boii-400|Boii]] were a Celtic people of the [[e:la-tene-culture|La Tène culture]] who appear in written sources from the 4th century BCE. One branch settled in the Po valley of northern [[e:italy|Italy]], where it fought [[e:rome|Rome]] until defeated in 191 BCE; another held [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] and spread along the [[e:danube|Danube]] into what is now [[e:austria|Austria]], [[e:slovakia|Slovakia]] and western [[e:hungary|Hungary]].
boii.r: Like other late Celtic peoples, the [[s:boii-400|Boii]] lived in a world of chieftains, warrior elites and druids. They built oppida, large fortified towns such as [[e:zavist|Závist]] near [[e:prague|Prague]] and the settlement at [[e:bratislava|Bratislava]], where they minted [[e:silver|silver]] coins, some bearing the name [[e:biatec|Biatec]]. [[e:iron-technology|Ironworking]], glass bracelets and long-distance trade with the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] world marked their prosperity in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.
boii.e: Around 60 BCE the [[s:boii-400|Boii]] were crushed by the Dacian king [[e:burebista|Burebista]], and part of the people joined the [[s:helvetii|Helvetii]] in their failed migration of 58 BCE. Germanic [[s:marcomanni|Marcomanni]] later occupied [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]], but the [[e:latin|Latin]] name [[e:boiohaemum|Boiohaemum]], 'home of the Boii', lives on as [[e:bohemia|Bohemia]], and possibly in [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]].

buria-state.t: A Sikh chiefship on the upper Yamuna, one of the small Cis-Sutlej holdings formed after the fall of Mughal Sirhind.
buria-state.o: Buria arose around 1760, when [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] [[e:sardar|sardars]] seized lands between the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] and the [[e:yamuna|Yamuna]] as Mughal and [[e:durrani-empire|Durrani]] authority collapsed in the region.
buria-state.r: Like the other [[e:cis-sutlej-states|Cis-Sutlej]] chiefs, the family of Buria accepted British protection in 1809. Its holding was small, and under British rule it lost most of its sovereign powers, surviving as a privileged estate. Little else about its administration is recorded.
buria-state.e: After independence Buria's lands were absorbed into [[e:east-punjab|East Punjab]]; the town of Buria is now in [[e:yamunanagar-district|Yamunanagar district]] of [[e:haryana|Haryana]].

british-occupation-of-manila.t: Brief British rule of Manila during the Seven Years War, which exposed the weakness of Spanish power in the Philippines.
british-occupation-of-manila.o: After [[e:spain|Spain]] entered the [[e:seven-years-war|Seven Years War]], a British expedition from [[e:chennai|Madras]] under [[e:william-draper|William Draper]] and [[e:samuel-cornish|Samuel Cornish]] attacked [[e:manila|Manila]] in September 1762. The city fell on 6 October, and the acting governor, Archbishop [[e:manuel-rojo-del-rio-y-vieyra|Manuel Rojo]], agreed a capitulation and a large ransom that was never fully paid.
british-occupation-of-manila.r: British control barely extended beyond [[e:manila|Manila]] and Cavite. [[e:dawsonne-drake|Dawsonne Drake]] of the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] governed as deputy, while [[e:simon-de-anda-y-salazar|Simón de Anda y Salazar]] organised Spanish resistance from [[e:bacolor|Bacolor]] in [[e:pampanga|Pampanga]]. The occupation encouraged uprisings, notably that of [[e:diego-silang|Diego Silang]] in [[e:ilocos|Ilocos]], who sought British support and was assassinated in 1763.
british-occupation-of-manila.e: The [[e:treaty-of-paris-1763|Treaty of Paris]] of 1763 returned [[e:manila|Manila]] to [[e:spain|Spain]], and the British left in April 1764. The episode prompted Spanish reforms and fortification, and revolts it had encouraged foreshadowed later Filipino resistance to Spanish rule.

bogd-khanate-of-mongolia.t: The Buddhist monarchy under the Bogd Khan that declared Mongolia's independence from the Qing in 1911, the forerunner of the modern Mongolian state.
bogd-khanate-of-mongolia.o: As the [[e:xinhai-revolution|Xinhai Revolution]] broke Qing authority, [[e:khalkha-mongols|Khalkha]] nobles and lamas, with Russian encouragement, declared independence in December 1911 and enthroned the [[e:bogd-khan|Eighth Jebtsundamba Khutughtu]], the leading lama of [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]], as Bogd Khan in [[e:ulaanbaatar|Niislel Khüree]] (Urga). The new state hoped to unite all [[e:mongols|Mongols]], including those of [[e:inner-mongolia|Inner Mongolia]].
bogd-khanate-of-mongolia.r: It was a theocratic monarchy with ministries headed by nobles and lamas, among them the prime minister [[e:togs-ochiryn-namnansuren|Sain Noyon Khan Namnansüren]]. Monasteries held great wealth and a large share of the male population. The [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] supported it, but the [[e:treaty-of-kyakhta-1915|Kyakhta treaty]] of 1915 reduced it to autonomy under Chinese suzerainty. In 1919 the Chinese general [[e:xu-shuzheng|Xu Shuzheng]] abolished the autonomy.
bogd-khanate-of-mongolia.e: In 1921 the White Russian [[e:roman-von-ungern-sternberg|Baron Ungern-Sternberg]] expelled the Chinese and restored the [[e:bogd-khan|Bogd Khan]], before the [[e:mongolian-peoples-party|Mongolian People's Party]] and the [[e:red-army|Red Army]] took [[e:ulaanbaatar|Urga]] that July. The Bogd Khan reigned as a limited monarch until his death in 1924, when the [[s:mongolian-peoples-republic|Mongolian People's Republic]] was proclaimed.

bali-nyonga.t: A Chamba warrior kingdom in the Cameroon Grassfields that became Germany's key ally in the region in the 1890s.
bali-nyonga.o: Bali-Nyonga descends from the [[s:chamba-state|Chamba]], mounted raiders who left the upper [[e:benue-river|Benue]] region in the early 19th century, perhaps fleeing the [[e:fulani-war|Fulani jihad]], and swept into the western [[e:cameroon-grassfields|Grassfields]]. After the death of their leader the raiders split, and one group, named after its leader Nyonga, settled near what is now [[e:bamenda|Bamenda]] in the 1830s or later.
bali-nyonga.r: The [[s:chamba-state|Chamba]] conquerors adopted many [[e:cameroon-grassfields|Grassfields]] institutions, including palace societies and the title [[e:fon-title|Fon]], while dominating local peoples by force. Under Fon Galega I, who ruled from about 1856 to 1901, [[e:bali|Bali]] became the strongest power in the area. In 1889 Galega allied with the German explorer [[e:eugen-zintgraff|Eugen Zintgraff]], and Bali forces fought with the Germans against Mankon in 1891.
bali-nyonga.e: The alliance brought [[e:bali|Bali]] into [[s:kamerun|Kamerun]] as a favoured German ally, supplied with guns and authority over its neighbours. After 1916 it passed to the [[s:british-cameroons|British Cameroons]], and the [[e:fon-title|Fon]] of Bali-Nyonga still reigns.

bosnia-and-herzegovina-austro-hungarian.t: Former Ottoman province occupied and then annexed by Austria-Hungary, whose rule modernised Sarajevo and ended with the shots that started the First World War.
bosnia-and-herzegovina-austro-hungarian.o: After uprisings in [[e:herzegovina|Herzegovina]] and [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] from 1875 and the [[e:russo-turkish-war-1877-1878|Russo-Turkish War]], the [[e:congress-of-berlin|Congress of Berlin]] in 1878 gave [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] a mandate to occupy and administer Bosnia and Herzegovina, which remained nominally Ottoman. Austro-Hungarian troops crushed fierce Muslim and [[e:serbs|Serb]] resistance in the summer of 1878.
bosnia-and-herzegovina-austro-hungarian.r: As neither [[e:austria|Austria]] nor [[e:hungary|Hungary]] would let the other have it, the province was run jointly through the common finance ministry, notably by [[e:benjamin-kallay|Benjamin Kállay]] from 1882 to 1903, who promoted a shared Bosnian identity. Railways, mines, forestry and schools developed, and [[e:sarajevo|Sarajevo]] gained European-style buildings such as the City Hall. The Ottoman landholding system with its Christian serfs was largely kept.
bosnia-and-herzegovina-austro-hungarian.e: [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] annexed the territory in 1908, provoking the Bosnian Crisis, and granted a diet in 1910. On 28 June 1914 [[e:gavrilo-princip|Gavrilo Princip]] assassinated Archduke [[e:archduke-franz-ferdinand-of-austria|Franz Ferdinand]] in [[e:sarajevo|Sarajevo]]. In 1918 [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] joined the [[s:state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs|State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs]] and then the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]].
bosnia-and-herzegovina-austro-hungarian.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

beri-state.t: A small chiefship of the Bundelkhand Agency, known mainly from British lists of the minor states of central India.
beri-state.o: Beri took shape as a separate holding in the mid-18th century as the [[e:bundela|Bundela]] kingdoms broke up, and its chief was confirmed by a British sanad in the early 19th century.
beri-state.r: Few details of its internal history are recorded. It was a non-salute state covering a handful of villages in [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]].
beri-state.e: After independence Beri was merged with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]], and its lands were absorbed into the Indian administration by 1950.

bundi-state.t: The Hada Chauhan Rajput kingdom of Hadoti in south-eastern Rajasthan, known for the Taragarh fort, its step-wells and the Bundi school of painting.
bundi-state.o: In 1342 [[e:rao-deva|Rao Deva]], of the [[e:hada-chauhans|Hada]] branch of the [[e:chauhan|Chauhans]], took the Bundi area from local [[e:meena-people|Meena]] chiefs and made it his capital. The surrounding region became known as [[e:hadoti|Hadoti]] after his clan.
bundi-state.r: Bundi's Raos often fought [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]] and later served the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]]: [[e:rao-surjan|Rao Surjan]] surrendered [[e:ranthambore-fort|Ranthambore]] to [[e:akbar|Akbar]] in 1569, and [[e:rao-chhatrasal-of-bundi|Rao Chhatrasal]] was killed at [[e:battle-of-samugarh|Samugarh]] in 1658 fighting for [[e:dara-shikoh|Dara Shikoh]]. The neighbouring [[s:kotah-state|Kotah State]] split off in 1631. The court sponsored a distinctive school of [[e:persian-miniature|miniature painting]], and Bundi is known for its step-[[e:well|wells]] and the [[e:taragarh-fort-bundi|Taragarh]] fort.
bundi-state.e: Bundi suffered [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] raids and signed a treaty with the British in 1818. It joined the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in 1948 and is now a district of [[e:rajasthan|Rajasthan]].

bhadarva-state.t: A minor Rajput chiefship of the Rewa Kantha country in central Gujarat, near the Mahi river.
bhadarva-state.o: Bhadarva was one of the small estates of the [[e:rewa-kantha-agency|Rewa Kantha]] region, held by a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family from around 1600. Its founding is not well documented.
bhadarva-state.r: The ruler held a few villages and paid tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]]. In the British period it was grouped in the [[e:rewa-kantha-agency|Rewa Kantha Agency]]. Little else is recorded in standard references.
bhadarva-state.e: Bhadarva was merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in present [[e:vadodara|Vadodara]] district.

bemba-kingdom.t: The kingdom of the Chitimukulu on the plateau of north-eastern Zambia, which grew powerful through warfare and the 19th-century ivory and slave trade.
bemba-kingdom.o: Bemba tradition traces the royal Crocodile clan to [[e:luba-empire|Luba]] lands in the [[e:congo-basin|Congo basin]], from which its founders migrated east and settled on the [[e:lubemba|Lubemba]] plateau. The paramount title Chitimukulu was established by the early 18th century, with related chiefs governing surrounding territories.
bemba-kingdom.r: The Chitimukulu was a sacred ruler, with royal relics and the advice of hereditary priest-councillors (bakabilo), while senior chiefs such as the [[e:mwamba-bemba-title|Mwamba]] held great power. Farming used the chitemene system of burning cut branches to fertilise poor soils. In the 19th century, under [[e:chileshe-chepela|Chileshe Chepela]] and [[e:chitapankwa|Chitapankwa]], the Bemba expanded by raiding and traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and captives with Swahili-Arab merchants.
bemba-kingdom.e: Succession disputes after the deaths of [[e:chitimukulu-sampa|Chitimukulu Sampa]] in 1896 and [[e:mwamba-bemba-title|Mwamba]] in 1898 allowed the [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company]] to take control by 1899. The Chitimukulu remains the Bemba paramount chief in [[e:zambia|Zambia]].

british-occupation-of-havana.t: Eleven months of British rule over Havana during the Seven Years' War, which opened Cuba to trade and spurred sweeping Spanish reforms.
british-occupation-of-havana.o: After [[e:spain|Spain]] entered the [[e:seven-years-war|Seven Years' War]], a British expedition under [[e:george-keppel-3rd-earl-of-albemarle|George Keppel]], Earl of Albemarle, and Admiral Sir [[e:george-pocock|George Pocock]] landed near [[e:havana|Havana]] in June 1762. After a siege in which the defender [[e:luis-vicente-de-velasco|Luis Vicente de Velasco]] died at the [[e:morro-castle-havana|Morro Castle]], the city surrendered on 13 August 1762, with much of the Spanish fleet.
british-occupation-of-havana.r: [[e:george-keppel-3rd-earl-of-albemarle|Albemarle]] governed [[e:havana|Havana]] and its surroundings as military governor, levying heavy contributions on the city. British merchants poured in, trade with the British colonies opened, and several thousand enslaved Africans were imported, a sign of the later growth of Cuban [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]]. Catholic institutions continued, though friction with the [[e:bishop|bishop]] led to his expulsion. Disease killed many British soldiers.
british-occupation-of-havana.e: Under the [[e:treaty-of-paris-1763|Treaty of Paris]] in 1763 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] returned [[e:havana|Havana]] to [[e:spain|Spain]] in exchange for [[e:florida|Florida]]. Shocked by the loss, Spain fortified the city with [[e:la-cabana|La Cabaña]] fortress, reorganised its colonial militias and began liberalising Cuban trade as part of the [[e:bourbon-reforms|Bourbon reforms]].

british-central-africa-protectorate.t: The British protectorate around Lake Malawi, established through wars against slave-trading chiefs and later renamed Nyasaland.
british-central-africa-protectorate.o: Scottish missions at [[e:blantyre|Blantyre]] and [[e:livingstonia|Livingstonia]] and the [[e:african-lakes-company|African Lakes Company]] drew [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] into the [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]] region. To block Portuguese claims, [[e:britain|Britain]] declared the [[e:shire-highlands|Shire Highlands]] a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1889 and in 1891 proclaimed the British [[e:central-africa|Central Africa]] Protectorate, under Commissioner [[e:harry-johnston|Harry Johnston]] with his headquarters at [[e:zomba|Zomba]].
british-central-africa-protectorate.r: [[e:harry-johnston|Johnston]] and his successor [[e:alfred-sharpe|Alfred Sharpe]] used [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] and African troops to defeat Yao slave-trading chiefs such as [[s:makanjira-chiefdom|Makanjira]], the [[s:jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota|Jumbe State of Nkhotakota]] and the [[s:maseko-ngoni-kingdom|Maseko Ngoni Kingdom]]. European planters grew [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] in the [[e:shire-highlands|Shire Highlands]], relying on labour [[e:tenancy|tenancy]] known as thangata, and a hut tax pushed men into wage work.
british-central-africa-protectorate.e: In 1907 the territory was renamed the [[s:nyasaland|Nyasaland Protectorate]], with a governor and legislative council. Its borders became those of modern [[e:malawi|Malawi]], and its planter economy and migrant labour persisted into the colonial period.

byelorussian-ssr.t: Soviet Belarus, devastated in the Second World War and a founding member of the United Nations, which became the independent Republic of Belarus in 1991.
byelorussian-ssr.o: After the [[e:red-army|Red Army]] retook [[e:minsk|Minsk]] from [[e:poland|Poland]] in 1920, the [[e:byelorussian-ssr|Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic]] was proclaimed again on 31 July 1920, replacing the [[s:lithuanian-byelorussian-ssr|Lithuanian-Byelorussian SSR]]. The [[e:peace-of-riga|Peace of Riga]] in 1921 divided Belarusian lands between it and the [[s:second-polish-republic|Second Polish Republic]], and in 1922 it became a founding member of the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]].
byelorussian-ssr.r: The 1920s brought Belarusian-language schools and culture, followed by collectivisation and [[e:joseph-stalin|Stalin]]'s purges, whose victims lie at [[e:kurapaty|Kurapaty]] near [[e:minsk|Minsk]]. The republic absorbed western [[e:belarus|Belarus]] in 1939. German occupation from 1941 to 1944 killed perhaps a quarter of the population and destroyed hundreds of villages, among them [[e:khatyn-massacre|Khatyn]]. It gained a seat in the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] in 1945 and was industrialised under leaders such as [[e:pyotr-masherov|Pyotr Masherov]].
byelorussian-ssr.e: Heavily affected by fallout from [[e:chernobyl-disaster|Chernobyl]] in 1986, the republic declared [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] in 1990 and independence on 25 August 1991. Renamed the Republic of [[e:belarus|Belarus]], it signed the [[e:belovezha-accords|Belovezha Accords]] dissolving the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] in December 1991.

bulala-sultanate.t: A Muslim dynasty of the Lake Fitri region that drove the Sayfawa kings out of Kanem in the 14th century and survived as the Sultanate of Fitri.
bulala-sultanate.o: The [[e:bulala|Bulala]] were a people around [[e:lake-fitri|Lake Fitri]] in central [[e:chad|Chad]] whose ruling house was related to the [[e:sayfawa-dynasty|Sayfawa dynasty]] of the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]]. In the second half of the 14th century they waged repeated wars on [[e:kingdom-of-kanem|Kanem]], killing several Sayfawa kings and forcing the dynasty to abandon its capital [[e:njimi|Njimi]] and move west of [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]] to [[e:bornu|Bornu]].
bulala-sultanate.r: For over a century the [[e:bulala|Bulala]] ruled [[e:kingdom-of-kanem|Kanem]] from bases near [[e:lake-fitri|Lake Fitri]], controlling trade routes between the [[e:nile|Nile]] and the [[e:chad|Chad]] basin. Their state was a Muslim sultanate supported by [[e:cattle|cattle]]-keeping and agricultural subjects. Few internal details survive; most information comes from [[e:bornu|Bornu]] chronicles hostile to them.
bulala-sultanate.e: [[e:bornu|Bornu's]] [[e:idris-katakarmabi|Idris Katakarmabi]] defeated the [[e:bulala|Bulala]] in the early 16th century and reoccupied [[e:njimi|Njimi]], and [[e:idris-alooma|Idris Alooma]] later pushed them back further. The Bulala retreated to Fitri, later paying tribute to the [[s:wadai-empire|Wadai Empire]]. The Sultanate of Fitri at Yao came under French rule around 1900 and survives as a traditional authority in [[e:chad|Chad]].

barony-of-arcadia.t: Barony in the south-western Peloponnese around the castle of Arcadia (Kyparissia), the last refuge of the last prince of Achaea.
barony-of-arcadia.o: [[e:arcadia|Arcadia]], the medieval name of [[e:kyparissia|Kyparissia]], was one of the domains held by the Villehardouin family after the conquest of the [[e:peloponnese|Morea]], together with [[e:kalamata|Kalamata]], and was organised as a barony of the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] in the early 13th century.
barony-of-arcadia.r: The barony centred on the coastal castle above [[e:kyparissia|Kyparissia]] and its fertile surroundings, and was held by a succession of Frankish families, among them the Le Maure. In the late 14th century it passed to the Genoese [[e:zaccaria|Zaccaria family]] through [[e:andronikos-asen-zaccaria|Andronikos Asen Zaccaria]], whose son [[e:centurione-ii-zaccaria|Centurione II Zaccaria]] became Prince of [[e:achaea|Achaea]] in 1404.
barony-of-arcadia.e: As the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] of the [[s:despotate-of-the-morea|Despotate of the Morea]] conquered the rest of the principality, [[e:centurione-ii-zaccaria|Centurione II]] retreated to [[e:arcadia|Arcadia]]. After his death in 1432 [[e:thomas-palaiologos|Thomas Palaiologos]] took it over, ending [[e:latin|Latin]] rule in the region.

cr.a: Eric Gaba (Sting - fr:Sting); derivative work by Constantine

bishopric-of-samland.t: Prince-bishopric of the Sambian peninsula and Königsberg, whose bishop was the first in Europe to hand his lands to a Protestant duke.
bishopric-of-samland.o: Founded in 1243 as one of [[e:william-of-modena|William of Modena's]] four Prussian dioceses, [[e:sambia-peninsula|Samland]] took shape after the conquest of the [[s:sambians|Sambians]] in 1255. The [[e:bishop|bishop]] received a third of the diocese, with residence at [[e:primorsk-kaliningrad-oblast|Fischhausen]] and a cathedral on the [[e:kneiphof|Kneiphof]] island in [[e:konigsberg|Königsberg]].
bishopric-of-samland.r: Like [[s:pomesanians|Pomesania]], its cathedral chapter was incorporated into the [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]], and the [[e:bishop|bishops]] worked closely with the grand masters. The bishopric's lands included rich amber-gathering coasts, though the amber monopoly belonged to the Order.
bishopric-of-samland.e: [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:georg-von-polentz|Georg von Polentz]] adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1523 and in 1525 transferred his secular rule to [[e:albert-duke-of-prussia|Duke Albert]] when the Order's state became [[s:duchy-of-prussia|Ducal Prussia]], the first Protestant state. [[e:sambia-peninsula|Samland]] became part of the duchy, and its lands later lay in [[e:east-prussia|East Prussia]].

british-cyprus.t: Cyprus under British rule from 1878 to 1960, a strategic base whose Greek Cypriot campaign for union with Greece led to independence.
british-cyprus.o: By the [[e:cyprus-convention|Cyprus Convention]] of 1878, the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] allowed [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] to occupy and administer [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]], while keeping formal [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], in return for British support against [[e:russia|Russia]]. [[e:garnet-wolseley|Sir Garnet Wolseley]] became the first high commissioner. [[e:britain|Britain]] annexed the island when the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] entered the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] in 1914 and made it a crown colony in 1925.
british-cyprus.r: A British governor ruled with a partly elected legislative council, abolished after the 1931 riots, when Government House was burned. The population, about four-fifths Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] and one-fifth Turkish Muslim, was divided by the Greek demand for enosis, union with [[e:greece|Greece]]. Agriculture, mining and later British military bases shaped the economy.
british-cyprus.e: From 1955 the [[e:eoka|EOKA]] [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] movement under [[e:george-grivas|George Grivas]], backed by [[e:makarios-iii|Archbishop Makarios]] III, fought British rule. The Zurich and [[e:london|London]] agreements of 1959 created the Republic of [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]], which became independent in August 1960, with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] keeping two sovereign base areas.

benares-state.t: The kingdom of the Maharajas of Benares at Ramnagar fort, famous for its Ramlila and for Chait Singh's revolt against Warren Hastings.
benares-state.o: [[s:mansa-state|Mansa]] Ram, a [[e:bhumihar|Bhumihar]] landholder, obtained the zamindari of [[e:varanasi|Benares]] around 1737 under the Nawab of [[e:awadh|Awadh]]. His son [[e:balwant-singh-of-benares|Balwant Singh]] built a semi-independent principality and the fort of [[e:ramnagar-varanasi|Ramnagar]] across the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] from Varanasi. In 1775 the Nawab ceded [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] over the area to the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]].
benares-state.r: [[e:chait-singh|Chait Singh's]] resistance to [[e:warren-hastings|Warren Hastings's]] heavy demands led to his rising and flight in 1781, a key charge in Hastings's later impeachment. The family kept large estates as zamindars, and in 1911 part of these lands, [[e:ramnagar-varanasi|Ramnagar]] and [[e:bhadohi|Bhadohi]], was made a princely state. The [[e:maharaja|Maharajas]] were patrons of [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] learning, and the month-long [[e:ramnagar-ramlila|Ramnagar Ramlila]] they sponsor remains famous.
benares-state.e: [[e:vibhuti-narayan-singh|Vibhuti Narayan Singh]] acceded to [[e:india|India]] and [[e:varanasi|Benares]] State was merged into [[e:uttar-pradesh|Uttar Pradesh]] in 1949. The family still hosts the [[e:ramlila|Ramlila]] and keeps a museum at [[e:ramnagar-varanasi|Ramnagar]] fort.

bilaspur-state.t: The Chandela Rajput hill state of Kahlur on the Sutlej, a rival of Guru Gobind Singh and briefly a separate state of the Indian Union before joining Himachal Pradesh.
bilaspur-state.o: Tradition dates Kahlur to 697, when Bir Chand, a Chandela [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] from central [[e:india|India]], carved out a domain on the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] in the lower [[e:himalayas|Himalaya]]. The town of [[e:bilaspur-himachal-pradesh|Bilaspur]], which gave the state its later name, was founded as the capital in the mid-17th century.
bilaspur-state.r: Kahlur was one of the leading [[e:shimla|Shimla]] hill states, ruled by Rajas who held land through local [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] and [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] families. Raja [[e:bhim-chand-of-kahlur|Bhim Chand]] fought [[e:guru-gobind-singh|Guru Gobind Singh]] in the 1680s and 1690s, and the state was later overrun by the [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]]. After the [[e:anglo-nepalese-war|Anglo-Nepalese War]] of 1814–1816 the British restored the Raja under a sanad.
bilaspur-state.e: Raja Anand Chand kept [[e:bilaspur-himachal-pradesh|Bilaspur]] apart after 1947, and it was run as a separate centrally administered state until it joined [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in 1954. The old town of Bilaspur was submerged in the 1960s by the [[e:gobind-sagar|Gobind Sagar]] reservoir of the [[e:bhakra-dam|Bhakra Dam]], and a new town was built above it.

banu-kanz-emirate.t: An Arab-Nubian dynasty of Aswan that guarded Egypt's southern frontier and eventually claimed the throne of Makuria.
banu-kanz-emirate.o: The [[e:banu-kanz|Banu Kanz]] descended from [[e:arabs|Arabs]] of the [[e:rabia|Rabi'a]] tribe who settled in the Aswan region and the gold mines of the [[e:eastern-desert|Eastern Desert]] in the 9th century and intermarried with [[e:nubians|Nubians]] and Beja. In 1006 the Fatimid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Hakim gave their leader [[e:abu-al-makarim-hibat-allah|Abu al-Makarim Hibat Allah]] the title Kanz al-Dawla for capturing the rebel [[e:abu-rakwa|Abu Rakwa]].
banu-kanz-emirate.r: The Kanz al-Dawla chiefs ruled the southern marches around Aswan as hereditary [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimid Caliphate]], controlling trade with [[e:nubia|Nubia]] and the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] and the gold of the [[e:wadi-allaqi|Wadi Allaqi]]. In 1174 they rebelled against [[e:saladin|Saladin]] and were crushed. Moving southwards, they grew close to the Makurian royal family, and in 1317 to 1323 a Kanzi prince, Kanz al-Dawla, ruled [[s:makuria|Makuria]].
banu-kanz-emirate.e: The [[e:banu-kanz|Banu Kanz]] helped spread [[e:islam|Islam]] and Arabic among the [[e:nubians|Nubians]] but clashed repeatedly with the [[s:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Sultanate]], which broke their power around 1412. Their name survives in the Kenzi Nubians of the Aswan region.

barony-of-karytaina.t: Frankish barony in the mountains of central Peloponnese, guarded by the castle of Karytaina and celebrated through its lord Geoffrey of Bruyeres in the Chronicle of the Morea.
barony-of-karytaina.o: The barony of [[e:karytaina|Karytaina]], also called [[e:skorta|Skorta]] after its mountainous district, was created around 1209 in the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] and granted to [[e:hugh-of-bruyeres|Hugh of Bruyeres]]. With 22 knight's fiefs it was one of the largest baronies, set to control the unruly highlands of the upper [[e:alpheios|Alpheios]] valley.
barony-of-karytaina.r: Hugh's son [[e:geoffrey-of-bruyeres|Geoffrey of Bruyeres]] built the castle of [[e:karytaina|Karytaina]] on a crag above the [[e:alpheios|Alpheios]] around 1254. He was the model knight of the [[e:chronicle-of-the-morea|Chronicle of the Morea]], admired for his courage despite rebelling against Prince [[e:william-ii-of-villehardouin|William II]] and eloping with a [[e:vassal|vassal]]'s wife. Greek villagers and local archons held land under the barons.
barony-of-karytaina.e: After Geoffrey died in 1275 without a male heir, half the barony reverted to the prince and its fortunes declined. In 1320 [[e:andronikos-asen|Andronikos Asen]], the Byzantine governor of [[e:mystras|Mistras]], took [[e:karytaina|Karytaina]] and much of [[e:skorta|Skorta]], ending Frankish rule there.

cr.a: Eric Gaba (Sting - fr:Sting); derivative work by Constantine

basotho-kingdom.t: The mountain kingdom Moshoeshoe built from refugees of the 1820s wars, the forerunner of modern Lesotho.
basotho-kingdom.o: [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]], a junior [[s:bakwena-chiefdom|Kwena]] chief, gathered followers at [[e:butha-buthe|Butha-Buthe]] in the early 1820s and in 1824 moved them to the flat-topped mountain of [[e:thaba-bosiu|Thaba Bosiu]], which proved impregnable. As the wars of the [[e:mfecane|Lifaqane]] scattered communities across the highveld, he welcomed refugees from many groups, lending them [[e:cattle|cattle]] and building a kingdom from them.
basotho-kingdom.r: [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]] ruled through his sons and allied chiefs, with public assemblies, pitso, to debate policy. He used diplomacy as much as war, invited missionaries of the [[e:paris|Paris]] Evangelical Missionary Society to [[e:morija|Morija]] in 1833 and acquired guns and horses. Grain farming in the fertile [[e:caledon-river|Caledon]] valley fed his people, and he defeated [[e:sekonyela|Sekonyela]] of the [[s:batlokwa-chiefdom|Batlokwa Chiefdom]] in 1853.
basotho-kingdom.e: Wars with the [[s:orange-free-state|Orange Free State]] in 1858 and 1865-1866 cost the [[e:sotho-people|Basotho]] much of their lowland farmland. To save the rest, [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]] sought British protection, and the kingdom was annexed as [[s:basutoland|Basutoland]] in 1868, two years before his death.

bishopric-of-semigallia.t: Short-lived missionary bishopric for the unconquered Semigallians, created in 1218 and merged into the see of Riga in 1251.
bishopric-of-semigallia.o: In 1218 [[e:albert-of-riga|Bishop Albert of Riga]] obtained permission to create a new diocese for [[s:semigallians|Semigallia]], still largely pagan. Bernhard zur Lippe, a [[e:saxons|Saxon]] nobleman turned Cistercian abbot, became its first [[e:bishop|bishop]]. As the [[e:semigallians|Semigallians]] resisted, the bishops based themselves at [[e:selpils|Selburg]] (Sēlpils) in the land of the [[s:selonians|Selonians]].
bishopric-of-semigallia.r: The bishopric existed mainly on paper, since most of [[s:semigallians|Semigallia]] remained independent. Its [[e:bishop|bishops]] controlled a few districts along the [[e:western-dvina|Daugava]], depending on support from Riga and the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]]. A papal legate, [[e:baldwin-of-alna|Baldwin of Alna]], briefly tried to reorganise the see in the 1230s.
bishopric-of-semigallia.e: In 1251 [[e:pope-innocent-iv|Pope Innocent IV]] united the diocese with Riga, which shortly afterwards became the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]]. [[s:semigallians|Semigallia]] itself was conquered only in 1290, and its land was divided between the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]] and the archbishop.

brazilian-military-dictatorship.t: The 21-year military regime that ruled Brazil from 1964, combining rapid economic growth with censorship, torture and repression.
brazilian-military-dictatorship.o: The coup of 1964 against [[e:joao-goulart|João Goulart]] ended the [[s:fourth-brazilian-republic|Fourth Brazilian Republic]]. Marshal [[e:humberto-castelo-branco|Humberto Castelo Branco]] became the first of five generals who ruled as president. [[e:institutional-acts|Institutional Acts]] gave the regime extraordinary powers, abolished the old parties and created two official ones, ARENA and the [[e:brazilian-democratic-movement|MDB]].
brazilian-military-dictatorship.r: In 1968 [[e:institutional-act-number-five|Institutional Act Number Five]] closed Congress, suspended habeas corpus and imposed censorship. Under General [[e:emilio-garrastazu-medici|Emílio Garrastazu Médici]], the regime used torture and killings against opponents and [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrillas]], while the 'economic miracle' brought growth of around ten per cent a year. Large projects such as the [[e:itaipu-dam|Itaipú]] dam and the [[e:trans-amazonian-highway|Trans-Amazonian Highway]] were launched. [[e:ernesto-geisel|Ernesto Geisel]] began a slow opening in 1974, and [[e:joao-figueiredo|João Figueiredo]] granted an amnesty in 1979.
brazilian-military-dictatorship.e: The [[e:diretas-ja|Diretas Já]] campaign of 1984 demanded direct elections. In January 1985 an electoral college chose the civilian [[e:tancredo-neves|Tancredo Neves]], ending military rule and beginning the [[s:new-republic-brazil|New Republic (Brazil)]]. A [[e:national-truth-commission-brazil|National Truth Commission]] reported on the regime's crimes in 2014.

bavand-dynasty.t: One of the longest-lived Iranian dynasties, ruling parts of Tabaristan on the Caspian for almost seven centuries from the Arab conquest to the Mongol age.
bavand-dynasty.o: Tradition traces the Bavandids to Bav, a descendant of the Sasanian prince [[e:kawus-son-of-kavad-i|Kawus]], who established himself in the mountains of [[e:tabaristan|Tabaristan]] after the fall of the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] around 651. The family survived the Abbasid conquest of the lowlands in 760 by holding the highland region of Firim.
bavand-dynasty.r: The dynasty ruled in three main branches: the Kayusiyya (to 1074), the Ispahbadiyya (1074 to 1210), centred on [[e:sari-iran|Sari]] and [[e:amol|Amol]], and the Kinkhwariyya (1238 to 1349). Its rulers kept the ancient title ispahbad and long remained Zoroastrian, converting to [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 9th century and later favouring Shia Islam. Sharvin I fought the [[e:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasids]] alongside the [[s:qarinvand-dynasty|Qarinvand dynasty]]. They were [[e:vassal|vassals]] in turn of the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyid dynasty]], the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] and the [[s:khwarazmian-empire|Khwarazmian Empire]], while patronising Persian letters.
bavand-dynasty.e: In 1349 the last ruler, [[e:fakhr-al-dawla-hasan|Fakhr al-Dawla Hasan]], was murdered by [[e:kiya-afrasiyab|Afrasiyab Chelavi]], founder of the [[s:afrasiyabids-of-mazandaran|Afrasiyabids of Mazandaran]], ending the line.

batavian-republic.t: The Dutch revolutionary republic set up with French help in 1795, which created the first unitary Dutch state and a modern constitution.
batavian-republic.o: In January 1795 French armies crossed the frozen rivers into the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]], and stadtholder William V fled to [[e:england|England]]. [[e:dutch|Dutch]] Patriots, exiled since 1787, proclaimed the Batavian Republic, named after the ancient [[s:batavi|Batavians]]. The [[e:treaty-of-the-hague-1795|Treaty of The Hague]] bound it to [[e:france|France]] and imposed a heavy indemnity.
batavian-republic.r: After fierce debate a constitution of 1798 replaced the old federation with a unitary state, separated church and state and gave [[e:jews|Jews]] equal rights. Coups followed in 1798 and 1801. The fleet was destroyed at [[e:battle-of-camperdown|Camperdown]] in 1797, colonies were lost to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], and trade suffered. In 1805 [[e:rutger-jan-schimmelpenninck|Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck]] became [[e:grand-pensionary|Grand Pensionary]] with wide powers.
batavian-republic.e: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], wanting firmer control, turned the republic into the [[s:kingdom-of-holland|Kingdom of Holland]] in 1806 under his brother [[e:louis-bonaparte|Louis Bonaparte]]. Its administrative reforms, national taxes and codified law survived into the later [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Kingdom of the Netherlands]].

bituriges-cubi.t: Powerful Gallic people of Berry whose capital Avaricum, modern Bourges, was stormed by Caesar in one of the bloodiest sieges of the Gallic War.
bituriges-cubi.o: The Bituriges, whose name means 'kings of the world', occupied the middle [[e:loire|Loire]] and [[e:cher-river|Cher]] basins around [[e:avaricum|Avaricum]] ([[e:bourges|Bourges]]). [[e:livy|Livy]] tells a legend that in the 6th century BCE their king [[e:ambigatus|Ambigatus]] held supremacy over the [[e:celts|Celts]] and sent his nephews [[e:bellovesus|Bellovesus]] and [[e:segovesus|Segovesus]] to lead migrations into [[e:italy|Italy]] and the [[e:hercynian-forest|Hercynian Forest]]. A related branch, the [[s:bituriges-vivisci|Bituriges Vivisci]], later settled at [[e:bordeaux|Bordeaux]].
bituriges-cubi.r: Their land was rich in iron ore, and the Bituriges were renowned smiths and metalworkers. [[e:avaricum|Avaricum]], defended by a massive [[e:timber|timber]]-laced murus gallicus rampart, was one of the largest and wealthiest oppida in [[e:gaul|Gaul]].
bituriges-cubi.e: In 52 BCE they joined [[e:vercingetorix|Vercingetorix]] and burned some twenty of their own towns to starve the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]], but spared [[e:avaricum|Avaricum]], which [[e:julius-caesar|Caesar]] took after a hard siege, killing most of its inhabitants. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their territory became a civitas of [[e:gallia-aquitania|Aquitania]], the origin of the province of [[e:berry-province|Berry]].

cr.a: The Department of History, United States Military Academy

british-kaffraria.t: A British territory carved from Xhosa land on the Eastern Cape frontier, scene of the Xhosa cattle-killing of 1856-1857.
british-kaffraria.o: After the War of the Axe of 1846-1847, Governor [[e:sir-harry-smith-1st-baronet|Sir Harry Smith]] annexed the land between the [[e:keiskamma-river|Keiskamma]] and Kei rivers in December 1847, reviving the abandoned [[s:province-of-queen-adelaide|Province of Queen Adelaide]]. Governed from [[e:king-williams-town|King William's Town]], it was a separate dependency under the Cape governor rather than part of the colony.
british-kaffraria.r: British magistrates gradually took power from [[e:xhosa-people|Xhosa]] chiefs, and a further war in 1850-1853 tightened control. In 1856-1857 a prophecy by the girl [[e:nongqawuse|Nongqawuse]] led many Xhosa to kill their [[e:cattle|cattle]] and destroy their grain; tens of thousands died of hunger. Governor [[e:george-grey|Sir George Grey]] used the catastrophe to push survivors into wage labour and to settle German military veterans and immigrants on confiscated land.
british-kaffraria.e: British Kaffraria became a [[e:crown-colony|Crown colony]] in 1860 but could not pay its way, and it was annexed to the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]] in 1866. Towns such as East [[e:london|London]], [[e:stutterheim|Stutterheim]] and [[e:berlin|Berlin]] preserve the marks of its settlement schemes.

cr.a: I created the map, based partly on the source map: Eastern frontier of the Colony of the Cape of Good Hope from Algoa Bay to the …

bidar-sultanate.t: The Barid Shahi sultanate, heir to the Bahmani capital of Bidar, whose ministers ruled the last Bahmani sultans as puppets.
bidar-sultanate.o: [[e:qasim-barid|Qasim Barid]], a Turkic noble, became chief minister of the declining [[s:bahmani-sultanate|Bahmani Sultanate]] in the 1490s and controlled its last sultans from [[e:bidar|Bidar]]. His son [[e:amir-barid-i|Amir Barid]] continued this role, and after the last Bahmani ruler fled around 1527 the family ruled openly; [[e:ali-barid-shah-i|Ali Barid Shah]] took the royal title in the 1540s.
bidar-sultanate.r: The [[e:barid-shahi-dynasty|Barid Shahi]] state was small, centred on [[e:bidar|Bidar]] and its fort, and depended on the balance between the larger [[e:deccan-sultanates|Deccan sultanates]]. The Barid Shahs patronised architecture, including the tomb of [[e:ali-barid-shah-i|Ali Barid]] and the [[e:rangin-mahal|Rangin Mahal]] with its inlaid mother-of-pearl decoration. Bidar was also known for bidriware, a craft of [[e:silver|silver]] inlay on blackened metal.
bidar-sultanate.e: The [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]] annexed [[e:bidar|Bidar]] in 1619, ending the dynasty. The city later fell to the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] in 1656. Its tombs and the bidriware craft are its chief legacy.

british-solomon-islands-protectorate.t: A British protectorate in the Solomon Islands for 85 years, scene of the Guadalcanal campaign and of the Maasina Rule movement, now the Solomon Islands.
british-solomon-islands-protectorate.o: To control the labour recruitment trade to [[s:colony-of-queensland|Queensland]] and [[e:fiji|Fiji]], and in competition with [[s:german-new-guinea|German New Guinea]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] declared a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the southern [[e:solomon|Solomons]] in 1893. It was extended in 1898 and 1899, and in 1900 [[e:germany|Germany]] transferred [[e:santa-isabel-island|Santa Isabel]], [[e:choiseul-island|Choiseul]] and other northern islands to [[e:britain|Britain]]. [[e:charles-woodford|Charles Woodford]] became the first Resident Commissioner at [[e:tulagi|Tulagi]] in 1896.
british-solomon-islands-protectorate.r: The administration was tiny and relied on head taxes and on plantation companies such as [[e:levers-pacific-plantations|Lever's Pacific Plantations]] to develop copra. Christian missions spread widely. Resistance continued, notably on [[e:malaita|Malaita]], where [[e:kwaio|Kwaio]] warriors killed the district officer [[e:william-r-bell|William Bell]] in 1927. [[e:japan|Japan]] invaded in 1942, and the [[e:guadalcanal-campaign|Guadalcanal campaign]] of 1942 and 1943 turned the war in the Pacific. After the war the [[e:maasina-rule|Maasina Rule]] movement on Malaita challenged British authority.
british-solomon-islands-protectorate.e: The capital moved to [[e:honiara|Honiara]], built on the wartime American base. A legislative council and self-government followed, and the islands became independent as [[e:solomon|Solomon]] Islands on 7 July 1978, with [[e:peter-kenilorea|Peter Kenilorea]] as prime minister.

basohli-state.t: A small Rajput hill state on the Ravi whose court gave its name to the bold, brightly coloured Basohli school of Pahari painting.
basohli-state.o: Basohli was ruled by a Balauria branch of [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]]; tradition places the state's foundation in 765, but little is known before the 17th century. Raja Bhupat Pal is credited with founding the town of Basohli on the [[e:ravi|Ravi]] as his capital in the 1630s.
basohli-state.r: Under Raja Kirpal Pal, in the late 17th century, the court patronised painters who developed the Basohli style: strong reds, yellows and greens, flat backgrounds and jewel-like beetle-wing details, used for series such as the [[e:rasamanjari|Rasamanjari]]. The style spread to neighbouring courts. Politically, Basohli was a minor state between [[s:chamba-state|Chamba]] and [[e:jammu|Jammu]].
basohli-state.e: In the early 19th century Basohli fell under the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] and was granted to the [[e:dogras|Dogra]] rulers of [[e:jammu|Jammu]], who absorbed it in 1836. It later became part of [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir (princely state)]]. The town is now in [[e:kathua|Kathua]] district.

bituriges-vivisci.t: Offshoot of the Bituriges settled on the Gironde estuary, whose trading port of Burdigala grew into Bordeaux.
bituriges-vivisci.o: [[e:strabo|Strabo]] notes that the Bituriges Vivisci were the only Celtic people living among the [[e:aquitani|Aquitani]], which suggests they migrated from the [[s:bituriges-cubi|Bituriges Cubi]] of [[e:berry-province|Berry]] to the lower [[e:garonne|Garonne]], perhaps in the 3rd or 2nd century BCE. Their emporium [[e:bordeaux|Burdigala]] stood on a bend of the Garonne.
bituriges-vivisci.r: [[e:bordeaux|Burdigala]] was a trading port linking the Atlantic with the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] by the [[e:garonne|Garonne]] and [[e:aude-river|Aude]] route, handling [[e:tin|tin]], metals and Italian wine. Caesar does not name them, perhaps because they did not resist him.
