banten-sultanate.t: The pepper sultanate of western Java, a leading Asian port of the 17th century until the Dutch East India Company reduced it to a vassal.
banten-sultanate.o: Around 1527 forces from [[s:demak-sultanate|Demak]] and [[e:cirebon|Cirebon]], led by [[e:sunan-gunung-jati|Sunan Gunung Jati]] and his son [[e:maulana-hasanuddin|Maulana Hasanuddin]], took the port of [[e:banten|Banten]] from the [[s:sunda-kingdom|Sunda Kingdom]]. Hasanuddin became its first ruler. In 1579 his son [[e:maulana-yusuf|Maulana Yusuf]] captured [[e:pakuan-pajajaran|Pakuan Pajajaran]], ending the Sunda Kingdom.
banten-sultanate.r: [[e:banten|Banten]] became one of [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia's]] great [[e:pepper|pepper]] markets, drawing Chinese, Indian, English and Danish merchants; the first [[e:dutch|Dutch]] fleet arrived in 1596, and the English opened a factory in 1602. [[e:sultan-ageng-tirtayasa|Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa]], from 1651, built canals and a navy and challenged [[e:batavia|Dutch Batavia]]. The Surosowan palace and Great Mosque date from the 16th century.
banten-sultanate.e: In 1682 [[e:sultan-ageng-tirtayasa|Ageng]]'s son, [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Haji, sought [[e:dutch|Dutch]] help against his father, and the Company won control of [[e:banten|Banten's]] trade. [[e:herman-willem-daendels|Herman Willem Daendels]] destroyed the palace in 1808, and [[e:stamford-raffles|Thomas Stamford Raffles]] abolished the sultanate in 1813.

byzantium.t: Megarian colony on the Bosporus that controlled the passage to the Black Sea and later became Constantinople.
byzantium.o: Settlers from [[s:megara|Megara]], led according to tradition by [[e:byzas|Byzas]], founded [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantium]] c. 667 BCE on the European promontory between the [[e:golden-horn|Golden Horn]] and the [[e:sea-of-marmara|Sea of Marmara]]. The site commanded the [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporus]], the only sea route between the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] and the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]].
byzantium.r: [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantium]] grew rich from tuna fishing and tolls on shipping, especially the grain trade. It came under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]], was taken by the Spartan regent [[e:pausanias-general|Pausanias]] in 478 BCE and then joined the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]], revolting in 440 BCE. Its resistance to [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]]'s siege of 340 to 339 BCE was celebrated. In 220 BCE [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] went to war over its new tolls.
byzantium.e: [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantium]] allied with [[e:rome|Rome]] in the 2nd century BCE and kept its freedom until Vespasian brought it into a Roman province c. 73 CE. Constantine refounded it as [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in 330 CE, capital of the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]].

banat-of-craiova.t: Habsburg-ruled Oltenia, the western third of Wallachia, held by Austria for two decades after the Treaty of Passarowitz.
banat-of-craiova.o: In the [[e:austro-turkish-war-1716-1718|Austro-Turkish war of 1716 to 1718]] [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] forces occupied [[e:oltenia|Oltenia]], the part of [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]] west of the [[e:olt-river|Olt]] river. The [[e:treaty-of-passarowitz|Treaty of Passarowitz]] in 1718 ceded it to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburg]] monarchy, which organised it as a province with its seat at [[e:craiova|Craiova]], the traditional residence of the Wallachian bans.
banat-of-craiova.r: The province was governed by an imperial administration with a local boyar, [[e:gheorghe-cantacuzino|Gheorghe Cantacuzino]], as ban at first. [[e:vienna|Vienna]] introduced a [[e:census|census]], regular taxes, a postal service and stricter control over boyars and monasteries, reforms that curbed noble privileges but raised burdens; many peasants fled across the [[e:olt-river|Olt]]. [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] religion and Romanian-speaking society remained unchanged.
banat-of-craiova.e: [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] defeat in the war of 1737 to 1739 led to the [[e:treaty-of-belgrade|Treaty of Belgrade]] in 1739, which returned [[e:oltenia|Oltenia]] to [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]] under Ottoman suzerainty. The episode left detailed Austrian maps and surveys of the region.

baghat-state.t: A small Rajput hill state of the Shimla hills whose capital at Solan grew into one of the main towns of Himachal Pradesh.
baghat-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins. Its name is often explained as 'many passes'.
baghat-state.r: Baghat was a small hill state on the road from [[e:kalka|Kalka]] to [[e:shimla|Shimla]]. It was occupied by [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. With the coming of the [[e:kalka-shimla-railway|Kalka-Shimla]] road and railway, Solan became its capital and grew as a market town.
baghat-state.e: Baghat merged into [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948, and Solan is now the headquarters of Solan district.

bozhou-chiefdom.t: The hereditary domain of the Yang family in northern Guizhou, which ruled for seven centuries as a native chieftaincy under Chinese dynasties until its destruction in 1600.
bozhou-chiefdom.o: According to family tradition, [[e:yang-duan|Yang Duan]], a man from [[e:taiyuan|Taiyuan]], recovered Bozhou, around modern [[e:zunyi|Zunyi]], from [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] forces in 876 and was granted hereditary authority over it. His descendants ruled the mountainous region as local lords, accepting nominal titles from successive Chinese courts.
bozhou-chiefdom.r: The Yang lords governed a mixed population of Han settlers and [[e:miao-people|Miao]], [[e:gelao-people|Gelao]] and other peoples as tusi, native chieftains who paid tribute and supplied troops while running their own affairs. The [[e:song-dynasty|Song]], Yuan and [[e:ming-empire|Ming]] dynasties confirmed their titles. During the Mongol wars the [[s:southern-song|Southern Song]] built the mountain fortress of [[e:hailongtun|Hailongtun]] in 1257, later the seat of the Yang family.
bozhou-chiefdom.e: [[e:yang-yinglong|Yang Yinglong]] rebelled against the [[s:ming-empire|Ming Empire]] in 1589. In 1600 a large [[e:ming-empire|Ming]] army under [[e:li-hualong|Li Hualong]] stormed [[e:hailongtun|Hailongtun]] and Yang Yinglong killed himself. The chieftaincy was abolished and replaced by regular prefectures under direct imperial rule.

bedulu-kingdom.t: The Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Bali under the Warmadewa line, ruling from Bedulu and Pejeng until Majapahit's conquest in 1343.
bedulu-kingdom.o: The [[e:belanjong-pillar|Belanjong pillar]] of 914 at [[e:sanur|Sanur]] records [[e:sri-kesari-warmadewa|Sri Kesari Warmadewa]], the first known Balinese king, campaigning on the island. His [[e:warmadewa-dynasty|Warmadewa dynasty]] ruled from the Pejeng and [[e:bedulu|Bedulu]] area, the fertile heart of [[e:bali|Bali]] near modern [[e:ubud|Ubud]], for over three centuries.
bedulu-kingdom.r: Royal charters in Old Balinese, later [[e:old-javanese|Old Javanese]], show irrigation communities, ancestors of the subak system, and temples endowed with land. King [[e:udayana-warmadewa|Udayana]] married the Javanese princess [[e:mahendradatta|Mahendradatta]], and their son [[e:airlangga|Airlangga]] later ruled [[s:kahuripan|Kahuripan]] in [[e:java|Java]]. The rock-cut sanctuaries of [[e:goa-gajah|Goa Gajah]] and [[e:gunung-kawi|Gunung Kawi]], the latter linked to King [[e:anak-wungsu|Anak Wungsu]], date from this period.
bedulu-kingdom.e: In 1343 [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]] troops under [[e:gajah-mada|Gajah Mada]], joined according to Balinese tradition by Arya Damar, defeated the last king, remembered as Sri Astasura Ratna Bumi [[e:banten|Banten]]. Majapahit installed a Javanese dynasty that ruled from Samprangan and then the [[s:kingdom-of-gelgel|Kingdom of Gelgel]], shaping later Balinese court culture.

bishopric-of-culm.t: One of the four Prussian dioceses set up in 1243, ruling the land of Löbau and passing under the Polish crown in 1466.
bishopric-of-culm.o: In 1243 the papal legate [[e:william-of-modena|William of Modena]] divided conquered [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] into four dioceses: [[e:chelmno|Culm]], [[s:pomesanians|Pomesania]], [[s:prince-bishopric-of-warmia|Warmia]] and Samland. Culm covered the [[e:chelmno-land|Chełmno land]], which [[e:konrad-i-of-masovia|Konrad of Masovia]] had granted to the [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]], and the [[e:bishop|bishop]] received a third of the diocese as his own territory, chiefly around [[e:lubawa|Löbau]].
bishopric-of-culm.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]]' cathedral stood at [[e:chelmza|Culmsee]] (Chełmża), while they resided at the castle of [[e:lubawa|Löbau]]. The cathedral chapter was incorporated into the [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]] in the 13th century, tying the bishopric closely to the Order's state. [[e:chelmno-law|Chełmno law]], granted in the [[e:chelmno|Culm]] charter of 1233, became the model for town and land rights across [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]].
bishopric-of-culm.e: During the Thirteen Years' War, the Prussian estates rebelled against the Order, and the [[e:second-peace-of-thorn|Second Peace of Thorn]] in 1466 placed the [[e:chelmno-land|Chełmno land]] under the [[e:kingdom-of-poland|Polish crown]] as part of [[s:royal-prussia|Royal Prussia]]. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] became Polish senators, and the diocese continued as a church province.

bructeri.t: A Germanic people of Westphalia who fought Rome alongside Arminius and sheltered the seeress Veleda during the Batavian revolt.
bructeri.o: The Bructeri lived between the upper Ems and the [[e:lippe-river|Lippe]], in what is now [[e:westphalia|Westphalia]]. They appear in Roman sources from 12 BCE, when [[e:nero-claudius-drusus|Drusus]] fought them on the Ems. In 9 CE they joined [[e:arminius|Arminius]] against [[e:publius-quinctilius-varus|Varus]] and captured the eagle of the Nineteenth [[e:legion|Legion]], which [[e:germanicus|Germanicus]]' general [[e:lucius-stertinius|Stertinius]] recovered in 15.
bructeri.r: Their leadership was in the hands of chiefs and an influential religious figure: the seeress [[e:veleda|Veleda]], who lived in a tower near the [[e:lippe-river|Lippe]], foretold the success of the Batavian revolt of 69 and was consulted by other peoples. Around 98, [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] reports that neighbouring tribes had nearly wiped out the Bructeri while [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] watched.
bructeri.e: The Bructeri survived that defeat and are mentioned again in the 4th century as part of the [[s:franks|Franks]]. Their district, the Boructuari, was among the peoples evangelised by Saint [[e:suitbert|Suitbert]] around 700, before the [[s:saxons|Saxons]] overran it.

brunei-sultanate.t: A Malay sultanate of northern Borneo which in the 16th century ruled coasts from Sarawak to Manila and survives as the independent state of Brunei.
brunei-sultanate.o: Chinese records mention a kingdom called Po-ni in northwest [[e:borneo|Borneo]] from the 10th century. Brunei tradition holds that its ruler [[e:muhammad-shah-of-brunei|Awang Alak Betatar]] accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] and became [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Muhammad Shah, the register dating this to 1368. The early capital was [[e:kota-batu|Kota Batu]] on the Brunei River.
brunei-sultanate.r: Under [[e:bolkiah|Sultan Bolkiah]] around 1500 Brunei reached its height, controlling much of [[e:borneo|Borneo's]] coast and allied ports in the [[s:philippines|Philippines]], including [[s:kingdom-of-maynila|Maynila]]. Its wealth came from trade in [[e:camphor|camphor]], [[e:pepper|pepper]] and Chinese goods, and its water village impressed [[e:antonio-pigafetta|Antonio Pigafetta]] in 1521. [[e:spain|Spain]] attacked in the Castilian War of 1578.
brunei-sultanate.e: In the 19th century Brunei lost [[s:raj-of-sarawak|Sarawak]] to [[e:james-brooke|James Brooke]] and [[e:sabah|Sabah]] to the [[e:british-north-borneo-company|British North Borneo Company]]. It became a British [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1888, oil was found at [[e:seria|Seria]] in 1929, and it declined to join [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]] in 1963. Brunei became fully independent in 1984 under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:hassanal-bolkiah|Hassanal Bolkiah]].

bigerriones.t: Aquitanian people of the high Pyrenean valleys around Tarbes, who gave their name to Bigorre.
bigerriones.o: The Bigerriones lived in the upper [[e:adour|Adour]] valley and the Pyrenean foothills of the modern [[e:hautes-pyrenees|Hautes-Pyrénées]]. Caesar lists them among the Aquitanian peoples who surrendered to [[e:publius-licinius-crassus|Publius Crassus]] in 56 BCE.
bigerriones.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Like other [[e:aquitani|Aquitani]] they spoke a language related to Basque, and their economy combined mountain herding with farming in the valleys.
bigerriones.e: Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their chief town was [[e:tarbes|Turba]], later Tarbes, within the province of [[e:gallia-aquitania|Aquitania]] and then [[e:novempopulania|Novempopulana]]. Their name passed to the medieval [[s:county-of-bigorre|County of Bigorre]].

banganapalle-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state in the Rayalaseema country of Andhra, best known for the mango variety that bears its name.
banganapalle-state.o: Banganapalle was granted in the 1660s by the [[e:bijapur|Bijapur]] sultanate, then under Mughal pressure, to a Muslim officer whose descendants became its Nawabs. After a period of disputed succession the line of the Nawabs was confirmed under British protection.
banganapalle-state.r: The Nawabs ruled a small enclave surrounded by the [[s:madras-presidency|Madras Presidency]], with a mostly [[e:telugu-language|Telugu]]-speaking [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] population. It was one of the few [[e:princely-state|princely states]] attached to the [[e:chennai|Madras]] government. The region's orchards produced the Banganapalle mango, now one of [[e:india|India's]] best-known varieties.
banganapalle-state.e: The last Nawab acceded to [[e:india|India]], and Banganapalle merged into [[s:madras-presidency|Madras Province]] in 1948. It became part of [[e:andhra-state|Andhra State]] in 1953 and now lies in [[e:andhra-pradesh|Andhra Pradesh]].

buayan-sultanate.t: An upriver Maguindanao sultanate on the Pulangi River of Mindanao, long the rival of the coastal Maguindanao Sultanate.
buayan-sultanate.o: Buayan was the upstream, sa raya, state of the Pulangi river basin in central [[e:mindanao|Mindanao]], while [[s:maguindanao-sultanate|Maguindanao]] held the coast, sa ilud. Both traced their [[e:islam|Islam]] to [[e:sharif-kabungsuan|Sharif Kabungsuan]], a Johor-born preacher of the early 16th century. Buayan's rulers controlled the [[e:rice|rice]]-growing interior and its links with highland peoples.
buayan-sultanate.r: Buayan's datus governed through kinship networks and controlled trade in [[e:rice|rice]], slaves and forest goods passing down the river. In the 19th century, as [[s:maguindanao-sultanate|Maguindanao]] weakened under Spanish pressure, [[e:datu-uto|Datu Uto]] of Buayan became the strongest leader in the Pulangi valley and acquired firearms through traders.
buayan-sultanate.e: Spanish expeditions in the 1880s forced [[e:datu-uto|Datu Uto]] to submit, though he kept much of his power. After 1899 the Americans took over [[e:mindanao|Mindanao]], and by 1905 Buayan's independence was ended. The area is now part of the [[e:bangsamoro|Bangsamoro]] region.

british-somaliland.t: A British protectorate on the Gulf of Aden coast of Somalia, which fought a 20-year war with the Dervishes and became independent as Somaliland in 1960.
british-somaliland.o: [[e:britain|Britain's]] interest in the northern [[e:somalis|Somali]] coast came from [[e:aden|Aden]], which depended on Somali livestock. Between 1884 and 1886 British officers signed treaties with the [[s:isaaq-sultanate|Isaaq]], [[e:gadabuursi|Gadabuursi]], [[s:warsangali-sultanate|Warsangali]] and other clans, and after [[e:egypt|Egypt]] withdrew from [[e:zeila|Zeila]] and [[e:berbera|Berbera]] the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] was established, run at first from [[s:british-raj|British India]].
british-somaliland.r: British rule was thin and cheap, aimed at keeping the coast secure and the meat trade flowing. From 1899 the [[s:dervish-state|Dervish State]] of [[e:mohammed-abdullah-hassan|Mohammed Abdullah Hassan]] fought a long war against the British, ended in 1920 by a campaign that used aircraft. Pastoral clans kept their customary institutions under appointed elders and Islamic courts. [[e:italy|Italy]] occupied the territory briefly in 1940 to 1941.
british-somaliland.e: On 26 June 1960 British [[s:state-of-somaliland|Somaliland]] became independent as the State of [[e:italian-somaliland|Somaliland]], which five days later united with the former [[s:trust-territory-of-somaliland|Trust Territory of Somaliland]] to form the [[s:somali-republic|Somali Republic]]. Its borders were revived by the [[s:republic-of-somaliland|Republic of Somaliland]] in 1991.

baku-commune.t: A Bolshevik-led government that ruled Baku for a few months in 1918 and whose leaders became Soviet martyrs as the 26 Baku Commissars.
baku-commune.o: In March 1918 the [[e:baku|Baku]] Soviet, dominated by [[e:communist-party-of-the-soviet-union|Bolsheviks]] and supported by [[e:armenian-revolutionary-federation|Armenian Dashnak]] forces, defeated Azerbaijani [[e:musavat|Musavat]] units in fighting known as the March Days, in which thousands of Muslims were killed. In April it formed the Baku [[e:council-of-peoples-commissars|Council of People's Commissars]] under [[e:stepan-shaumian|Stepan Shaumian]], part of the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]].
baku-commune.r: The Commune nationalised the oil industry and the Caspian fleet and tried to supply [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]] with oil. Its forces were mostly Armenian, and it was opposed by the Azerbaijani population. It faced an advance on [[e:baku|Baku]] by the Ottoman-led [[e:caucasus-army-of-islam|Army of Islam]], which defeated its troops in June and July 1918.
baku-commune.e: On 31 July 1918 the Commune resigned after the [[e:baku|Baku]] Soviet voted to invite British help, and the [[s:centrocaspian-dictatorship|Centrocaspian Dictatorship]] took over. Its leaders fled, were captured and shot near [[e:turkmenbasy|Krasnovodsk]] in September 1918, becoming the [[e:26-baku-commissars|26 Baku Commissars]] of Soviet legend.

cr.a: Неизвестный художник (не указан в выходных данных плаката; отсутствует авторская монограмма или подпись)

begteginid-dynasty.t: A Turkmen dynasty of atabegs at Erbil whose ruler Gökböri, Saladin's brother-in-law, made the city famous for celebrating the Prophet's birthday.
begteginid-dynasty.o: [[e:zayn-al-din-ali-kuchuk|Zayn al-Din Ali Kuchuk]], son of Begtegin, was a [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] officer of [[e:imad-al-din-zengi|Imad al-Din Zengi]] who became governor of [[e:erbil|Erbil]] and other towns around 1144. Under the [[s:zengid-dynasty-of-mosul|Zengid dynasty of Mosul]] he built up a personal domain in the plains east of the [[e:tigris|Tigris]], which his descendants inherited.
begteginid-dynasty.r: His son [[e:muzaffar-al-din-gokbori|Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri]] married [[e:rabia-khatun|Rabi'a Khatun]], sister of [[e:saladin|Saladin]], fought at the [[e:battle-of-hattin|Battle of Hattin]] in 1187 and received [[e:erbil|Erbil]] as an Ayyubid ally in 1190. He ruled until 1233, building hospitals, hostels for travellers, schools and orphanages, and staging lavish public celebrations of the [[e:mawlid|Mawlid]], the Prophet's birthday, among the earliest recorded. The biographer [[e:ibn-khallikan|Ibn Khallikan]], a native of Erbil, praised his generosity.
begteginid-dynasty.e: [[e:muzaffar-al-din-gokbori|Gökböri]] died without a male heir in 1233 and bequeathed [[e:erbil|Erbil]] to the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] [[e:al-mustansir-i|al-Mustansir]], who annexed it. The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] took the city in 1258.

basoda-state.t: A small Pathan Nawabi state in Malwa, a branch of the family that ruled Kurwai.
basoda-state.o: Basoda was founded around 1753 by a member of the Afghan family of [[s:kurwai-state|Kurwai]], one of several Pathan chiefships established in the area during the decline of Mughal power.
basoda-state.r: The Nawab ruled a small farming territory around the town of Basoda in the [[e:bhopal-agency|Bhopal Agency]]. Few details of its internal history are recorded.
basoda-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Basoda was merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and joined [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 1956; its lands are in [[e:vidisha|Vidisha]] district.

bolognese-republic.t: The brief republic set up in Bologna in 1796 after the French expelled papal rule, which soon merged into the Cispadane Republic.
bolognese-republic.o: In June 1796 French troops entered [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]], part of the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]], and the papal legate left. The city's Senate, under French protection, took over the government, and [[e:bologna|Bologna]] declared itself a free republic.
bolognese-republic.r: [[e:bologna|Bologna's]] old ruling families kept much of their influence, governing through the Senate and new committees while meeting French demands for money and art. The republic drafted a constitution in late 1796. It sent delegates to the congresses that united [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]] with [[e:ferrara|Ferrara]], [[e:modena|Modena]] and [[e:reggio-emilia|Reggio]].
bolognese-republic.e: By the end of 1796 [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]] had joined the [[s:cispadane-republic|Cispadane Republic]], which in 1797 became part of the [[s:cisalpine-republic|Cisalpine Republic]].

bar-kokhba-state.t: The short-lived Jewish state of Simon bar Kosiba, whose revolt against Hadrian was the last great Jewish rising against Rome.
bar-kokhba-state.o: The revolt broke out in 132, probably provoked by Hadrian's plan to refound [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]] as the Roman colony [[e:aelia-capitolina|Aelia Capitolina]], and possibly by a ban on circumcision. Its leader, [[e:simon-bar-kokhba|Simon bar Kosiba]], was hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', a messianic title reportedly endorsed by [[e:rabbi-akiva|Rabbi Akiva]].
bar-kokhba-state.r: [[e:simon-bar-kokhba|Simon]] styled himself [[e:nasi-title|Nasi]] (prince) of [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] and dated documents by the 'redemption of Israel'. Coins overstruck on Roman issues showed the Temple facade and the slogan 'for the freedom of [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]]'. Letters and contracts found in caves of the Judaean Desert, notably [[e:nahal-hever|Nahal Hever]], show a working administration that leased state land, collected produce and gave terse orders to commanders, written in [[e:hebrew|Hebrew]], [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] and Greek.
bar-kokhba-state.e: Hadrian brought in [[e:sextus-julius-severus|Julius Severus]] from [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], who wore the rebels down with a war of sieges. The fortress of [[e:betar|Betar]] fell in 135 or 136. [[e:judaea|Judea]] was devastated, renamed [[e:syria-palaestina|Syria Palaestina]], and [[e:jews|Jews]] were barred from [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]].

bit-dakkuri.t: A Chaldean tribe settled south of Babylon around Borsippa, often in conflict with the old cities over land.
bit-dakkuri.o: Bit-Dakkuri, 'House of Dakkuru', was one of the leading [[e:chaldean-tribes|Chaldean tribes]] of [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]], settled along the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] between [[e:babylon|Babylon]] and [[e:borsippa|Borsippa]]. It first appears in 850 BCE, when its chief Adinu paid tribute of gold, [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] to [[e:shalmaneser-iii|Shalmaneser III]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]].
bit-dakkuri.r: Like other Chaldean groups, Bit-Dakkuri was ruled by sheikhs from walled towns, living from date groves, herding and trade. Its proximity to [[e:babylon|Babylon]] and [[e:borsippa|Borsippa]] led to disputes with city dwellers over farmland. Its sheikhs swung between Assyrian loyalty and support for Babylonian rebels.
bit-dakkuri.e: [[e:esarhaddon|Esarhaddon of Assyria]] removed its chief Shamash-ibni around 678 BCE and returned seized lands to the citizens of [[e:babylon|Babylon]] and [[e:borsippa|Borsippa]]. The tribe fades from the sources by the mid-7th century BCE.

beylik-of-mani.t: Semi-autonomous Ottoman principality of the Mani peninsula, whose last bey, Petrobey Mavromichalis, helped launch the Greek War of Independence.
beylik-of-mani.o: The [[e:maniots|Maniots]] of the southern [[e:peloponnese|Peloponnese]] had always resisted Ottoman control. After the failed [[e:orlov-revolt|Orlov revolt]] of 1770 and the Russo-Turkish peace of 1774, the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] gave up direct rule and in 1776 created a [[e:beylik|Beylik]] of [[e:mani|Mani]] under the authority of the [[e:kapudan-pasha|Kapudan Pasha]], the Ottoman admiral, with a Maniot bey.
beylik-of-mani.r: The bey, chosen from the [[e:maniots|Maniot]] clans, paid a modest tribute and kept order, but power remained with the feuding chieftain families in their stone tower houses. Notable beys included [[e:tzanetos-grigorakis|Tzanetos Grigorakis]] and, from 1815, [[e:petrobey-mavromichalis|Petros Mavromichalis]]. The [[e:mani|Mani]] was poor, with [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]], piracy and a strong warrior tradition shaping its society.
beylik-of-mani.e: In March 1821 [[e:petrobey-mavromichalis|Petrobey Mavromichalis]] declared revolt at [[e:areopolis|Areopolis]] and [[e:kalamata|Kalamata]], joining the [[e:greek-war-of-independence|Greek War of Independence]]. The [[e:beylik|beylik]] ended, and the [[e:mani|Mani]] became part of the [[s:first-hellenic-republic|First Hellenic Republic]], though its clans long resisted central government.

banka-pahari-state.t: A very small chiefship of the Bundelkhand Agency, known almost only from British lists of the minor states of central India.
banka-pahari-state.o: Banka-Pahari was confirmed as a separate holding by the British in the early 19th century, as one of several small estates left from the break-up of [[e:bundela|Bundela]] power.
banka-pahari-state.r: It comprised only a handful of villages under a hereditary chief. Nothing else of note is recorded in standard sources.
banka-pahari-state.e: After independence Banka-Pahari was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

barca.t: A Greek city of Cyrenaica founded by rebel Battiad princes, remembered for its brutal destruction by the Persians.
barca.o: [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] relates that around 560 BCE the brothers of King [[e:arcesilaus-ii|Arcesilaus II]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-cyrene|Kingdom of Cyrene]] quarrelled with him and founded Barca, on the plain inland from the coast (near modern [[e:al-marj|al-Marj]]), with the support of local [[s:libu|Libyans]]. The city soon became a rival of its mother city.
barca.r: Barca was a Greek city of mixed Greek and Libyan population, ruled at first by kings; [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] names a king Alazeir, whose daughter married [[e:arcesilaus-iii|Arcesilaus III of Cyrene]]. It was known for [[e:horse-breeding|horse breeding]] and [[e:chariot|chariots]]. When Arcesilaus III was murdered there, his mother [[e:pheretime|Pheretime]] called in the Persian governor of [[e:egypt|Egypt]], [[e:aryandes|Aryandes]], whose army took Barca around 515 BCE by trickery after a long siege.
barca.e: Many Barcaeans were deported to [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]]. The city recovered as a member of the Cyrenaican cities, but declined as its port, Ptolemais, grew. It passed to the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]] in 322 BCE.

blackfoot-confederacy.t: The alliance of the Siksika, Kainai and Piikani, horse-mounted bison hunters who dominated the north-western Plains from the Saskatchewan River to the Missouri.
blackfoot-confederacy.o: The Niitsitapi, Algonquian-speaking peoples of the plains and parklands at the foot of the Rocky Mountains, had long hunted bison on foot. In the early 18th century they acquired horses from the south and guns from [[e:cree|Cree]] middlemen trading with the [[e:hudsons-bay-company|Hudson's Bay Company]], and the [[e:siksika|Siksika]], [[e:kainai-nation|Kainai]] and Piikani emerged as an allied military power.
blackfoot-confederacy.r: Each nation was divided into bands led by chiefs chosen for skill in war and generosity, and men's societies policed the summer camps and the communal hunt. Bison provided nearly everything: food, tipis, clothing and tools. The confederacy traded [[e:fur-trade|furs]] at [[e:hudsons-bay-company|Hudson's Bay Company]] and [[e:north-west-company|North West Company]] posts but kept American trappers out of its lands for decades. [[e:smallpox|Smallpox]] epidemics in 1781, 1837 and 1869 killed many.
blackfoot-confederacy.e: The Blackfoot had signed the [[e:lame-bull-treaty|Lame Bull Treaty]] with the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1855; weakened by the [[e:marias-massacre|Marias Massacre]] of 1870 and the near extinction of the bison, they signed Treaty 7 with [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]] in 1877, negotiated by [[e:crowfoot|Crowfoot]]. Today they live on the [[e:siksika|Siksika]], [[e:kainai-nation|Kainai]] and Piikani reserves in [[e:alberta|Alberta]] and the [[e:blackfeet-reservation|Blackfeet Reservation]] in [[e:montana|Montana]].

cr.a: Blackfoot Confederacy. "The tipi ring is captured on the Blackfoot Confederacy Flag, designed by Blood Tribe Grandfat...

bhor-state.t: A Maratha state in the Sahyadri hills south of Pune, ruled by the hereditary Pant Sachiv ministers of the Maratha court.
bhor-state.o: Bhor was granted in 1697 to [[e:shankaraji-narayan|Shankaraji Narayan]], appointed [[e:pant-sachiv|Sachiv]] (minister) by the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] king [[e:rajaram-i|Rajaram]]. His [[e:deshastha-brahmin|Deshastha Brahmin]] family held the office of Pant Sachiv and the lands that supported it.
bhor-state.r: The [[e:pant-sachiv|Pant Sachivs]] ruled a hilly territory of forts and small farms along the [[e:western-ghats|Western Ghats]], including [[e:rohida-fort|Rohida]] and [[e:rajgad|Rajgad]]. After 1818 they came under British protection and later the [[e:deccan-states-agency|Deccan States Agency]]. The state introduced some representative institutions before independence.
bhor-state.e: Bhor merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:maharashtra|Maharashtra]] in 1960, in [[e:pune|Pune]] district.

batlokwa-chiefdom.t: The Sotho-speaking Tlokwa chiefdom led by the regent MaNthatisi and her son Sekonyela, a major power and raider during the wars of the 1820s.
batlokwa-chiefdom.o: The Tlokwa were a Sotho-speaking people of the upper [[e:wilge-river|Wilge]] and [[e:caledon-river|Caledon]] river region. When [[s:hlubi-chiefdom|Hlubi]] and [[s:swazi-kingdom|Ngwane]] refugees broke into the highveld in the early 1820s, the regent MaNthatisi led the Tlokwa on a long series of migrations and raids that made her name feared across the interior, before they settled around the mountain fortresses of Joalaboholo and Marabeng near modern [[e:ficksburg|Ficksburg]].
batlokwa-chiefdom.r: Power rested on [[e:cattle|cattle]], mountain strongholds and fighting men drawn from many uprooted groups. MaNthatisi handed authority to her son [[e:sekonyela|Sekonyela]], whose rivalry with [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]] of the [[s:basotho-kingdom|Basotho Kingdom]] dominated the [[e:caledon-river|Caledon]] valley for two decades. Sekonyela received Wesleyan missionaries but kept to traditional religion, and he clashed in turn with the [[e:voortrekkers|Voortrekkers]]: around the end of 1837 [[e:piet-retief|Piet Retief]] tricked him into handing over cattle taken from the [[e:zulu-kingdom|Zulu]] king [[e:dingane|Dingane]], along with his horses and guns.
batlokwa-chiefdom.e: In 1853 [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]] stormed the Tlokwa strongholds and [[e:sekonyela|Sekonyela]] fled; he died in the [[s:orange-free-state|Orange Free State]]. Most of his people were absorbed into the [[e:sotho-people|Basotho]], while others later settled at Witsieshoek in the Free State, where a Tlokwa chieftaincy survives.

barghawata.t: A Berber confederation on Morocco's Atlantic coast that followed its own prophet and scripture for over three centuries.
barghawata.o: The Barghawata emerged in the [[e:tamesna|Tamesna]] plain between [[e:sale|Salé]] and [[e:safi-morocco|Safi]] after the [[e:berbers|Berber]] revolt of 740 against the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]]. Their first leader, Tarif, took part in the revolt, and around 744 his son [[e:salih-ibn-tarif|Salih ibn Tarif]] proclaimed himself a prophet, founding a new religion for his people.
barghawata.r: [[s:salihids|Salih]] gave the Barghawata a Berber-language scripture of eighty suras and distinct laws, including fasting in the month of [[e:rajab|Rajab]], prayers at different times and food taboos, according to the 11th-century geographer al-Bakri. His successors, such as [[e:yunus-ibn-ilyas|Yunus ibn Ilyas]], spread the faith by force. The confederation of farming and herding tribes fought the [[s:idrisid-dynasty|Idrisid dynasty]], the [[s:banu-ifran-emirate|Banu Ifran emirate]] and the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]].
barghawata.e: The [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]] attacked them from 1058; their spiritual leader [[e:abdallah-ibn-yasin|Abdallah ibn Yasin]] was killed fighting them in 1059, but the Barghawata were broken. Remnants were finally wiped out by the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] in the mid-12th century.

blambangan-kingdom.t: The last Hindu kingdom of Java, on the island's eastern tip, which held out against Muslim Mataram until conquered by the Dutch in 1768.
blambangan-kingdom.o: [[e:blambangan|Blambangan]] emerged in the eastern salient of [[e:java|Java]] as a province of [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]], and after Majapahit's decline in the 15th and 16th centuries it became an independent [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] kingdom, with its early capital near [[e:panarukan|Panarukan]]. Javanese legend remembers its ruler Menak Jingga as the enemy in the Damarwulan story.
blambangan-kingdom.r: [[e:blambangan|Blambangan]] was a sparsely populated realm of forests and small ports, caught between Muslim [[e:java|Java]] and [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] [[e:bali|Bali]]. It fought repeated wars with the [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram Sultanate]] and often accepted Balinese protection, especially from [[s:kingdom-of-buleleng|Buleleng]] and [[s:kingdom-of-mengwi|Mengwi]]. In the 17th century Prabu Tawang Alun founded a new capital at Macan Putih.
blambangan-kingdom.e: The [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] invaded in 1767 to 1768 to keep out the British, and suppressed the [[e:puputan-bayu|Puputan Bayu]] rising of 1771 to 1772 with heavy loss of life. The region became [[e:banyuwangi|Banyuwangi]], where the [[e:osing-people|Osing people]] preserve a distinct language and culture.

batawana-chiefdom.t: A Tswana chiefdom of Ngamiland around the Okavango delta, founded by a breakaway branch of the Bangwato.
batawana-chiefdom.o: Around 1795 Tawana, a son of the [[e:bamangwato|Bangwato]] chief, broke away after a succession dispute and led his followers north-west. They eventually settled near [[e:lake-ngami|Lake Ngami]] at the edge of the [[e:okavango-delta|Okavango]] delta, where they established authority over the [[e:wayeyi|BaYei]], [[e:hambukushu|Hambukushu]] and other local peoples.
batawana-chiefdom.r: Batawana chiefs ruled from towns near [[e:lake-ngami|Lake Ngami]], drawing tribute in labour and goods from subject peoples. [[e:ngamiland|Ngamiland]] was rich in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and [[e:ostrich-feather|ostrich feathers]], and the chiefdom traded with Cape and [[e:griqua|Griqua]] hunters and merchants. [[e:david-livingstone|David Livingstone]] reached Lake Ngami in 1849 during the reign of [[e:letsholathebe-i|Letsholathebe I]].
batawana-chiefdom.e: [[e:ngamiland|Ngamiland]] was brought into the [[s:bechuanaland-protectorate|Bechuanaland Protectorate]] in the 1880s and 1890s, and the chiefdom continued under colonial rule. In 1915 the Batawana capital moved to [[e:maun|Maun]], which grew into the main town of north-western [[e:botswana|Botswana]].

billung-march.t: A Saxon frontier march facing the Obotrites along the lower Elbe, held by the Billung family until the great Slavic revolt of 1066.
billung-march.o: Around 936 [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] entrusted [[e:hermann-billung|Hermann Billung]] with command against the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] along the lower [[e:elbe|Elbe]], from [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] to the [[e:peene|Peene]]. This frontier region, later called the Billung March, covered roughly modern [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] and eastern Holstein, inhabited mainly by [[s:obotrite-confederation|Obotrites]] and other Wendish peoples who paid tribute.
billung-march.r: The march was less a settled territory than a zone of military overlordship and tribute collection. The [[e:house-of-billung|Billungs]], who also became dukes of [[e:saxony|Saxony]], controlled it from strongholds along the [[e:elbe|Elbe]]. Bishoprics such as [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] in [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] were founded to convert the [[e:slavs|Slavs]], but German control remained loose and the Obotrite princes kept considerable power.
billung-march.e: The [[e:great-slav-rising|Great Slav Rising]] of 983 shook German control, and after the murder of the Christian Obotrite prince [[e:gottschalk-obotrite-prince|Gottschalk]] in 1066 the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] expelled German influence and destroyed churches. The march ceased to exist; German rule returned only with [[e:henry-the-lion|Henry the Lion]] in the 12th century, leading to the [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Lordship of Mecklenburg]].

bacan-sultanate.t: The southernmost of the four kingdoms of the North Moluccas, on the islands of Bacan south of Halmahera.
bacan-sultanate.o: Bacan was one of the [[e:moloku-kie-raha|Moloku Kie Raha]], the four Moluccan kingdoms with [[s:ternate-sultanate|Ternate]], [[s:tidore-sultanate|Tidore]] and [[s:jailolo-sultanate|Jailolo]]. Its rulers adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the late 15th century, like their neighbours, as Javanese and Malay traders sought Moluccan [[e:cloves|cloves]]. Local tradition traces the four royal houses to a common ancestor.
bacan-sultanate.r: Bacan was smaller and poorer than [[s:ternate-sultanate|Ternate]] and [[s:tidore-sultanate|Tidore]] but grew [[e:cloves|cloves]] and controlled islands to the south and the Obi group. In 1557 its sultan accepted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] under Portuguese influence, though later rulers were Muslim. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] built [[e:fort-barneveld|Fort Barneveld]] on Bacan in the early 17th century, and the sultanate was often a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of Ternate.
bacan-sultanate.e: Bacan came under [[e:dutch|Dutch]] control in the 19th century and its sultan became a colonial client. After [[e:indonesian-independence|Indonesian independence]] the sultanate was absorbed into the new state's administration around 1950; the royal family keeps a ceremonial role in [[e:north-maluku|North Maluku]].

bencoolen.t: British East India Company pepper settlement on the south-west coast of Sumatra, later governed by Stamford Raffles.
bencoolen.o: Expelled from [[e:banten|Banten]] in 1682, the [[e:east-india-company|English East India Company]] sought a new source of [[e:pepper|pepper]] and in 1685 founded a post at [[e:bengkulu|Bencoolen]] (Bengkulu) by agreement with local chiefs. It became the Company base in the Malay archipelago, and between 1714 and 1719 the garrison built Fort Marlborough, one of the largest British forts in Asia.
bencoolen.r: The settlement was run by a Company resident and council, later a lieutenant-governor, who forced local farmers to grow [[e:pepper|pepper]] for fixed prices. It was unhealthy and lost money for most of its history, and convicts and slaves from [[e:india|India]] and [[e:africa|Africa]] were used as labour. [[e:stamford-raffles|Thomas Stamford Raffles]] governed from 1818 to 1824, abolishing [[e:slavery|slavery]] and promoting new crops.
bencoolen.e: Under the [[e:anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1824|Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824]] [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] exchanged [[e:bengkulu|Bencoolen]] for [[s:dutch-malacca|Dutch Malacca]], and the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] took over in 1824 and 1825, folding it into the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]]. Fort Marlborough still stands in Bengkulu.

bassa-cove.t: A settlement for freed Black Americans on the Liberian coast, founded by Pennsylvania and New York colonisation societies on Quaker principles of peace and temperance.
bassa-cove.o: In the early 1830s the Young Men's Colonization Society of [[e:pennsylvania|Pennsylvania]], together with the [[e:new-york|New York]] colonisation society, founded a settlement at the mouth of the [[e:st-john-river-liberia|St John]] river, first called Port Cresson after the [[e:quakers|Quaker]] colonisation advocate [[e:elliott-cresson|Elliott Cresson]]. Its settlers were free Black Americans and emancipated slaves.
bassa-cove.r: The colony was run on [[e:quakers|Quaker]] principles: it forbade arms for aggression and banned the sale of alcohol, which also limited its trade with neighbours. In 1835 local [[e:bassa-people-liberia|Bassa]] forces, angered by the colony's opposition to the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]], destroyed the settlement and killed many settlers. It was refounded as Bassa Cove, and [[e:thomas-buchanan-governor|Thomas Buchanan]] became its governor in 1836.
bassa-cove.e: In 1839 [[e:bassa-people-liberia|Bassa]] Cove joined the [[s:colony-of-liberia|Colony of Liberia]] in the Commonwealth of [[s:liberia|Liberia]], with Buchanan as governor of the whole. The town of Buchanan in [[e:grand-bassa-county|Grand Bassa County]] stands near the site.

burgundian-state.t: The patchwork realm of the Valois dukes of Burgundy, from Dijon to the North Sea, whose court set the fashion of 15th-century Europe.
burgundian-state.o: In 1363 [[e:john-ii-of-france|John II of France]] gave the [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Duchy of Burgundy]] to his son [[e:philip-the-bold|Philip the Bold]]. Philip's marriage to [[e:margaret-iii-countess-of-flanders|Margaret of Male]] brought [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]], [[s:county-of-artois|Artois]] and the [[s:free-county-of-burgundy|Free County of Burgundy]] in 1384. His grandson [[e:philip-the-good|Philip the Good]] added [[s:county-of-namur|Namur]], [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]], Holland, [[s:county-of-zeeland|Zeeland]], [[s:county-of-hainaut|Hainaut]] and [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]] between 1421 and 1443.
burgundian-state.r: The dukes held their lands by different titles under [[e:france|France]] and the Empire and tried to bind them with common institutions, a Chamber of Accounts, the [[e:states-general-of-the-netherlands|States General]] from 1464 and the [[e:order-of-the-golden-fleece|Order of the Golden Fleece]], founded in 1430. Flemish and Brabantine towns supplied wealth from cloth and trade, and painters such as [[e:jan-van-eyck|Jan van Eyck]] and [[e:rogier-van-der-weyden|Rogier van der Weyden]] worked for the court.
burgundian-state.e: [[e:charles-the-bold|Charles the Bold]] sought a crown but was killed at [[e:battle-of-nancy|Nancy]] in 1477. [[e:louis-xi|Louis XI]] seized the duchy; [[e:mary-of-burgundy|Mary of Burgundy]] married [[e:maximilian-i-holy-roman-emperor|Maximilian of Austria]], and after her death in 1482 the [[e:treaty-of-arras-1482|Treaty of Arras]] split the inheritance, the [[e:low-countries|Low Countries]] passing to the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]].

banu-khalid-emirate.t: The Bedouin emirate that ruled eastern Arabia from Hofuf after expelling the Ottomans, until the first Saudi state absorbed it.
banu-khalid-emirate.o: The Banu Khalid were a powerful tribal confederation of eastern [[e:arabia|Arabia]]. In 1670 their chief [[e:barrak-ibn-ghurayr|Barrak ibn Ghurayr]] expelled the Ottoman garrison of the [[s:lahsa-eyalet|Lahsa Eyalet]] and made [[e:hofuf|Hofuf]] the centre of an [[e:emirate|emirate]] controlling the coast from [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] to [[s:sheikhdom-of-qatar|Qatar]] and the oases of [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Hasa]] and [[e:qatif|Qatif]].
banu-khalid-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] governed through tribal alliances, taxing oasis farmers, pearl divers and caravans while keeping nominal ties with the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]]. Under their protection, clans of the [[e:bani-utbah|Bani Utbah]] settled at [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] and later [[e:zubarah|Zubarah]] in [[s:sheikhdom-of-qatar|Qatar]]. [[e:sulayman-ibn-muhammad-al-hamid|Sulayman ibn Muhammad]], emir in the mid-18th century, pressured the town of [[e:uyayna|Uyayna]] to expel the reformer [[e:muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab|Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab]].
banu-khalid-emirate.e: Family feuds after 1752 weakened the [[e:emirate|emirate]]. The [[s:emirate-of-diriyah|Emirate of Diriyah]] defeated the Banu Khalid in a series of campaigns and conquered [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Hasa]] by 1796, though the tribe remained important in the region.

balearica.t: The late Roman province of the Balearic Islands, separated from Carthaginiensis in the 4th century and lost to the Vandals in 455.
balearica.o: The [[e:balearic-islands|Balearic Islands]], conquered by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 123 BCE, belonged to [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]], [[s:hispania-tarraconensis|Tarraconensis]] and then [[s:carthaginiensis|Carthaginiensis]]. Around 369 they became a separate province, Balearica, under a governor in the [[s:diocese-of-hispania|Diocese of Hispania]].
balearica.r: The islands lived from farming, fishing and trade, with towns such as [[e:palma|Palma]], [[e:pollentia|Pollentia]] and on [[e:menorca|Menorca]] [[e:mahon|Mago]] and [[e:ciutadella-de-menorca|Iamo]]. [[e:christianity|Christianity]] was well established by the 5th century. A letter of [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:severus-of-minorca|Severus of Minorca]] describes the forced conversion of the [[e:jews|Jews]] of Mago in 418, a rare window on island life.
balearica.e: Vandal raids from [[e:africa|Africa]] struck the islands from 425. Around 455 the [[e:vandals|Vandals]] under Gaiseric took control, ending Roman rule. The islands passed to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] after [[e:belisarius|Belisarius]]' reconquest of Africa in 534.

barony-of-kalavryta.t: Short-lived Frankish barony in the mountains of northern Peloponnese, one of the first lost to the reviving Byzantines.
barony-of-kalavryta.o: Kalavryta was one of the twelve baronies set up in the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] around 1209. It was granted to [[e:otho-of-tournay|Otho of Tournay]] and covered the mountainous district around the town of Kalavryta in the northern [[e:peloponnese|Peloponnese]], with twelve knight's fiefs.
barony-of-kalavryta.r: Like other baronies, it was held by a French [[e:knighthood|knightly]] family owing military service and counsel to the prince and governing a Greek peasant population from a castle. Records say little more about it than the name of its lords.
barony-of-kalavryta.e: After the Principality ceded [[e:mystras|Mistras]] and other forts to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] in 1262, Byzantine forces pushed north. Kalavryta was taken around 1270 and the barony ceased to exist, though the area later changed hands again before passing permanently to the [[s:despotate-of-the-morea|Despotate of the Morea]].

cr.a: Eric Gaba (Sting - fr:Sting); derivative work by Constantine

berziti.t: Slavic tribe of western Macedonia, the Brsjaci, caught between Byzantium and Bulgaria until absorbed by the Bulgarian state in the 9th century.
berziti.o: The Berziti were among the Slavic groups that settled in [[e:macedonia-region|Macedonia]] in the 7th century, in the region around [[e:ohrid|Ohrid]], [[e:prilep|Prilep]] and [[e:bitola|Bitola]]. Byzantine sources refer to their land as Berzitia; the later Macedonian ethnographic name Brsjaci is often traced to them.
berziti.r: Known only from a few Byzantine notices, they lived under their own chiefs (archons), at times tributary to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. In the 770s the Bulgarian ruler [[e:telerig|Telerig]] planned to resettle them in [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]], and the Byzantine emperor Constantine V campaigned in the region.
berziti.e: During the reigns of [[e:presian-i|Presian]] and [[e:boris-i-of-bulgaria|Boris I]] in the mid-9th century their territory passed to the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]], and the name disappears.

belegezites.t: Slavic tribe settled in Thessaly in the 7th century, remembered for trading grain with besieged Thessalonica.
belegezites.o: The [[s:berziti|Belegezites]] were one of the Slavic groups that settled in the [[e:balkans|Balkans]] during the great migrations of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They occupied lands in [[e:thessaly|Thessaly]] around Phthiotic [[s:thebes|Thebes]] and [[e:demetrias|Demetrias]] on the [[e:pagasetic-gulf|Gulf of Volos]]. Almost everything known about them comes from the [[e:miracles-of-saint-demetrius|Miracles of Saint Demetrius]], a Byzantine collection of stories about [[e:thessaloniki|Thessalonica]].
belegezites.r: They lived as farming communities under their own chiefs, partly independent of [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. During the Slavic siege of [[e:thessaloniki|Thessalonica]] in the 670s they did not join the attackers but sold grain to the starving city, a sign of their prosperity and pragmatic relations with the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]]. Their name probably survives in Velegezitia, a district named in later Byzantine sources.
belegezites.e: Over the 8th and 9th centuries [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] reasserted control over [[e:greece|Greece]] through the [[e:theme-system|theme system]], and the [[s:berziti|Belegezites]] were gradually brought under imperial administration, converted to [[e:christianity|Christianity]] and absorbed into the Greek-speaking population. They leave few traces apart from place names.
belegezites.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

bengal-sultanate.t: The independent Muslim kingdom that united Bengal for two centuries, nurtured Bengali literature and built the mosques of Gaur and Pandua.
bengal-sultanate.o: [[e:shamsuddin-ilyas-shah|Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah]], ruler of [[e:gaur|Lakhnauti]], conquered [[e:satgaon|Satgaon]] and the [[s:sonargaon-sultanate|Sonargaon Sultanate]] and in 1352 united [[e:bengal|Bengal]] as an independent state. He withstood an invasion by [[e:firuz-shah-tughluq|Firuz Shah Tughluq]] of the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] in 1353 to 1354, and a second invasion against his son [[e:sikandar-shah-bengal|Sikandar Shah]] also failed, securing Bengal's independence; the [[e:ilyas-shahi-dynasty|Ilyas Shahi dynasty]] ruled from [[e:pandua-malda|Pandua]] and later Gaur.
bengal-sultanate.r: Several dynasties ruled, including the [[e:ilyas-shahi-dynasty|Ilyas Shahis]], the line of [[e:raja-ganesha|Raja Ganesha]] and the [[e:husain-shahi-dynasty|Husain Shahis]]. [[e:bengal|Bengal]] exported muslin, [[e:silk|silk]], [[e:rice|rice]] and [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] through [[e:chittagong|Chittagong]], and Chinese envoys of the Ming visited. The sultans patronised Bengali translations of the [[e:ramayana|Ramayana]] and [[e:mahabharata|Mahabharata]]. Brick mosques such as the [[e:adina-mosque|Adina Mosque]] at [[e:pandua-malda|Pandua]] and the [[e:sixty-dome-mosque|Sixty Dome Mosque]] at [[e:bagerhat|Bagerhat]] date from this period.
bengal-sultanate.e: [[e:sher-shah-suri|Sher Shah Suri]] seized [[e:gaur|Gaur]] in 1538 and [[e:bengal|Bengal]] became part of the [[s:sur-empire|Sur Empire]]. Afghan Karrani rulers then governed it until the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] defeated [[e:daud-khan-karrani|Daud Khan Karrani]] in 1576. Resistance continued under the [[s:baro-bhuyans|Baro-Bhuyans]].

beylik-of-the-west.t: The western province of Ottoman Algiers, governed from Mazouna, Mascara and finally Oran, on the frontier with Spain and Morocco.
beylik-of-the-west.o: The [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]] created the western [[e:beylik|beylik]] in 1563, with its first seat at [[e:mazouna|Mazouna]]. As the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] consolidated control over the former [[s:zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen|Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen]], the capital moved to [[e:mascara-algeria|Mascara]] around 1700, closer to [[s:spanish-oran|Spanish Oran]], which the beys sought to recapture.
beylik-of-the-west.r: The beys governed the plains and highlands of western [[e:algeria|Algeria]] through makhzen tribes, collecting taxes in grain and livestock. [[e:mustapha-bouchelaghem|Mustapha Bouchelaghem]] captured [[e:oran|Oran]] in 1708, though [[e:spain|Spain]] retook it in 1732. [[e:mohammed-el-kebir|Mohammed el-Kebir]] took possession of Oran in 1792, made it his capital and built mosques there.
beylik-of-the-west.e: After the fall of [[e:algiers|Algiers]] in 1830, the last bey, Hassan, surrendered [[e:oran|Oran]] to the French in January 1831. The western tribes soon rallied to the [[s:emirate-of-abdelkader|Emirate of Abdelkader]], while the territory became part of [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]].

burid-emirate-of-damascus.t: The dynasty of Tughtekin that ruled Damascus for half a century, resisting both the Crusaders and the Zengids.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.o: [[e:tughtekin|Tughtekin]], the Turkish atabeg of the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuk]] prince [[e:duqaq|Duqaq]], took power in [[e:damascus|Damascus]] after Duqaq's death in 1104. The dynasty takes its name from his son [[e:taj-al-muluk-buri|Taj al-Muluk Buri]], who succeeded him in 1128.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.r: The Burids governed with the support of the Damascene notables and the urban militia. [[e:tughtekin|Tughtekin]] fought and negotiated with the [[s:kingdom-of-jerusalem|Kingdom of Jerusalem]], while [[e:taj-al-muluk-buri|Buri]], after the [[e:nizari-ismailism|Nizari Ismailis]] gained influence in the city, allowed a massacre of them in 1129. To resist [[e:imad-al-din-zengi|Zengi]] of [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], the regent [[e:muin-al-din-unur|Mu'in al-Din Unur]] allied with [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]], but the [[e:second-crusade|Second Crusade]] nonetheless besieged [[e:damascus|Damascus]] in July 1148 and withdrew after five days.
burid-emirate-of-damascus.e: Weakened by internal rivalries, [[e:mujir-al-din-abaq|Mujir al-Din Abaq]] lost the support of the city, which opened its gates to [[e:nur-al-din|Nur al-Din]] in April 1154, uniting Muslim [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] under the [[s:zengid-dynasty|Zengid dynasty]].

beylik-of-constantine.t: The eastern province of Ottoman Algiers, the largest and richest, whose last bey made Constantine the final stronghold against the French.
beylik-of-constantine.o: The [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]] organised the eastern [[e:beylik|beylik]] in 1567, with its seat in the ancient rock-top city of Constantine. It covered eastern [[e:algeria|Algeria]] from [[e:kabylia|Kabylia]] to the Tunisian border and south to the Saharan oases such as [[s:sultanate-of-touggourt|Touggourt]].
beylik-of-constantine.r: The beys ruled through local great families and makhzen tribes, collecting taxes in grain, wool and livestock and paying heavy tribute to [[e:algiers|Algiers]]. [[e:salah-bey|Salah Bey]], who ruled from 1771 to 1792, built mosques, [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] and bridges and is remembered in local song. Constantine was a centre of learning, crafts and leather work.
beylik-of-constantine.e: After [[e:algiers|Algiers]] fell in 1830, [[e:ahmed-bey-of-constantine|Ahmed Bey]] held Constantine and repulsed a French assault in 1836. The French stormed the city in October 1837, and the [[e:beylik|beylik]] was absorbed into [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]]; Ahmed Bey fought on until 1848.

bishopric-of-pomesania.t: Prussian prince-bishopric on the lower Vistula, closely tied to the Teutonic Order, whose bishop embraced the Reformation in the 1520s.
bishopric-of-pomesania.o: The diocese was one of four created in [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] by [[e:william-of-modena|William of Modena]] in 1243, covering the land of the [[s:pomesanians|Pomesanians]]. The [[e:bishop|bishop]] received a third of the territory as his own principality, with the castle of [[e:prabuty|Riesenburg]] (Prabuty) as residence and a cathedral at [[e:kwidzyn|Marienwerder]] (Kwidzyn).
bishopric-of-pomesania.r: Its cathedral chapter belonged to the [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]] from 1285, and the [[e:bishop|bishops]] were usually loyal to the Order. [[e:kwidzyn|Marienwerder]] became the centre of the cult of [[e:dorothea-of-montau|Dorothea of Montau]], a local mystic. After 1466 the bishopric remained in the Order's part of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], under Polish overlordship.
bishopric-of-pomesania.e: [[e:bishop|Bishop]] [[e:erhard-von-queis|Erhard von Queis]] adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] and, after the secularisation of the Order's state into [[s:duchy-of-prussia|Ducal Prussia]] in 1525, surrendered his secular rule to [[e:albert-duke-of-prussia|Duke Albert]] in 1527. The territory became part of [[e:duchy-of-prussia|Ducal Prussia]], and the Protestant bishopric was later abolished.

bastetani.t: An Iberian people of the Granada highlands, whose capital Basti yielded the seated stone goddess known as the Lady of Baza.
bastetani.o: The Bastetani occupied the uplands of eastern [[e:andalusia|Andalusia]], in modern [[e:granada|Granada]], [[e:almeria|Almería]] and [[e:jaen|Jaén]], from the mid-first millennium BCE. Their main town was [[e:basti-iberia|Basti]], near [[e:baza|Baza]], and they bordered the [[s:oretani|Oretani]], [[s:contestani|Contestani]] and coastal [[s:bastuli|Bastuli]].
bastetani.r: They lived in fortified towns on hills controlling routes between the coast and the [[e:guadalquivir|Guadalquivir]] valley. Their elites were buried in rich chamber tombs, as at Tútugi (Galera) and [[e:basti-iberia|Basti]], where the [[e:lady-of-baza|Lady of Baza]], a painted stone statue of an enthroned woman used as a cinerary urn, was found in 1971. Their economy combined farming, herding and esparto working.
bastetani.e: After Carthaginian control, the Bastetani passed under [[e:rome|Rome]] during the Second Punic War and joined the great revolt of 197 BCE before being pacified. Their region was divided between [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]] and [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]] in Roman times.

beylik-of-chaka.t: The Aegean emirate of Chaka Bey, the first Turkish ruler to build a fleet and threaten Constantinople from the sea.
beylik-of-chaka.o: [[e:tzachas|Chaka]], called Tzachas by the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]], was a Turkish commander who had been a captive at the Byzantine court of [[e:nikephoros-iii-botaneiates|Nikephoros III]]. After his release he seized [[s:smyrna|Smyrna]] and the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] coast of western [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], probably in the late 1080s.
beylik-of-chaka.r: With Greek shipwrights he built a fleet, took [[s:phocaea|Phocaea]], [[s:clazomenae|Clazomenae]] and the islands of [[e:lesbos|Lesbos]], [[s:chios|Chios]] and [[s:principality-of-samos|Samos]], and styled himself emperor. In 1090-1091 he allied with the [[s:pechenegs|Pechenegs]], who were then besieging [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], but the Byzantine navy and the [[e:pechenegs|Pecheneg]] defeat at [[e:battle-of-levounion|Levounion]] in 1091 ended the threat. Little is known of his government.
beylik-of-chaka.e: Alexios I persuaded [[e:tzachas|Chaka]]'s son-in-law, the [[e:sultanate-of-rum|Rum Seljuk]] [[e:kilij-arslan-i|Kilij Arslan I]], to kill him at a banquet around 1093. After the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]], the Byzantine general [[e:john-doukas-megas-doux|John Doukas]] recovered [[s:smyrna|Smyrna]] in 1097-1098.

bhauma-kara-dynasty.t: A dynasty of coastal Odisha that patronised great Buddhist monasteries and was ruled for long periods by queens.
bhauma-kara-dynasty.o: The Bhauma-Karas came to power in coastal [[e:odisha|Odisha]] in the 8th century, replacing the [[s:shailodbhava-dynasty|Shailodbhava dynasty]]. Their capital was Guhadeva-pataka, near modern [[e:jajpur|Jajpur]]. The dynasty founded an era beginning around 736 that dates their inscriptions.
bhauma-kara-dynasty.r: The early kings were Buddhists who supported monasteries at [[e:ratnagiri-odisha|Ratnagiri]], [[e:lalitagiri|Lalitagiri]] and Udayagiri; Shubhakara I is thought to be the king of Wu-cha who sent a Buddhist [[e:manuscript|manuscript]] to the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] emperor in 795. Later rulers turned to [[e:shaivism|Shaivism]]. Unusually, several queens ruled in their own right, including Tribhuvana Mahadevi I and Dandi Mahadevi. Temples such as the [[e:vaital-deul|Vaital Deul]] in [[e:bhubaneswar|Bhubaneswar]] date from this period.
bhauma-kara-dynasty.e: After a series of weak rulers the dynasty declined in the 10th century, and the [[s:somavamshi-dynasty|Somavamshi dynasty]] took over coastal [[e:odisha|Odisha]].

bhopal-state.t: An Afghan-founded Muslim state of central India, famous for its century of rule by four successive women, the Begums of Bhopal.
bhopal-state.o: [[e:dost-mohammad-khan-of-bhopal|Dost Mohammad Khan]], an Afghan soldier who had served the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]], took advantage of imperial decline after 1707 to seize lands in [[e:malwa|Malwa]]. He fortified the old town of Bhopal and built the fort of Fatehgarh, establishing a Muslim dynasty over a largely [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] population.
bhopal-state.r: Bhopal resisted [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] pressure and allied with the British in 1818. From 1819 to 1926 four women ruled in turn: [[e:qudsia-begum|Qudsia Begum]], [[e:sikandar-begum|Sikandar Begum]], [[e:shah-jahan-begum|Shah Jahan Begum]] and [[e:sultan-jahan-begum|Sultan Jahan Begum]], who built mosques, schools, railways and the [[e:taj-ul-masajid|Taj-ul-Masajid]]. It was a nineteen-gun salute state.
bhopal-state.e: Nawab [[e:hamidullah-khan|Hamidullah Khan]] held out against accession until 1949, when Bhopal became a centrally administered state of [[e:india|India]]. In 1956 it became the capital of [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]].

baraundha-state.t: A small Raghuvanshi Rajput principality in the hills of Bundelkhand, reputed one of the oldest ruling houses of the region.
baraundha-state.o: The ruling family were Raghuvanshi [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]] who held lands around Patharkachar in the rugged country south of the [[e:yamuna|Yamuna]], in what became [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]]. Their traditional history places the founding of the state in the mid-16th century, but details of its early rulers are sparse.
baraundha-state.r: Baraundha was a small, largely rural state of forest and upland villages ruled by a Raja. After British supremacy in [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] in the early 19th century it was confirmed by sanad and supervised through the Bundelkhand and later [[s:rewa-state|Baghelkhand]] agencies of the [[e:central-india-agency|Central India Agency]].
baraundha-state.e: After [[e:indian-independence|Indian independence]] its ruler acceded to [[e:india|India]], and in 1948 Baraundha was merged into the new union of [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]]. Its territory now lies in [[e:satna-district|Satna district]] of [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]].

bremen-soviet-republic.t: Council republic in the port city of Bremen in early 1919, suppressed after a few weeks by government troops.
bremen-soviet-republic.o: After the [[e:german-revolution-of-1918-1919|November revolution]] of 1918, workers' and soldiers' councils took power in [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]]. On 10 January 1919, after the [[e:spartacist-uprising|Spartacist rising]] in [[e:berlin|Berlin]], left-wing radicals and Communists proclaimed a Soviet Republic, dissolving the city's senate and parliament.
bremen-soviet-republic.r: The council government, dominated by Communists and [[e:independent-social-democratic-party-of-germany|Independent Socialists]], controlled the city for less than a month. It faced shortages of money and food, as banks refused credit, and opposition from the middle classes and moderate Social Democrats. Its leaders tried to negotiate with the national government but refused to disarm.
bremen-soviet-republic.e: On 4 February 1919 the [[e:freikorps|Freikorps]] Division Gerstenberg, sent by [[e:gustav-noske|Gustav Noske]], stormed [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]]. About 80 people died, and the Soviet Republic ended. [[e:bremen|Bremen]] resumed as a city-state within the [[s:weimar-republic|Weimar Republic]].

barony-of-vostitsa.t: Barony of the Principality of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, centred on Vostitsa, the modern Aigio.
barony-of-vostitsa.o: After the Frankish conquest of the [[e:peloponnese|Peloponnese]], the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] was divided into twelve baronies around 1209. Vostitsa, with a modest number of knight's fiefs, was granted to the Charpigny family from [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]], who held it through the 13th century.
barony-of-vostitsa.r: The barons held the castle and town on the south shore of the [[e:gulf-of-corinth|Gulf of Corinth]], owed military service to the prince and sat in his high court, while Greek villagers farmed the land under them. Little detail of daily government survives beyond mentions in the [[e:chronicle-of-the-morea|Chronicle of the Morea]] and Angevin records.
barony-of-vostitsa.e: In the 14th century the barony passed by inheritance and sale among several lords and was caught up in the struggles of the [[e:navarrese-company|Navarrese Company]]. It came to an end in the early 15th century, as the principality crumbled.

cr.a: Eric Gaba (Sting - fr:Sting); derivative work by Constantine

belize.t: Central America's only English-speaking country, independent since 1981, home to the world's second-longest barrier reef and a long border dispute with Guatemala.
belize.o: [[s:british-honduras|British Honduras]] was renamed Belize in 1973, and despite [[e:guatemala|Guatemala's]] claim to the territory it became independent on 21 September 1981 under [[e:george-cadle-price|George Price]] of the [[e:peoples-united-party|People's United Party]], with the British monarch as head of state. British troops stayed to guard it against [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]].
belize.r: Power has alternated between the [[e:peoples-united-party|People's United Party]] and the [[e:united-democratic-party-belize|United Democratic Party]], under prime ministers such as [[e:manuel-esquivel|Manuel Esquivel]], [[e:said-musa|Said Musa]], [[e:dean-barrow|Dean Barrow]] and [[e:johnny-briceno|Johnny Briceño]]. [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] recognised Belize's independence in 1991, though not its borders, and the British garrison largely left in 1994. Tourism to the reef and Maya sites, [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], citrus, bananas and seafood support the economy. Its population mixes Kriol, Mestizo, Maya, [[e:garifuna|Garifuna]] and Mennonite communities.
belize.e: In 2018 and 2019 both [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] and Belize voted to submit the territorial dispute to the [[e:international-court-of-justice|International Court of Justice]]. [[e:belmopan|Belmopan]], built after [[e:hurricane-hattie|Hurricane Hattie]], is the capital, though [[e:belize-city|Belize City]] is the largest town.

bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.t: An Afghan principality in the Ganges Doab founded by Muhammad Khan Bangash, a soldier of fortune in the late Mughal Empire.
bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.o: [[e:muhammad-khan-bangash|Muhammad Khan Bangash]], an Afghan commander who served the Mughal emperor [[e:farrukhsiyar|Farrukhsiyar]], was granted lands in the [[e:ganges-yamuna-doab|Doab]] and founded the town of [[e:farrukhabad|Farrukhabad]] in 1714, naming it after the emperor. He later served as Mughal governor of [[e:prayagraj|Allahabad]] and [[e:malwa|Malwa]], and built a hereditary principality.
bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.r: The Bangash nawabs ruled a territory between the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] and [[e:yamuna|Yamuna]] populated by Afghan settlers and [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] farmers. They fought the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] and the [[s:awadh-state|Awadh State]]; [[e:ahmad-khan-bangash|Ahmad Khan Bangash]] defeated an [[e:awadh|Awadh]] army in 1750 but was then crushed by a Maratha and Awadh alliance. [[e:farrukhabad|Farrukhabad]] became a centre of textile [[e:printing-press|printing]] and trade.
bangash-nawabs-of-farrukhabad.e: From the 1770s the nawabs depended on [[e:awadh|Awadh]], and in 1802 Nawab Imdad Husain Khan ceded his territory to the [[e:east-india-company|British East India Company]] in exchange for a pension. The last nawab joined the 1857 rebellion and was exiled.

bangwaketse-chiefdom.t: A Tswana chiefdom centred on Kanye whose rulers helped secure British protection rather than Company rule for Botswana.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.o: The [[e:bangwaketse|Bangwaketse]] separated from the [[e:bakwena|Bakwena]] in the 18th century and settled in south-eastern [[e:botswana|Botswana]]. Under [[e:makaba-ii|Makaba II]] in the late 18th and early 19th centuries they became one of the strongest [[e:tswana-people|Tswana]] states, until Makaba was killed in 1824 during the wars of that era.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled from a large town through ward heads and the kgotla, drawing wealth from [[e:cattle|cattle]] and trade in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and skins with the Cape. After years of displacement, Gaseitsiwe re-established the chiefdom at [[e:kanye|Kanye]], a defensible hill town. Missionaries of the [[e:london-missionary-society|London Missionary Society]] were influential.
bangwaketse-chiefdom.e: The chiefdom joined the [[s:bechuanaland-protectorate|Bechuanaland Protectorate]] in 1885. In 1895 [[e:bathoen-i|Bathoen I]] travelled to [[e:london|London]] with [[e:khama-iii|Khama III]] and [[e:sebele-i|Sebele I]] to oppose transfer to the [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company]], and the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] was preserved. [[e:bangwaketse|Ngwaketse]] is now a district of [[e:botswana|Botswana]].

bagratid-armenia.t: The medieval Armenian kingdom of the Bagratids, whose capital Ani became famous as the city of a thousand and one churches.
bagratid-armenia.o: [[e:ashot-i-of-armenia|Ashot Bagratuni]], recognised as prince of princes in 862, received a royal crown from the [[e:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid]] [[e:caliphate|caliph]] around 884 with Byzantine approval, reviving the Armenian monarchy after more than four centuries. The kingdom grew out of the [[s:principality-of-armenia|Principality of Armenia]] and the family's vast estates in [[e:shirak|Shirak]] and [[e:ayrarat|Ayrarat]].
bagratid-armenia.r: The kingdom was a federation of noble houses and rival kingdoms under the [[e:bagratuni-dynasty|Bagratid]] [[e:negus-nagast|king of kings]]. [[e:smbat-i-of-armenia|Smbat I]] was executed by the [[e:sajid-dynasty|Sajid]] emir Yusuf in 914, but [[e:ashot-ii-of-armenia|Ashot II the Iron]] restored royal power. [[e:ashot-iii-of-armenia|Ashot III]] moved the capital to Ani in 961, which grew wealthy on trade between [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and [[e:iran|Iran]]. Under [[e:gagik-i-of-armenia|Gagik I]] the architect [[e:trdat-the-architect|Trdat]] completed [[e:ani-cathedral|Ani Cathedral]] in 1001.
bagratid-armenia.e: [[e:hovhannes-smbat-iii|Hovhannes-Smbat]] bequeathed his kingdom to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], and in 1045 [[e:gagik-ii-of-armenia|Gagik II]] was forced to surrender Ani to the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]]. The [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]] sacked Ani in 1064, and many [[e:armenians|Armenians]] moved west towards [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]].

barcid-iberia.t: The Carthaginian domain built in Iberia by Hamilcar Barca and his heirs, the silver-rich base from which Hannibal set out to invade Italy.
barcid-iberia.o: After losing [[e:sicily|Sicily]] in the First Punic War, [[e:carthage|Carthage]] sent [[e:hamilcar-barca|Hamilcar Barca]] to [[e:iberia|Iberia]] in 237 BCE. Landing at [[s:gadir|Gadir]], he conquered the [[e:guadalquivir|Guadalquivir]] valley and its mines. After his death in about 229 BCE, his son-in-law [[e:hasdrubal-the-fair|Hasdrubal]] extended Carthaginian power by diplomacy and founded [[e:carthago-nova|Qart Hadasht]], later Carthago Nova, around 227 BCE.
barcid-iberia.r: [[e:barcid-family|Barcid]] [[e:iberia|Iberia]] was run almost as a family dominion of the Barcids, nominally under [[e:carthage|Carthage]]. [[e:silver|Silver]] from mines near [[e:carthago-nova|Qart Hadasht]] and the [[e:sierra-morena|Sierra Morena]] paid for armies of Iberian, Celtiberian and African troops. Alliances with local rulers were sealed by marriages, such as [[e:hannibal|Hannibal's]] to [[e:himilce|Himilce of Castulo]]. In 226 BCE the [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] treaty with [[e:rome|Rome]] fixed a northern limit.
barcid-iberia.e: [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]], in command from 221 BCE, took [[s:saguntum|Saguntum]] in 219 BCE, starting the [[e:second-punic-war|Second Punic War]]. [[e:scipio-africanus|Scipio]] captured [[e:carthago-nova|Qart Hadasht]] in 209 BCE and won at [[e:battle-of-ilipa|Ilipa]] in 206 BCE, ending Carthaginian rule. The territory became the Roman provinces of [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]] and [[e:hispania-ulterior|Ulterior]].

barony-of-patras.t: The largest barony of the Principality of Achaea, centred on the port of Patras, later sold to its Latin archbishop.
barony-of-patras.o: When the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] was organised around 1209, [[s:patrae|Patras]], the main port of the north-western [[e:peloponnese|Peloponnese]], was granted as a barony with 24 knight's fiefs to [[e:william-aleman|William Aleman]], a knight possibly of German or Provencal origin. He fortified the ancient citadel above the town.
barony-of-patras.r: The barons held the castle and city, owed service to the prince and shared the town with the [[e:latin|Latin]] archbishop, who was the senior Catholic prelate in the principality. [[s:patrae|Patras]] was a commercial centre for [[e:silk|silk]], currants and trade with [[e:italy|Italy]], with a Greek majority under Latin lords.
barony-of-patras.e: Over the 13th century the archbishops acquired the baronial rights. Around 1276 the barony passed to the archbishop, creating the [[s:latin-archbishopric-of-patras|Latin Archbishopric of Patras]], a church-ruled state that lasted until 1430.

cr.a: Eric Gaba (Sting - fr:Sting); derivative work by Constantine

bonai-state.t: A hilly princely state on the Brahmani river in northern Odisha, ruled from Bonaigarh until 1948.
bonai-state.o: The ruling family claimed descent from the [[s:kadamba-dynasty|Kadamba dynasty]], and tradition dates the state to around 1500. Its early history is poorly documented.
bonai-state.r: Bonai was a rugged, forested state with a largely Adivasi population, including [[e:bhuyan|Bhuyan]] and [[e:munda-people|Munda]] communities. It was counted among the [[e:chota-nagpur-plateau|Chota Nagpur]] tributary states until 1905, when it was transferred to the [[e:orissa-tributary-states|Orissa Tributary States]]. Its hills contain iron ore deposits.
bonai-state.e: Bonai merged into [[e:odisha|Orissa]] on 1 January 1948 and is now part of [[e:sundargarh|Sundargarh]] district.

cr.a: Govern britànic de l'Índia / Government of British India

bit-adini.t: Bit Adini, an Aramaean kingdom on the Euphrates bend whose fall in 856 BCE opened Syria to Assyrian armies.
bit-adini.o: After the [[e:late-bronze-age-collapse|Late Bronze Age collapse]], [[e:til-barsip|Til Barsip]] at Tell Ahmar was the Luwian city of Masuwari. In the 10th century BCE Aramaean tribes took control, and the land on both banks of the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] became Bit Adini, the House of Adini, controlling a key river crossing.
bit-adini.r: Bit Adini combined Aramaean tribal leadership with older Luwian urban traditions, and its rulers raised fortified towns. King [[e:ahuni|Ahuni]] led resistance to [[e:ashurnasirpal-ii|Ashurnasirpal II]] and [[e:shalmaneser-iii|Shalmaneser III]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]], forming alliances with [[s:kingdom-of-carchemish|Carchemish]] and other Syrian kingdoms.
bit-adini.e: [[e:shalmaneser-iii|Shalmaneser III]] captured [[e:til-barsip|Til Barsip]] in 856 BCE, renamed it Kar-Shalmaneser and made it an Assyrian base, with palaces decorated with wall paintings. [[e:ahuni|Ahuni]] was deported to [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]].

byzantine-spania.t: The East Roman foothold on Spain's south-east coast, won by Justinian in 552 and held for some seventy years against the Visigoths.
byzantine-spania.o: In 552 the Visigothic noble [[e:athanagild|Athanagild]], rebelling against King [[e:agila-i|Agila]], sought help from Justinian. An imperial force under the elderly patrician [[e:liberius-praetorian-prefect|Liberius]] landed in the south-east, and in the following years the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] seized a coastal strip from around Cartagena to Málaga and beyond, organised as the province of Spania.
byzantine-spania.r: Spania was run by a magister militum based at [[e:carthago-nova|Carthago Nova]], and an inscription of 589 records the governor Comenciolus repairing the city's defences. It formed part of Justinian's restoration of the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]] in the West, linked to [[s:praetorian-prefecture-of-africa|Byzantine Africa]]. Its population was Hispano-Roman and Catholic, and Byzantine authority was mainly military and fiscal.
byzantine-spania.e: Visigothic kings steadily pushed the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] back. [[e:liuvigild|Leovigild]] retook inland areas, [[e:sisebut|Sisebut]] captured Málaga around 615, and [[e:suintila|Suintila]] expelled the last imperial forces around 624. [[e:carthago-nova|Carthago Nova]] was destroyed in the fighting.

brandenburger-gold-coast.t: Brandenburg-Prussia's short-lived colony on the Gold Coast, centred on the fort of Gross Friedrichsburg near Cape Three Points.
brandenburger-gold-coast.o: The Elector [[e:frederick-william-elector-of-brandenburg|Frederick William]] of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] chartered the [[e:brandenburg-african-company|Brandenburg African Company]] in 1682, hoping to share in the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|Atlantic trade]]. An expedition under [[e:otto-friedrich-von-der-groeben|Otto Friedrich von der Groeben]] reached the [[e:ahanta-people|Ahanta]] coast and in 1683 founded [[e:gross-friedrichsburg|Gross Friedrichsburg]] at [[e:princes-town-ghana|Pokesu]] (Princes Town), after treaties with local chiefs. Smaller posts followed at Takrama and at Accada, where [[e:fort-dorothea|Fort Dorothea]] was built.
brandenburger-gold-coast.r: The colony traded guns and cloth for gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and slaves, many of them shipped to the Danish island of [[e:saint-thomas-u-s-virgin-islands|St Thomas]] in the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]]. Its garrisons were tiny and depended on alliances with [[e:ahanta-people|Ahanta]] leaders. The company was always short of capital and ships, and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] rivals from the [[s:dutch-gold-coast|Dutch Gold Coast]] obstructed its trade.
brandenburger-gold-coast.e: King [[e:frederick-william-i-of-prussia|Frederick William I of Prussia]], uninterested in overseas ventures, sold the posts to the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] in 1717.
