The [[e:ahanta-people|Ahanta]] merchant [[e:jan-conny|Jan Conny]] held [[e:gross-friedrichsburg|Gross Friedrichsburg]] against them until 1724. The fort, renamed Fort [[e:jayapura|Hollandia]], survives as a ruin at [[e:princes-town-ghana|Princes Town]].

baghal-state.t: A Panwar Rajput hill state of the Simla Hills, ruled from Arki, whose palace holds noted Pahari murals.
baghal-state.o: Baghal was one of the [[e:simla-hill-states|Simla Hill States]], ruled by [[e:parmar-rajputs|Panwar]] [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]] who claimed descent from the Paramaras of Dhar. Rana [[e:sabha-libya|Sabha]] Chand founded the capital at Arki in 1643.
baghal-state.r: The Ranas ruled a small hill territory of terraced farms. [[s:gorkha-kingdom|Gorkha]] forces from [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] occupied it from 1803 until the British expelled them in 1815, after which Baghal held a sanad of British protection. The Arki palace is known for its 19th century wall paintings in the Pahari style.
baghal-state.e: Baghal joined the new province of [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in 1948. Arki is now a town in Solan district.

bruttii.t: Oscan-speaking people who broke away from the Lucanians in 356 BCE and dominated the toe of Italy, Hannibal's last stronghold.
bruttii.o: [[e:diodorus-siculus|Diodorus]] says that in 356 BCE runaway slaves and herdsmen in the mountains of [[e:calabria|Calabria]], then under Lucanian control, rebelled and formed a new people, the Bruttii. The story may simplify a revolt of a subject population, but by the late 4th century BCE they were an independent federation.
bruttii.r: Their capital was [[e:cosenza|Consentia]] (Cosenza). They lived in hill towns and drew wealth from the [[e:sila-calabria|Sila]] forest, producing pitch and [[e:timber|timber]]. They captured Greek cities including [[s:hipponion|Hipponion]] and [[e:terina|Terina]] and minted fine coins. They fought [[e:alexander-i-of-epirus|Alexander of Epirus]] and joined Pyrrhus against [[e:rome|Rome]].
bruttii.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] subdued them by 270 BCE and took half the [[e:sila-calabria|Sila]]. They joined [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] after Cannae, and [[e:bruttium|Bruttium]] was his last base in [[e:italy|Italy]] until he left in 203 BCE. As punishment they lost land and status; Roman writers said they were reduced to serving as attendants to magistrates.

bazi-dynasty.t: A short Babylonian dynasty of three kings from the house of Bazi, reigning for about twenty years around 1000 BCE.
bazi-dynasty.o: The Bazi Dynasty took its name from Bit-Bazi, a family or tribal group probably of Kassite descent. Its founder, [[e:eulmash-shakin-shumi|Eulmash-shakin-shumi]], became king of [[e:babylon|Babylon]] around 1004 BCE after the end of the [[s:second-sealand-dynasty|Second Sealand Dynasty]].
bazi-dynasty.r: Very little is known of these reigns beyond king lists and a few chronicle entries and kudurru inscriptions. [[e:eulmash-shakin-shumi|Eulmash-shakin-shumi]] ruled for about seventeen years; he was followed briefly by [[e:ninurta-kudurri-usur-i|Ninurta-kudurri-usur I]] and [[e:shirikti-shuqamuna|Shirikti-Shuqamuna]]. [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]] remained weakened by Aramean settlement and poor harvests, and the kings had limited authority beyond the main cities.
bazi-dynasty.e: Around 985 BCE the dynasty was followed by a single Elamite king, [[e:mar-biti-apla-usur|Mar-biti-apla-usur]], and then by the [[s:dynasty-of-e|Dynasty of E]].

bara-kingdom.t: The cattle-herding Bara people of southern-central Madagascar, ruled by Zafimanely nobles in several rival kingdoms.
bara-kingdom.o: The Bara occupied the grasslands of south-central [[e:madagascar|Madagascar]] around [[e:ihosy|Ihosy]], where a ruling house, the Zafimanely, established authority over [[e:cattle|cattle]]-herding clans by the 17th century. Tradition links the Zafimanely to the dynasties of the south-east.
bara-kingdom.r: Bara society was organised around [[e:cattle|cattle]], which measured wealth and were central to ritual, and around warrior values, including cattle raiding as a test of manhood. Power was divided among several Zafimanely chiefs rather than a single state. Little written evidence exists before the 19th century.
bara-kingdom.e: The [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]] established posts in Bara country in the 19th century but never fully controlled it. French forces subdued the region around 1900. The Bara remain one of [[e:madagascar|Madagascar's]] main pastoral peoples.

british-togoland.t: The western part of German Togoland, ruled by Britain from the Gold Coast, whose 1956 plebiscite made it the first trust territory to join an independent state.
british-togoland.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and [[e:france|France]] divided [[s:german-togoland|German Togoland]] in 1916, [[e:britain|Britain]] taking a strip along the western border with the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast Colony]]. In 1922 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] confirmed it as a British mandate, and after 1946 it became a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory. It included part of the [[e:ewe-people|Ewe]] [[e:bantustan|homeland]] and northern areas linked to [[s:kingdom-of-dagbon|Dagbon]] and [[s:mamprugu|Mamprugu]].
british-togoland.r: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] administered the territory as part of the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]], the north with the [[s:northern-territories-of-the-gold-coast|Northern Territories of the Gold Coast]] and the south from the colony, with Ho as the main southern centre. Cocoa farming spread in the south. The division of the [[e:ewe-people|Ewe]] between British [[s:german-togoland|Togoland]], [[s:french-togoland|French Togoland]] and the [[e:gold-coast|Gold Coast]] fed an Ewe unification movement that petitioned the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]].
british-togoland.e: In a UN plebiscite on 9 May 1956 a majority voted for union with the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]], though most southern [[e:ewe-people|Ewe]] districts voted against. The territory became part of independent [[e:ghana|Ghana]] in 1957; its southern part formed the core of the [[e:volta-river|Volta]] Region, while the north joined the Northern Region.

cr.a: Original: Acts of Union 1800 Vector: Yaddah

black-sea-soviet-republic.t: A short-lived Soviet republic of 1918 on the Black Sea coast around Novorossiysk, soon merged into the Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic.
black-sea-soviet-republic.o: In March 1918 the [[e:communist-party-of-the-soviet-union|Bolsheviks]] of [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] [[e:governorate|Governorate]], a narrow coastal province including [[e:novorossiysk|Novorossiysk]], [[e:tuapse|Tuapse]] and [[e:sochi|Sochi]], proclaimed the Black Sea Soviet Republic as an autonomous part of the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]] during the early months of the Civil War.
black-sea-soviet-republic.r: The republic was run by a council of commissars at [[e:novorossiysk|Novorossiysk]], relying on sailors of the [[e:black-sea-fleet|Black Sea Fleet]] and local [[e:red-guards-russia|Red Guards]]. It struggled with food shortages and with anti-Bolshevik forces. Little is known of its administration.
black-sea-soviet-republic.e: After about two months, in May 1918, it was merged with the [[s:kuban-soviet-republic|Kuban Soviet Republic]] to form the [[s:kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic|Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic]]. The coast passed to the [[e:white-movement|Whites]] later in 1918, and Soviet rule returned only in 1920.

bilkha-state.t: A small Kathi state near Junagadh, held by a branch of the Vala Kathis of Jetpur.
bilkha-state.o: Bilkha was formed around 1760 as a share of the lands of the Vala [[e:kathi-people|Kathis]], who also ruled [[s:jetpur-state|Jetpur State]]. It was one of many small Kathi holdings in south-central [[e:kathiawar|Saurashtra]].
bilkha-state.r: Little is recorded about Bilkha beyond its listing as a minor state of the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] held by [[e:kathi-people|Kathi Darbars]].
bilkha-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Bilkha was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948; the village is now in [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]] district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

bailiwick-of-jersey.t: The largest Channel Island, a self-governing Crown Dependency that has stayed loyal to the English crown since the loss of Normandy in 1204.
bailiwick-of-jersey.o: Jersey was part of the [[s:duchy-of-normandy|Duchy of Normandy]] from 933. After [[e:john-king-of-england|King John]] lost mainland Normandy in 1204, the island remained with the English crown and became a separate bailiwick under a warden, later a lieutenant governor, with a bailiff heading its Royal Court.
bailiwick-of-jersey.r: Jersey kept Norman customary law and its own States assembly. [[e:mont-orgueil|Mont Orgueil Castle]] defended it against frequent French attacks. The island traded in cod from [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]], knitted woollens and later [[e:potato|potatoes]] and [[e:cattle|cattle]], and grew into a financial centre. [[e:charles-ii-of-england|Charles II]] was proclaimed king there in 1649, and the French were defeated at the [[e:battle-of-jersey|Battle of Jersey]] in 1781.
bailiwick-of-jersey.e: [[e:germany|Germany]] occupied Jersey from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a [[e:crown-dependencies|Crown Dependency]] outside the [[s:united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-ireland|United Kingdom]], with its own parliament, the [[e:states-of-jersey|States Assembly]], and its own laws and taxes.

banate-of-severin.t: Hungarian frontier province at the Iron Gates of the Danube, a defensive march against Bulgarians, Cumans and later the Ottomans.
banate-of-severin.o: King [[e:andrew-ii-of-hungary|Andrew II's]] son [[e:bela-iv-of-hungary|Béla]] set up the banate around 1228–1233, in lands taken from [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] and the [[e:cumans|Cumans]] east of the [[e:iron-gates|Iron Gates]], around the fortress of [[e:drobeta-turnu-severin|Severin]] (Drobeta-Turnu Severin) built on Roman ruins. In 1247 Béla IV granted it to the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]], though they soon left.
banate-of-severin.r: A royal ban commanded the castle and the border, collecting tribute from the Romanian voivodes and knezes beyond, such as the [[s:voivodeship-of-litovoi|Voivodeship of Litovoi]]. Control shifted repeatedly with [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] and later the [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Principality of Wallachia]], whose rulers took the title ban of [[e:drobeta-turnu-severin|Severin]]. In the 15th century [[e:hungary|Hungary]] held it against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], and [[e:john-hunyadi|John Hunyadi]] was ban.
banate-of-severin.e: Ottoman raids steadily wore it down. [[e:drobeta-turnu-severin|Severin]] fortress fell to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1524, two years before [[e:battle-of-mohacs|Mohács]], and the banate ceased to exist. The region passed to [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]] as [[e:oltenia|Oltenia's]] western edge.

british-burma.t: Burma under British rule, built up through three wars from 1824 and governed as part of British India until 1937, then as a separate colony.
british-burma.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] took [[s:mrauk-u-kingdom|Arakan]] and [[e:tanintharyi-region|Tenasserim]] after the [[e:first-anglo-burmese-war|First Anglo-Burmese War]], settled by the [[e:treaty-of-yandabo|Treaty of Yandabo]] in 1826. The [[e:second-anglo-burmese-war|Second Anglo-Burmese War]] in 1852 added [[e:lower-burma|Lower Burma]] with [[e:yangon|Rangoon]]. In 1885 to 1886 [[e:britain|Britain]] annexed the rest of the [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]]'s kingdom after the [[e:third-anglo-burmese-war|Third Anglo-Burmese War]].
british-burma.r: [[s:myanmar|Burma]] was governed as a province of [[s:british-raj|British India]], with [[e:yangon|Rangoon]] as its capital. The [[e:irrawaddy-river|Irrawaddy]] delta was cleared for [[e:rice|rice]], making [[e:burma|Burma]] the world's largest rice exporter, worked by Burman migrants and financed by Indian [[e:chettiar|Chettiar]] moneylenders. Teak, oil and rubies were exploited. Buddhist associations and students led nationalist protests, and the [[e:saya-san|Saya San]] rebellion of 1930 to 1932 was suppressed.
british-burma.e: [[s:myanmar|Burma]] was separated from [[e:india|India]] in 1937. [[e:japan|Japan]] occupied it from 1942, creating the [[s:state-of-burma|State of Burma]], but [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] returned in 1945. Negotiations with [[e:aung-san|Aung San's]] [[e:anti-fascist-peoples-freedom-league|Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League]] led to independence on 4 January 1948 as the Union of [[e:burma|Burma]].

banu-ifran-emirate.t: A Zenata Berber emirate centred on Tlemcen, born from a Kharijite revolt and later a power in Morocco under Córdoba's overlordship.
banu-ifran-emirate.o: The [[e:banu-ifran|Banu Ifran]] were a [[e:zanata-berbers|Zenata Berber]] tribe of western [[e:algeria|Algeria]]. In the great [[e:berbers|Berber]] revolt against the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] from 740, they embraced [[e:sufriyya|Sufri Kharijism]], and around 742 their leader [[e:abu-qurra|Abu Qurra]] established a state at [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]], where he was proclaimed [[e:imam|imam]].
banu-ifran-emirate.r: [[e:abu-qurra|Abu Qurra]] raised large armies and joined the siege of the Abbasid governor at Tobna in 772. [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]] fell to Idris I of the [[s:idrisid-dynasty|Idrisid dynasty]] around 790, but the tribe stayed powerful. In the 10th century [[e:yala-ibn-muhammad|Ya'la ibn Muhammad]] founded the town of Ifkan and allied with the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]] against the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]]. Later [[e:banu-ifran|Ifranid]] [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled [[e:sale|Salé]] and [[e:chellah|Chellah]] and fought the [[s:barghawata|Barghawata]].
banu-ifran-emirate.e: The [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]] conquered the [[e:banu-ifran|Ifranid]] territories in the second half of the 11th century, and the tribe was dispersed or absorbed into the new order. Ifranid groups survived in the [[e:maghreb|Maghreb]] and [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]], where some served as soldiers.

bosporan-kingdom.t: Long-lived Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait that fed Athens with Black Sea grain and survived as a Roman client state until the coming of the Huns.
bosporan-kingdom.o: Greek colonies on both sides of the [[e:kerch-strait|Cimmerian Bosporus]], such as [[e:kerch|Panticapaeum]], [[e:phanagoria|Phanagoria]] and [[s:theodosia|Theodosia]], united under the [[e:archaeanactids|Archaeanactid dynasty]] around 480 BCE. In 438 BCE power passed to [[e:spartocus-i|Spartocus I]], whose [[e:spartocid-dynasty|Spartocid]] descendants ruled for more than three centuries from [[e:panticapaeum|Panticapaeum]], modern Kerch, extending control over local [[e:sindi|Sindians]] and [[e:maeotians|Maeotians]].
bosporan-kingdom.r: The [[e:spartocid-dynasty|Spartocids]] called themselves archons of the Greek cities and kings of the native peoples. Wealth came from grain, fish and slaves shipped to the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]: [[e:leucon-i|Leucon I]] (389-349 BCE) granted [[s:athens|Athens]] tax-free grain purchases and was honoured there. Rich kurgan burials show a blend of Greek and Scythian and Sarmatian culture.
bosporan-kingdom.e: Under pressure from the [[e:scythians|Scythians]], Paerisades V handed the kingdom to [[e:mithridates-vi-of-pontus|Mithridates VI of Pontus]] c. 108 BCE. Later kings, such as [[e:aspurgus|Aspurgus]] and his successors, ruled as clients of [[e:rome|Rome]]. The kingdom declined in the 3rd century CE and was overrun by the [[e:huns|Huns]] in the 370s.
bosporan-kingdom.re: Ancient Greek religion, later also Christianity and Judaism

bhoi-dynasty.t: A short-lived dynasty that took the throne of Odisha after the Gajapatis, whose fall opened the region to the Karrani Afghans.
bhoi-dynasty.o: [[e:govinda-vidyadhara|Govinda Vidyadhara]], a minister of the [[s:gajapati-kingdom|Gajapati Kingdom]], killed the last heirs of [[e:prataparudra-deva|Prataparudra Deva]] and seized the throne at [[e:cuttack|Cuttack]] in 1541. His family, the Bhoi dynasty, inherited a kingdom already reduced by losses to the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]] and the [[s:golconda-sultanate|Golconda Sultanate]].
bhoi-dynasty.r: The Bhoi rulers continued the Gajapati title and the royal role in the cult of [[e:jagannath|Jagannath]] at Puri, but faced constant revolts by nobles and pressure from the [[s:golconda-sultanate|Golconda Sultanate]] and the Afghan rulers of [[e:bengal|Bengal]]. Their short reigns were dominated by palace intrigue.
bhoi-dynasty.e: Around 1559 to 1560 the minister [[e:mukunda-deva|Mukunda Deva]] overthrew the last Bhoi rulers. He was defeated by the [[e:karrani-dynasty|Karrani Afghans]] of [[e:bengal|Bengal]] in 1568, ending independent [[e:odisha|Odisha]]. Bhoi descendants were later recognised as rajas of the [[s:kingdom-of-khurda|Kingdom of Khurda]].

bit-bahiani.t: Bit Bahiani, an Aramaean kingdom of the upper Khabur centred on Guzana, famous for the sculpted palace of King Kapara at Tell Halaf.
bit-bahiani.o: Aramaean tribes took over the upper [[e:khabur-river|Khabur]] in the 10th century BCE, and the House of Bahiani ruled from [[e:tell-halaf|Guzana]], at Tell Halaf on the Syrian-Turkish border. In 894 BCE its king Abi-salamu paid tribute to [[e:adad-nirari-ii|Adad-nirari II]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]].
bit-bahiani.r: King [[e:kapara|Kapara]] built a palace whose facade had colossal statues of gods on animals and dozens of carved stone reliefs. Excavated by [[e:max-von-oppenheim|Max von Oppenheim]] from 1911, they were shattered by bombing in [[e:berlin|Berlin]] in 1943 and painstakingly restored. A bilingual statue of the ruler [[e:hadad-yithi|Hadad-yith'i]] in Assyrian and [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] shows the kingdom adapting to Assyrian rule.
bit-bahiani.e: Bit Bahiani became an Assyrian [[e:vassal|vassal]] and finally a province c. 808 BCE. [[e:tell-halaf|Guzana]] is the Gozan of the Bible, where [[e:israelites|Israelites]] were deported after the fall of [[e:samaria|Samaria]].

bibroci.t: British people named only once by Julius Caesar, among the groups that surrendered to him during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
bibroci.o: Known only from [[e:commentarii-de-bello-gallico|Caesar's Gallic War]], the Bibroci were one of five British peoples, with the [[s:iceni|Cenimagni]], [[s:segontiaci|Segontiaci]], [[s:ancalites|Ancalites]] and [[s:cassi|Cassi]], who sent envoys to surrender to him in 54 BCE after the [[s:trinovantes|Trinovantes]] had come under his protection.
bibroci.r: Nothing is recorded of their government, rulers or way of life. Their territory is unknown; scholars have suggested places in the [[e:river-thames|Thames]] valley or in [[e:berkshire|Berkshire]] and [[s:kingdom-of-sussex|Sussex]], but no inscription or coin securely names them.
bibroci.e: They vanish from the record after [[e:julius-caesar|Caesar]]'s account. Their land was presumably absorbed by larger neighbours such as the [[s:atrebates-britain|Atrebates (Britain)]] or the [[s:catuvellauni|Catuvellauni]] before the Roman conquest of 43.

baramba-state.t: A small princely state on the Mahanadi in central Odisha, one of the Orissa Tributary States until 1948.
baramba-state.o: Tradition dates the state to the early 14th century, but little is reliably known about its founding.
baramba-state.r: Baramba was a small agricultural state west of [[e:cuttack|Cuttack]], known for its handloom weaving. It paid tribute to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] and from 1803 to the British as one of the [[e:orissa-tributary-states|Orissa Tributary Mahals]]. Its internal history is poorly recorded.
baramba-state.e: Baramba merged into [[e:odisha|Orissa]] on 1 January 1948 and is now in [[e:cuttack|Cuttack]] district.

basutoland.t: The British territory that preserved Moshoeshoe's mountain kingdom from absorption into South Africa, and became independent Lesotho.
basutoland.o: At [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]]'s request, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] annexed the [[s:basotho-kingdom|Basotho Kingdom]] in March 1868 to save it from conquest by the [[s:orange-free-state|Orange Free State]], which had already taken much of its lowland farmland. The boundaries were fixed by the [[e:second-treaty-of-aliwal-north|Convention of Aliwal North]] in 1869, and in 1871 the territory was handed to the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]].
basutoland.r: Cape attempts to disarm the [[e:sotho-people|Basotho]] caused the Gun War of 1880-1881, which the Basotho effectively won, and in 1884 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] resumed direct rule as a [[e:high-commission-territories|High Commission]] territory from [[e:maseru|Maseru]]. Paramount chiefs of [[e:moshoeshoe-i|Moshoeshoe]]'s line, among them [[e:letsie-i|Letsie I]] and [[e:lerotholi|Lerotholi]], kept wide authority, and a [[e:basutoland-national-council|Basutoland National Council]] was created in 1903. Hut tax and poor land made the territory a labour reserve for South African mines.
basutoland.e: Basutoland was never incorporated into [[s:republic-of-south-africa|South Africa]]. After the rise of parties such as the [[e:basotho-congress-party|Basutoland Congress Party]] and constitutional reforms, it became independent as the [[s:kingdom-of-lesotho|Kingdom of Lesotho]] on 4 October 1966 under [[e:moshoeshoe-ii|Moshoeshoe II]].

barolong-chiefdom.t: One of the oldest Tswana chiefdoms, whose branches at Thaba Nchu and Mafikeng were drawn into the struggles between Boers and Britain.
barolong-chiefdom.o: The [[e:barolong|Barolong]] are among the oldest [[e:tswana-people|Tswana]] groups, settled in the southern Kalahari margins and the [[e:molopo-river|Molopo]] valley. Under the 18th-century ruler Tau they became a powerful chiefdom, but after his death they split into branches, chief among them the Ratlou, Tshidi, Seleka and Rapulana.
barolong-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled large towns through ward headmen and the kgotla assembly, with [[e:cattle|cattle]] herding and cereal farming as the economy. During the wars of the 1820s the Seleka under [[e:moroka-ii|Moroka]] moved to [[s:thaba-nchu|Thaba Nchu]], where they aided the [[e:voortrekkers|Voortrekkers]] in 1836. [[e:methodism|Methodist]] missionaries had a strong influence. The Tshidi under [[e:montshiwa|Montshiwa]] settled at [[e:mahikeng|Mafikeng]] and resisted [[e:boers|Boer]] encroachment.
barolong-chiefdom.e: Conflict with the [[e:boers|Boer]] statelets of [[s:stellaland|Stellaland]] and [[s:goshen|Goshen]] led [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] to intervene, and in 1885 [[e:barolong|Barolong]] lands were divided between [[s:british-bechuanaland|British Bechuanaland]] and the [[s:bechuanaland-protectorate|Bechuanaland Protectorate]]. [[e:mahikeng|Mafikeng]] later became famous for its siege in the [[e:second-boer-war|Second Boer War]].

banate-of-bosnia.t: Medieval Bosnian state ruled by bans under nominal Hungarian overlordship, known for its silver mines and its own Bosnian Church.
banate-of-bosnia.o: [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] appears as a distinct land in the 10th century. In 1154 [[e:ban-boric|Ban Borić]] is the first named ruler, a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of [[e:hungary|Hungary]]. [[e:ban-kulin|Ban Kulin]] (c. 1180–1204) made it effectively independent, and his 1189 trade charter to [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]] is one of the oldest documents in the Serbian-Croatian language.
banate-of-bosnia.r: The ban ruled with a council of nobles from seats around [[e:visoko|Visoko]]. The [[e:bosnian-church|Bosnian Church]], an independent church condemned by [[e:rome|Rome]] as heretical, coexisted with [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] and Orthodoxy. Under [[e:stephen-ii-kotromanic|Stephen II Kotromanić]] (1322–1353) [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] annexed [[s:zachlumia|Zachlumia]] and the land up to the [[e:cetina|Cetina]], and [[e:saxons|Saxon]] miners opened [[e:silver|silver]] and lead mines at [[e:srebrenica|Srebrenica]] and [[e:fojnica|Fojnica]], trading through [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]].
banate-of-bosnia.e: In 1377 Ban [[e:tvrtko-i-of-bosnia|Tvrtko I]] had himself crowned king at Mile, claiming the Serbian crown as well, and the banate became the [[s:kingdom-of-bosnia|Kingdom of Bosnia]].

bhajji-state.t: A small Rajput hill state on the Sutlej north of Shimla, ruled from Seoni, one of the Simla Hill States.
bhajji-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500 and links it to the house of [[s:suket-state|Suket]], but little is reliably known of its origins.
bhajji-state.r: Bhajji was a small mountain state above the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]], with its capital at Seoni. It was occupied by the [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]] in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Its history is poorly recorded.
bhajji-state.e: Bhajji merged into [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948 and is now part of [[e:shimla|Shimla]] district.

banswara-state.t: A Guhila Rajput state in the Vagad hills of southern Rajasthan, created in the 16th century when Dungarpur was divided between two brothers.
banswara-state.o: After Rawal [[e:udai-singh-of-dungarpur|Udai Singh of Dungarpur]] State was killed at [[e:battle-of-khanwa|Khanwa]] in 1527, his lands were divided between his sons. [[e:jagmal-singh|Jagmal Singh]] took the eastern part across the Mahi river and founded Banswara, named, by tradition, for its bamboo forests.
banswara-state.r: Banswara was a hilly, forested state with a mostly [[e:bhils|Bhil]] population, crossed by the Mahi river. Its Maharawals accepted Mughal and then [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] overlordship and signed a treaty with the British in 1818. The state remained largely rural and poor, with temples and lakes around its capital.
banswara-state.e: Banswara joined the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in 1948 and is now a district of [[e:rajasthan|Rajasthan]], where the Mahi Bajaj Sagar dam was later built.

bit-amukani.t: A Chaldean tribal state of central Babylonia whose leader Nabu-mukin-zeri seized the throne of Babylon in 732 BCE.
bit-amukani.o: Bit-Amukani, 'House of Amukanu', was one of the three main [[e:chaldean-tribes|Chaldean tribes]] that settled in [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]] in the early first millennium BCE. It held land along the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] in central and southern Babylonia, around the town of Sapia (Shapiya). The [[e:chaldean-empire|Chaldeans]] first appear in Assyrian annals in the 9th century BCE.
bit-amukani.r: [[e:chaldean-tribes|Chaldean tribes]] were led by sheikhs who controlled walled towns, date groves and trade routes to the Gulf, and they adopted Babylonian names and culture while keeping tribal organisation. In 732 BCE, after [[e:nabonassar|Nabonassar's]] son had been murdered by a usurper, [[e:nabu-mukin-zeri|Nabu-mukin-zeri of Bit-Amukani]] seized the throne of [[e:babylon|Babylon]], ending the [[s:dynasty-of-e|Dynasty of E]].
bit-amukani.e: Tiglath-Pileser III of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] besieged Sapia in 731 BCE and by 729 BCE had overthrown [[e:nabu-mukin-zeri|Nabu-mukin-zeri]] and taken [[e:babylon|Babylon]]. Bit-Amukani later joined revolts against [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]], including that of [[e:shamash-shum-ukin|Shamash-shum-ukin]], and by the mid-7th century it vanished into Babylonian society.

belize-settlement.t: British logwood and mahogany cutters' settlement on the Bay of Honduras, tolerated by Spain for over a century and the origin of modern Belize.
belize-settlement.o: Tradition dates the first British settlement to 1638 and links it to the buccaneer Peter Wallace, but reliable evidence of logwood cutters, the [[e:baymen|Baymen]], on the [[s:belize|Belize]] River begins in the mid-17th century. Former buccaneers turned to cutting logwood, a valuable dye wood, on a coast [[e:spain|Spain]] claimed but did not occupy.
belize-settlement.r: [[e:spain|Spain]] never recognised British [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] but allowed [[e:timber|timber]] cutting under the treaties of [[e:paris|Paris]] in 1763 and [[e:versailles|Versailles]] in 1783 and the [[e:convention-of-london-1786|Convention of London]] of 1786. The [[e:baymen|Baymen]] governed themselves through a Public Meeting and elected magistrates, joined from 1786 by a British superintendent. The economy moved from logwood to mahogany, worked by enslaved Africans in small forest gangs. Settlers repulsed a Spanish attack at the [[e:battle-of-st-georges-caye|Battle of St George's Caye]] in 1798.
belize-settlement.e: After Central American independence, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] extended its control and the settlement's boundaries. [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] later claimed the territory, a dispute that still lingers. In 1862 the settlement was formally declared the [[s:british-honduras|Colony of British Honduras]].

british-military-administration-of-libya.t: British wartime and post-war rule over Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, which ended with Libya's UN-sponsored independence in 1951.
british-military-administration-of-libya.o: [[e:commonwealth-of-nations|British Commonwealth]] forces drove the [[e:axis-powers|Axis]] from [[e:cyrenaica|Cyrenaica]] in November 1942 and took [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] in January 1943. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] set up military administrations in both provinces, while [[e:france|France]] held the [[s:fezzan-ghadames-military-territory|Fezzan-Ghadames Military Territory]].
british-military-administration-of-libya.r: Under the laws of war, the British largely retained Italian law and administration and many Italian officials, while allowing Libyan political parties to form. The future of the former colony was debated by the victorious powers; in 1949 the [[e:bevin-sforza-plan|Bevin-Sforza plan]] for trusteeships was rejected by the [[e:united-nations-general-assembly|UN General Assembly]].
british-military-administration-of-libya.e: In November 1949 the UN decided that [[e:libya|Libya]] should become independent by 1952, sending [[e:adrian-pelt|Adrian Pelt]] as commissioner. [[e:cyrenaica|Cyrenaica]] became the [[s:emirate-of-cyrenaica|Emirate of Cyrenaica]] in 1949, and Libya gained independence as the [[s:kingdom-of-libya|Kingdom of Libya]] on 24 December 1951.

bijapur-sultanate.t: The Adil Shahi sultanate of the western Deccan, builder of the Gol Gumbaz, one of the largest domes in the world.
bijapur-sultanate.o: [[e:yusuf-adil-shah|Yusuf Adil Shah]], a Bahmani governor of reportedly Turkic or Persian origin, made himself independent at [[e:bijapur|Bijapur]] around 1490 as the [[s:bahmani-sultanate|Bahmani Sultanate]] disintegrated. He briefly held [[e:goa|Goa]], which was lost to the Portuguese in 1510, and founded a dynasty that dominated the western [[e:deccan|Deccan]] for nearly two centuries.
bijapur-sultanate.r: The [[e:adil-shah|Adil Shahs]] alternated between Shia and [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] allegiance and employed Persian, African and [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] officers; [[e:shahaji-bhonsle|Shahaji Bhonsle]], father of [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]], served them. [[e:ibrahim-adil-shah-ii|Ibrahim Adil Shah II]] was a musician and patron of the arts, author of the [[e:kitab-i-nauras|Kitab-i-Nauras]]. [[e:bijapur|Bijapur's]] [[e:ibrahim-rauza|Ibrahim Rauza]] and the [[e:gol-gumbaz|Gol Gumbaz]], tomb of [[e:muhammad-adil-shah|Muhammad Adil Shah]], are architectural highlights.
bijapur-sultanate.e: [[e:bijapur|Bijapur]] joined the coalition that defeated the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara Empire]] at [[e:battle-of-talikota|Talikota]] in 1565 and expanded south. Squeezed by the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] and the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha Kingdom]], it fell to [[e:aurangzeb|Aurangzeb]] after a long siege in 1686, and the region became a Mughal province.

byeonhan.t: A confederacy of twelve small states on the lower Nakdong river, famed for producing iron that it traded across the Korea Strait and to Chinese commanderies.
byeonhan.o: Byeonhan, also called Byeonjin, took shape in the 1st century BCE in the southeast of the peninsula as one of the three Samhan confederacies, alongside [[s:mahan|Mahan]] and [[s:jinhan|Jinhan]]. Chinese records list twelve member states, sharing customs and language closely with neighbouring Jinhan.
byeonhan.r: Each statelet was ruled by its own chief, with walled settlements and [[e:rice|rice]] and [[e:millet|millet]] farming. Its iron was its great asset: Byeonhan supplied iron to [[s:mahan|Mahan]], Wa in [[e:japan|Japan]] and the [[e:lelang-commandery|Lelang]] and [[e:daifang-commandery|Daifang]] [[e:commandery|commanderies]], and iron ingots served as currency. Chinese writers also mention the custom of flattening infants' heads and large bird feathers placed in burials.
byeonhan.e: From the 1st century CE the Byeonhan statelets developed into the [[s:gaya-confederacy|Gaya confederacy]], traditionally dated to 42 when [[e:suro-of-geumgwan-gaya|King Suro]] founded [[s:geumgwan-gaya|Geumgwan Gaya]] at [[e:gimhae|Gimhae]]. Archaeology shows a gradual change rather than a sharp break.

bakhtiari-confederation.t: A great confederation of Lur nomadic tribes in the Zagros whose khans grew rich from oil and helped win Iran's constitutional revolution.
bakhtiari-confederation.o: The [[e:bakhtiari|Bakhtiari]] are [[e:lurs|Lur]] tribes who migrate between winter pastures in [[e:khuzestan|Khuzestan]] and summer pastures in the high [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]]. By the 18th century they were organised into two main divisions, the [[e:haft-lang|Haft Lang]] and [[e:chahar-lang|Chahar Lang]], under khans who supplied troops to Safavid, [[e:afsharid-empire|Afsharid]] and [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] rulers.
bakhtiari-confederation.r: In 1867 [[e:hosseinqoli-khan-bakhtiari|Hossein Qoli Khan]] was recognised by the [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] state as ilkhan, paramount chief, unifying the confederation; he was executed in 1882 on the order of Prince [[e:zell-e-soltan|Zell-e Soltan]]. The khans negotiated with British companies over the Lynch road and, after oil was found at [[e:masjed-soleyman|Masjed Soleyman]] in 1908, received a share in the oil companies working their lands. In 1909 [[e:bakhtiari|Bakhtiari]] forces under [[e:ali-qoli-khan-bakhtiari|Sardar As'ad II]] and [[e:najaf-qoli-khan-bakhtiari|Samsam al-Saltaneh]] marched on [[e:tehran|Tehran]] and restored the constitution.
bakhtiari-confederation.e: [[e:reza-shah|Reza Shah's]] [[s:pahlavi-iran|Pahlavi Iran]] disarmed the tribes, forced settlement and executed or imprisoned leading khans by 1934. The [[e:bakhtiari|Bakhtiari]] remain a distinct people; [[e:soraya-esfandiary-bakhtiary|Queen Soraya]] of [[e:middle-persian|Pahlavi]] [[e:iran|Iran]] was of Bakhtiari descent.

bishopric-of-courland.t: Prince-bishopric in western Latvia, founded during the conquest of the Curonians, whose remnant survived as the District of Pilten.
bishopric-of-courland.o: The papal legate [[e:baldwin-of-alna|Baldwin of Alna]] created a bishopric for the [[s:curonians|Curonians]] in 1234 after treaties with Curonian leaders. When [[e:courland|Courland]] was conquered by the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]] in the 1250s and 1260s, the [[e:bishop|bishop]] received about a third of the land, scattered in several districts.
bishopric-of-courland.r: The [[e:bishop|bishop]]'s lands centred on [[e:piltene|Pilten]] and [[e:aizpute|Hasenpoth]], with the cathedral at Hasenpoth (Aizpute). Unlike other Livonian bishops, those of [[e:courland|Courland]] were closely tied to the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], and the chapter was for a time made up of Order priests. Curonian and Latvian peasants worked the estates of German [[e:vassal|vassals]].
bishopric-of-courland.e: In 1559 [[e:johann-von-munchhausen|Bishop Johann von Münchhausen]] sold the bishopric to [[e:frederick-ii-of-denmark|Frederick II of Denmark]], who gave it to his brother [[e:magnus-duke-of-holstein|Magnus of Holstein]]. After Magnus died in 1583, [[e:denmark|Denmark]] sold its rights to Poland-[[e:lithuania|Lithuania]] in 1585, and the territory became the [[s:district-of-pilten|District of Pilten]].

barotseland.t: The Lozi kingdom of the upper Zambezi floodplain, ruled by the Litunga, which kept a special status under British rule until Zambian independence.
barotseland.o: The [[e:lozi-people|Luyi]] (later Lozi) people settled the Bulozi floodplain of the upper [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]], with traditions linking their first ruler, Mbuyu, to the [[e:lunda-empire|Lunda]] world. By the 17th century the [[e:litunga|Litunga]] headed a centralised kingdom that drew on the floodplain's fish, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and cultivated mounds.
barotseland.r: The [[e:litunga|Litunga]] ruled through a council (kuta) of titled officials and a system of state-owned labour and tribute, and moved his court each year from the flooding plain to higher ground in the [[e:kuomboka|Kuomboka]] ceremony. [[e:mulambwa|Mulambwa]] reformed the law in the early 19th century. From about 1840 the kingdom was conquered by the [[s:kololo-kingdom|Makololo]] under [[e:sebetwane|Sebitwane]], but [[e:sipopa|Sipopa]] restored [[e:lozi-people|Lozi]] rule in 1864.
barotseland.e: [[e:lewanika|Lewanika]] signed a concession with the [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company]] in 1890, and Barotseland became a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] within [[s:northern-rhodesia|Northern Rhodesia]] with its own institutions. The 1964 [[e:barotseland-agreement-1964|Barotseland Agreement]] merged it into independent [[e:zambia|Zambia]], a settlement still disputed today.

belgian-congo.t: Belgium's vast central African colony, a paternalistic mining economy whose hasty independence in 1960 led to the Congo Crisis.
belgian-congo.o: After international outrage over abuses in the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]], the Belgian parliament annexed King [[e:leopold-ii|Leopold II's]] personal domain on 15 November 1908. A Colonial Charter placed it under the Belgian government, with a governor-general at [[e:boma|Boma]].
belgian-congo.r: Rule rested on the state, the Catholic missions and large companies, the so-called colonial trinity. [[e:union-miniere-du-haut-katanga|Union Minière du Haut Katanga]] mined [[e:copper|copper]] and cobalt, and uranium from [[e:shinkolobwe|Shinkolobwe]] supplied the [[e:manhattan-project|Manhattan Project]]. Primary schooling and health care spread widely, but Africans were barred from higher posts and university until the 1950s. [[e:simon-kimbangu|Simon Kimbangu's]] prophetic church was repressed. The capital moved to [[e:kinshasa|Léopoldville]] in the 1920s.
belgian-congo.e: Riots in [[e:kinshasa|Léopoldville]] in 1959 led [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]] to grant independence on 30 June 1960, with [[e:joseph-kasavubu|Joseph Kasavubu]] as president and [[e:patrice-lumumba|Patrice Lumumba]] as prime minister. Mutiny and the secession of [[e:katanga|Katanga]] followed within days.

barony-of-chalandritsa.t: Small Frankish barony in the hills south of Patras, one of the original fiefs of the Principality of Achaea.
barony-of-chalandritsa.o: Chalandritsa was among the baronies created in the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] around 1209. It was granted to Robert de la Tremouille, a knight from [[e:france|France]], and held a small number of knight's fiefs in the hill country of [[e:achaea|Achaea]] south of [[s:barony-of-patras|Patras]].
barony-of-chalandritsa.r: The barons owed military service to the prince and had seats in his high court. The Dramelay family later held it for much of the 13th and 14th centuries. Beyond these facts, recorded in the [[e:chronicle-of-the-morea|Chronicle of the Morea]] and Angevin documents, little is known of the barony's internal life.
barony-of-chalandritsa.e: In the final collapse of the principality, Chalandritsa was taken by the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] of the [[s:despotate-of-the-morea|Despotate of the Morea]], under [[e:constantine-xi-palaiologos|Constantine Palaiologos]], in 1429, at the same time as the campaign that won [[s:barony-of-patras|Patras]].

buton-sultanate.t: An island sultanate off southeast Sulawesi, known for its massive Wolio fortress and an unusual elected monarchy that lasted until 1960.
buton-sultanate.o: [[e:buton-island|Buton]]'s chronicles trace its kingdom to the 14th century and a legendary first queen, Wa Kaa Kaa. Placed on the sea route between [[e:java|Java]], [[s:gowa-sultanate|Makassar]] and the [[e:maluku-islands|Moluccas]], it grew as a port and a power over the nearby islands. Its sixth king, [[e:lakilaponto|Lakilaponto]], adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] around 1540 and became [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Murhum.
buton-sultanate.r: [[e:buton-island|Buton]] was governed by a written constitution, the [[e:martabat-tujuh|Martabat Tujuh]], adopted under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] La Elangi in the early 17th century and inspired by [[e:sufism|Sufi]] thought. Sultans were elected by a council of nobles from rotating royal houses and could be deposed. The Wolio fortress, with walls nearly three kilometres long, protected the capital.
buton-sultanate.e: Squeezed between Gowa and [[s:ternate-sultanate|Ternate]], [[e:buton-island|Buton]] allied with the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] from 1613. It kept internal autonomy under [[e:dutch|Dutch]] rule. After the death of the last sultan, [[e:muhammad-falihi-kaimuddin|Muhammad Falihi Kaimuddin]], in 1960, the sultanate ended and its lands became regencies of Southeast [[e:sulawesi|Sulawesi]].

borno-emirate.t: The Kanuri emirate under British rule that continued the ancient Kanem-Bornu monarchy from its new capital at Maiduguri.
borno-emirate.o: After [[s:rabih-az-zubayrs-state|Rabih az-Zubayr]] was killed in 1900, the French and British restored the al-Kanemi dynasty, rulers of the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]] since the early 19th century. In 1902 [[e:abubakar-garbai|Shehu Abubakar Garbai]] moved into British territory and was recognised as ruler of the British part of [[e:bornu|Bornu]]. In 1907 he founded a new capital at [[e:maiduguri|Yerwa]], which grew into the city of Maiduguri.
borno-emirate.r: Under [[e:indirect-rule|indirect rule]] the shehu governed through district heads and Islamic courts, supervised by British officials of the [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]] and later [[s:colonial-nigeria|Colonial Nigeria]]. The [[e:emirate|emirate]] kept [[e:bornu|Bornu's]] court titles and its tradition as a centre of Islamic scholarship. Its economy rested on farming, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and trade across [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]]. [[e:umar-sanda-kyarimi|Shehu Umar Sanda Kyarimi]] reigned from 1937 to 1968.
borno-emirate.e: With Nigerian independence in 1960 the [[e:emirate|emirate]] became part of the [[e:northern-region-nigeria|Northern Region]] and later of [[e:borno-state|Borno State]]. The [[e:shehu-of-borno|Shehu of Borno]] remains one of the most senior traditional rulers in [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]].

bourbon-restoration.t: The return of the Bourbon kings after Napoleon, a constitutional monarchy under Louis XVIII and Charles X that ended in the July Revolution of 1830.
bourbon-restoration.o: After [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] abdication in April 1814 the allies and the [[e:senat-conservateur|French Senate]] restored [[e:louis-xviii|Louis XVIII]], brother of [[e:louis-xvi|Louis XVI]]. He granted the Charter of 1814, which kept a parliament and many revolutionary gains. Napoleon's return in the Hundred Days of 1815 interrupted the regime until [[e:battle-of-waterloo|Waterloo]].
bourbon-restoration.r: [[e:france|France]] had a two-chamber parliament elected by a very small, wealthy electorate. Moderate ministers such as the [[e:armand-emmanuel-du-plessis-duc-de-richelieu|Duke of Richelieu]] paid off war indemnities and ended the allied occupation in 1818, while ultra-royalists pressed for revenge after the [[e:second-white-terror|White Terror]]. Charles X, crowned at [[e:reims|Reims]] in 1825, compensated émigrés and favoured the Church.
bourbon-restoration.e: In July 1830 Charles X issued ordinances dissolving parliament and curbing the press. Three days of revolt in [[e:paris|Paris]] drove him into exile, and [[e:louis-philippe-i|Louis-Philippe of Orléans]] became king, beginning the [[s:july-monarchy|July Monarchy]]. [[e:algiers|Algiers]] had been taken weeks earlier.

bonny-kingdom.t: Ijaw trading state of the eastern Niger delta, one of the busiest slave ports of the 18th century and then a centre of the palm oil trade.
bonny-kingdom.o: Bonny, called Ibani by its people, was founded by [[e:ijaw-people|Ijaw]] migrants on an island near the mouth of the Bonny river, traditionally in the 15th century. By the 17th century it was dealing with Portuguese, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English ships, buying captives from the [[e:igbo-people|Igbo]] hinterland through networks such as the [[s:aro-confederacy|Aro Confederacy]].
bonny-kingdom.r: The [[e:amanyanabo|Amanyanabo]] ruled with the heads of trading houses, which absorbed slaves and could be led by able former slaves. The Pepple dynasty, founded by Perekule in the 18th century, presided over a huge [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] and then a shift to [[e:palm-oil|palm oil]] after abolition. The British consul deposed King [[e:william-dappa-pepple|William Dappa Pepple]] in 1854.
bonny-kingdom.e: In 1869 the former slave and house head [[e:jaja-of-opobo|Jaja]] left Bonny to found the [[s:kingdom-of-opobo|Kingdom of Opobo]], taking much of its trade. Bonny signed a British protection treaty in 1884 and became part of the [[s:oil-rivers-protectorate|Oil Rivers Protectorate]]. It is now a key oil and gas terminal.

bikaner-state.t: The Rathore desert kingdom of northern Rajasthan, founded by a son of Rao Jodha, whose 20th-century Maharaja turned it green with the Ganga Canal.
bikaner-state.o: In 1465 [[e:rao-bika|Rao Bika]], a son of [[e:rao-jodha|Rao Jodha]] of [[s:jodhpur-state|Marwar]], led followers north into the [[e:jangladesh|Jangladesh]] region of the [[e:thar-desert|Thar]] and carved out a kingdom from local [[e:jats|Jat]] and Bhati lands. He founded the city of Bikaner in 1488.
bikaner-state.r: Raja [[e:rai-singh-of-bikaner|Rai Singh]] served [[e:akbar|Akbar]] as a general and built the [[e:junagarh-fort|Junagarh]] fort. Bikaner traded across the desert and was home to many Marwari merchant families. [[e:maharaja|Maharaja]] [[e:ganga-singh|Ganga Singh]] (r. 1887–1943) raised the [[e:ganga-risala|Ganga Risala]] [[e:camel|camel]] corps, sat in the Imperial War Cabinet during the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] and built the [[e:gang-canal|Ganga Canal]], opened in 1927 to irrigate the north of the state.
bikaner-state.e: Bikaner signed a treaty with the British in 1818 and acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1947. It merged into [[e:united-state-of-greater-rajasthan|Greater Rajasthan]] in 1949 and is now a district of [[e:rajasthan|Rajasthan]].

banu-qasi.t: A Muslim dynasty of Visigothic descent that dominated the upper Ebro for two centuries, allied by blood with the kings of Pamplona.
banu-qasi.o: The Banu Qasi claimed descent from a Visigothic count called Cassius who converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] after the conquest of 711 to 714, keeping his lands in the upper [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] valley. As muwallads, native Muslims, they became the leading family of the [[e:upper-march|Upper March]], based at [[e:tudela|Tudela]].
banu-qasi.r: They balanced between [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]], the [[s:franks|Franks]] and the Christian kingdoms, intermarrying with the Arista family of [[e:pamplona|Pamplona]], whose founder [[e:inigo-arista|Íñigo Arista]] was a half-brother of [[e:musa-ibn-musa|Musa ibn Musa]]. Musa ruled [[e:tudela|Tudela]], [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] and [[e:huesca|Huesca]] and was called the third king of [[e:spain|Spain]], until [[e:ordono-i-of-asturias|Ordoño I of Asturias]] defeated him at [[e:battle-of-albelda|Albelda]] in 859. Later family members fought Córdoba, the [[e:tujibids|Tujibids]] and [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]].
banu-qasi.e: Weakened by family divisions and wars with [[e:sancho-garces-i-of-pamplona|Sancho Garcés I of Pamplona]], the dynasty lost [[e:tudela|Tudela]] and its lands. [[e:abd-al-rahman-iii|Abd al-Rahman III]] ended its power in the 920s, and the [[e:tujibids|Tujibid]] family took over the [[e:upper-march|Upper March]].

brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.t: The last Hindu dynasty of Sindh, whose king Dahir fell in 712 to the Arab army of Muhammad ibn Qasim.
brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.o: According to the [[e:chach-nama|Chach Nama]], a 13th-century Persian history, [[s:principality-of-chach|Chach]], a [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] chamberlain at the court of the [[s:rai-dynasty|Rai dynasty]], married the widowed queen after the death of [[e:rai-sahasi-ii|Rai Sahasi II]] and seized the throne at [[e:aror|Aror]] around 632. He spent his reign subduing rebellious governors and fixing the borders of [[e:sindh|Sindh]].
brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.r: The [[e:chach-nama|Chach Nama]] describes a kingdom divided into provinces under governors, with a strong Buddhist population, many monasteries and powerful [[e:jats|Jat]] and [[e:lohana|Lohana]] groups in the countryside. [[s:principality-of-chach|Chach]] was succeeded by his brother Chandar and then by his sons, of whom [[e:raja-dahir|Dahir]] ruled from [[e:aror|Aror]] while his brother held [[e:brahmanabad|Brahmanabad]]. [[e:sindh|Sindh's]] ports, such as [[e:debal|Debal]], were active in [[e:indian-ocean-trade|Indian Ocean trade]].
brahman-dynasty-of-sindh.e: After attacks on Arab ships near [[e:debal|Debal]], the Umayyad governor of [[e:iraq|Iraq]], [[e:al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf|al-Hajjaj]], sent [[e:muhammad-ibn-qasim|Muhammad ibn Qasim]], who took Debal in 711 and defeated and killed [[e:raja-dahir|Dahir]] in 712. [[e:sindh|Sindh]] became a province of the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]], and later the [[s:habbari-dynasty|Habbari dynasty]] and the [[s:emirate-of-multan|Emirate of Multan]] arose there.
