banu-khattab-emirate.t: A Berber Ibadi dynasty of the Fezzan, ruling the Saharan slave-trade town of Zawila for over two centuries.
banu-khattab-emirate.o: [[e:zawila|Zawila]], in the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] of southern [[e:libya|Libya]], lay in the former lands of the [[s:garamantian-empire|Garamantian Empire]]. Around 918 Abd [[e:allah|Allah]] ibn al-Khattab of the [[e:hawwara|Hawwara]] [[e:berbers|Berbers]] established the dynasty there, controlling oases on the main caravan route between [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]] and the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
banu-khattab-emirate.r: The Banu Khattab were Ibadi Muslims who ruled a network of oases from [[e:zawila|Zawila]], which Arab geographers describe as a walled town with a mosque and markets. The [[e:emirate|emirate]] grew rich from the trade in enslaved people brought from [[e:kingdom-of-kanem|Kanem]] and the [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]] region, exchanged for horses, textiles and metal goods, and from date cultivation.
banu-khattab-emirate.e: In 1172 to 1176 [[s:qaraqushs-tripolitania|Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush]], a commander serving the [[s:ayyubid-empire|Ayyubid Empire]] of [[e:saladin|Saladin]], invaded the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] and killed the last Khattabid ruler. The [[e:fezzan|Fezzan]] later came under [[e:kingdom-of-kanem|Kanem]] and local dynasties.

balaton-principality.t: Frankish vassal principality around Lake Balaton where Pribina and Kocel built churches and welcomed Methodius's Slavonic liturgy.
balaton-principality.o: [[e:pribina|Pribina]], a Slavic prince expelled from [[e:nitra|Nitra]] by [[e:mojmir-i|Mojmir I]] of [[s:great-moravia|Moravia]] around 833, entered Frankish service. Around 839 [[e:louis-the-german|Louis the German]] granted him lands in Lower [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]], and he built a fortified seat at [[e:zalavar|Mosapurc]] (Zalavár) on the [[e:zala-river|Zala]] river near [[e:lake-balaton|Lake Balaton]].
balaton-principality.r: [[e:pribina|Pribina]] ruled as a Frankish [[e:vassal|vassal]], settling [[e:slavs|Slavs]] and [[e:bavarians|Bavarians]] and founding some 30 churches consecrated by the archbishops of [[e:salzburg|Salzburg]]. Under his son [[e:kocel|Kocel]], [[e:zalavar|Mosapurc]] was an important church centre. In 867 Kocel welcomed [[e:cyril-and-methodius|Cyril and Methodius]] and supported the Slavonic liturgy, and Methodius was made archbishop of [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]] in 870.
balaton-principality.e: [[e:pribina|Pribina]] was killed fighting Moravians in 861. After [[e:kocel|Kocel's]] death around 876 the principality returned to direct Frankish rule, and the Hungarian conquest of the 890s ended Frankish power in [[e:pannonia|Pannonia]].

british-seychelles.t: The Indian Ocean archipelago held by Britain from the Napoleonic Wars until 1976, a plantation colony and a place of exile.
british-seychelles.o: The French-settled [[e:seychelles|Seychelles]] surrendered to British warships several times during the [[e:napoleonic-wars|Napoleonic Wars]], while the French commandant [[e:queau-de-quinssy|Quéau de Quinssy]] stayed on to run the islands. After the capture of [[e:mauritius|Mauritius]] in 1810 they passed under British control, confirmed by the [[e:treaty-of-paris-1814|Treaty of Paris]] in 1814, and were governed as a dependency of Mauritius.
british-seychelles.r: French-speaking planters grew [[e:cotton|cotton]] and then coconuts, [[e:cinnamon|cinnamon]] and vanilla with enslaved labour until abolition in 1835; Africans freed from slave ships by the [[e:royal-navy|Royal Navy]] were later landed there. A [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] society formed, mostly Catholic. The islands became a separate [[e:crown-colony|Crown colony]] in 1903 with its capital at [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]], and served as a place of exile for figures such as [[e:prempeh-i|Prempeh I]] of [[e:ashanti-empire|Asante]] and [[e:makarios-iii|Archbishop Makarios]] of [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]].
british-seychelles.e: After internal self-government in 1970, the [[e:seychelles|Seychelles]] became independent on 29 June 1976 as a republic within the [[e:commonwealth-of-nations|Commonwealth]] under President [[e:james-mancham|James Mancham]], whose government was overthrown in a coup the next year by [[e:france-albert-rene|France-Albert René]].

brigantes-ireland.t: People of south-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, bearing the same name as the great Brigantes confederation of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.o: [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150 lists the [[s:brigantes|Brigantes]] in south-eastern Ireland, usually placed in the area of modern [[e:county-wexford|Wexford]] and [[e:waterford|Waterford]], near the [[s:coriondi|Coriondi]] and the [[s:usdiae|Usdiae]]. The name, meaning roughly 'the high ones' or linked to the goddess [[e:brigantia|Brigantia]], is the same as that of the Brigantes of northern [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
brigantes-ireland.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. The shared name has encouraged theories of migration from [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] to Ireland, or of a common cult of a goddess later remembered as [[e:brigid-goddess|Brigit]], but there is no evidence beyond the name. The south-east coast faced [[e:wales|Wales]] and [[e:gaul|Gaul]] and was open to sea trade.
brigantes-ireland.e: The Irish [[s:brigantes|Brigantes]] vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their area later lay within the [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Kingdom of Leinster]], the [[s:kingdom-of-osraige|Kingdom of Osraige]] and the lands of the [[s:deisi-muman|Deisi Muman]].

baban-emirate.t: A Kurdish emirate that founded the city of Sulaymaniyah and became a cradle of Sorani Kurdish literature between the Ottoman and Persian empires.
baban-emirate.o: The Baban family rose in the mountains of [[e:shahrizor|Shahrizor]] in the 17th century, recognised by the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] as hereditary lords. Their early centre was [[e:qalacholan|Qalacholan]]. In 1784 [[e:ibrahim-pasha-baban|Ibrahim Pasha Baban]] founded [[e:sulaymaniyah|Sulaymaniyah]], named after the [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] governor of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]], [[e:buyuk-suleyman-pasha|Büyük Süleyman Pasha]], as his new capital.
baban-emirate.r: The [[e:emirate|emirate]] was a frontier state caught between [[s:mamluk-iraq|Mamluk Iraq]] and [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]], each of which tried to choose its [[e:emir|emirs]]; family members often appealed to one side against the other. [[e:sulaymaniyah|Sulaymaniyah]] became a centre of learning, where poets such as [[e:nali-poet|Nali]], Salim and Kurdi wrote in Sorani Kurdish rather than Persian, founding a new literary tradition. The economy rested on agriculture, livestock and trade between [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] and [[e:persia|Persia]].
baban-emirate.e: As the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] centralised, they deposed the last emir, Ahmad Pasha, in 1850 and placed the region under a governor. The family remained influential in Kurdish politics.

buyid-dynasty.t: Daylamite Shia rulers who controlled the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad and most of Iran for over a century, the high point of the 'Iranian intermezzo'.
buyid-dynasty.o: Three sons of Buya, a Daylamite of modest origin, rose as officers under [[e:mardavij|Mardavij]] of the [[s:ziyarid-dynasty|Ziyarid dynasty]]. In 934 Ali took [[e:fars|Fars]] and made [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] his base; his brothers Hasan took [[e:rayy|Ray]] and [[e:isfahan|Isfahan]], and Ahmad entered [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] in 945. The [[e:caliphate|caliph]] gave them the titles [[e:imad-al-dawla|Imad al-Dawla]], [[e:rukn-al-dawla|Rukn al-Dawla]] and [[e:muizz-al-dawla|Mu'izz al-Dawla]].
buyid-dynasty.r: The Buyids kept [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliphs]] as figureheads while ruling as [[e:emir|emirs]] and later as shahanshah, a revived Persian title. They were Shia and sponsored public [[e:ashura|Ashura]] mourning and the [[e:eid-al-ghadir|feast of Ghadir]] in [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]]. [[e:adud-al-dawla|Adud al-Dawla]], who united the realm in 977 to 983, built the [[e:band-e-amir-dam|Band-e Amir]] dam in [[e:fars|Fars]] and the Adudi hospital in Baghdad. Their courts patronised scholars such as [[e:miskawayh|Miskawayh]] and the [[e:vizier|vizier]] [[e:al-sahib-ibn-abbad|al-Sahib ibn Abbad]], and they spread the [[e:iqta|iqta]] land-grant system.
buyid-dynasty.e: Family rivalries split the state. Mahmud of the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]] took [[e:rayy|Ray]] in 1029, and [[e:tughril|Tughril]] of the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] entered [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] in 1055. The last Buyid in [[e:fars|Fars]] was overthrown by the [[s:shabankara|Shabankara]] chief [[e:fadluya|Fadluya]] in 1062.

bahamas.t: Archipelago of some 700 islands off Florida, independent since 1973 and one of the wealthiest Caribbean states through tourism and finance.
bahamas.o: After winning majority rule in 1967, [[e:lynden-pindling|Lynden Pindling's]] [[e:progressive-liberal-party|Progressive Liberal Party]] led the [[s:colony-of-the-bahamas|Colony of the Bahamas]] to independence on 10 July 1973 as the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, a parliamentary monarchy with the British monarch as head of state.
bahamas.r: [[e:lynden-pindling|Pindling]], called the father of the nation, governed until 1992, expanding education and Bahamian ownership, though his government was tarnished by drug trafficking scandals in the 1980s, when the islands served as a transit route for cocaine to the [[s:united-states|United States]]. [[e:hubert-ingraham|Hubert Ingraham's]] [[e:free-national-movement|Free National Movement]] then alternated in power with the [[e:progressive-liberal-party|Progressive Liberal Party]]. Tourism, especially cruise and resort tourism on [[e:new-providence|New Providence]] and [[e:grand-bahama|Grand Bahama]], and offshore banking dominate the economy.
bahamas.e: The Bahamas remains a stable parliamentary democracy. [[e:hurricane-dorian|Hurricane Dorian]] devastated [[e:abaco-islands|Abaco]] and [[e:grand-bahama|Grand Bahama]] in 2019, and rising sea levels threaten the low-lying islands. [[e:philip-davis|Philip Davis]] became prime minister in 2021.

bahawalpur-state.t: The Abbasi Nawabs' desert kingdom along the Sutlej, the largest princely state to join Pakistan.
bahawalpur-state.o: The [[e:daudpota|Daudpota Abbasi]] clan, who claimed descent from the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliphs]], moved from [[e:sindh|Sindh]] to the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] valley in the early 18th century. Around 1748 [[e:bahawal-khan-i|Bahawal Khan I]] founded the town of Bahawalpur, and the Nawabs became independent of the declining [[s:durrani-empire|Durrani Empire]].
bahawalpur-state.r: The Nawabs signed a treaty with the British in 1833 and supported them in the Afghan and Anglo-[[e:sikhism|Sikh]] wars and in 1857. Much of the state was Cholistan desert, but the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] Valley Project of the 1920s greatly expanded irrigated farming. The Nawabs built palaces such as [[e:noor-mahal|Noor Mahal]] and held the old fort of [[e:derawar-fort|Derawar]].
bahawalpur-state.e: [[e:sadiq-muhammad-khan-v|Sadiq Muhammad Khan V]] acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] in October 1947 and gave the new state generous financial support. Bahawalpur was merged into [[e:west-pakistan|West Pakistan]] in 1955 and is now a division of [[e:punjab|Punjab]] province.

beikthano.t: One of the oldest Pyu cities in Myanmar, whose name means 'Vishnu city' and whose excavated monastery and burials show early contact with India.
beikthano.o: Beikthano grew up in the [[e:magway-region|Magway region]] of central [[s:myanmar|Myanmar]] from around the 2nd century BCE, making it among the earliest walled cities of the Pyu. Radiocarbon dates from excavations in the 1950s and 1960s place its main occupation between about 200 BCE and 400 CE.
beikthano.r: The city was enclosed by a large, roughly rectangular brick wall, with irrigation works feeding [[e:rice|rice]] fields around it. Excavators found a palace site, a monastery and stupa resembling those of [[e:nagarjunakonda|Nagarjunakonda]] in south [[e:india|India]], and many burial urns holding cremated remains, suggesting early Buddhist practice alongside local customs.
beikthano.e: Beikthano was abandoned or declined around the 4th or 5th century, possibly after a fire, as [[s:sri-ksetra-kingdom|Sri Ksetra]] rose as the leading Pyu centre. Local legend links its end to a princess named Panhtwa. It is now one of the three Pyu ancient cities on the [[e:unesco|UNESCO]] World Heritage List.

bahdinan-emirate.t: A Kurdish emirate in the mountains north of Mosul, centred on the clifftop town of Amadiya, that ruled for over four centuries.
bahdinan-emirate.o: The Bahdinan [[e:emir|emirs]] claimed descent from the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliphs]] through an ancestor named Baha al-Din, who gave the dynasty its name. They ruled from [[e:amadiya|Amadiya]] ([[s:bit-zamani|Amedi]]), a town on a sheer rock plateau in the mountains of northern [[e:iraq|Iraq]], from at least the late 14th century.
bahdinan-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] governed Kurdish tribes, Assyrian Christian and Jewish villages and Yazidi communities in the valleys between the [[e:great-zab|Great Zab]] and the [[e:khabur-river|Khabur]]. After the Ottoman conquest of the region in the 16th century they became hereditary [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], providing troops for its wars with the [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]]; [[e:sultan-husayn-wali|Sultan Husayn Wali]] was a notable ally of the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. [[e:amadiya|Amadiya]] was known for its [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] and its [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] scholars.
bahdinan-emirate.e: Weakened by internal feuds and attacks by the [[s:soran-emirate|Soran emirate]] in the 1830s, the [[e:emirate|emirate]] was abolished during Ottoman centralisation in the early 1840s, its lands placed under the governor of [[e:mosul|Mosul]].

banat-of-temeswar.t: Habsburg crown domain in the plain of the Banat, run directly from Vienna as a laboratory of colonisation and drainage after its conquest from the Ottomans.
banat-of-temeswar.o: [[e:prince-eugene-of-savoy|Prince Eugene of Savoy]] captured [[e:timisoara|Temeswar]] from the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1716, and the [[e:treaty-of-passarowitz|Treaty of Passarowitz]] in 1718 confirmed [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] possession of the [[e:banat|Banat]] between the [[e:mures-river|Mureș]], [[e:tisza|Tisza]] and [[e:danube|Danube]]. Rather than returning it to [[e:hungary|Hungary]], [[e:charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor|Charles VI]] kept it as a crown domain under military and court administration.
banat-of-temeswar.r: Governor [[e:claudius-florimund-mercy|Claudius Florimund Mercy]] rebuilt [[e:timisoara|Temeswar]] as a baroque fortress town, drained marshes, dug the [[e:bega-canal|Bega canal]] and promoted [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]] and mining. Tens of thousands of Catholic German settlers, later called [[e:danube-swabians|Danube Swabians]], were brought in alongside [[e:serbs|Serbs]], [[e:romanians|Romanians]] and Italians, while Hungarian nobles were largely excluded. The [[e:banat|Banat]] was governed by a provincial administration answering to [[e:vienna|Vienna]].
banat-of-temeswar.e: In 1778 [[e:maria-theresa|Maria Theresa]] returned the civil [[e:banat|Banat]] to [[e:hungary|Hungary]] as the counties of [[e:temes-county|Temes]], [[e:torontal-county|Torontál]] and Krassó, while its southern strip stayed in the [[s:military-frontier|Military Frontier]]. Its mixed population shaped the region until it was divided between [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]], [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] and Hungary in 1920.

balhae.t: A kingdom of Manchuria and northern Korea founded by Goguryeo and Mohe people, so prosperous that Tang China called it the flourishing land of the east.
balhae.o: After the fall of [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]], [[e:dae-joyeong|Dae Joyeong]] led Goguryeo refugees and [[e:mohe|Mohe]] tribesmen out of Tang-controlled Liaoxi, defeated a [[s:later-tang|Tang]] army at [[e:battle-of-tianmenling|Tianmenling]] and in 698 founded the state of Jin near the Dongmo mountain. In 713 Tang recognised him as king of Bohai, the name by which the state became known.
balhae.r: Balhae copied [[s:later-tang|Tang]] institutions, with [[e:three-departments-and-six-ministries|three departments and six ministries]], five capitals and fifteen prefectures, while its kings sometimes used their own era names. King Mun moved the court to [[e:sanggyeong|Sanggyeong]], laid out on the plan of [[e:changan|Chang'an]]. Its elite wrote Chinese and practised [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]], and some thirty-four embassies to [[e:japan|Japan]] carried [[e:fur-trade|furs]], honey and ginseng.
balhae.e: Weakened by internal conflict, Balhae fell in 926 to the Khitan under [[e:emperor-taizu-of-liao|Abaoji]], who made it the [[e:vassal|vassal]] kingdom of [[s:dongdan|Dongdan]]. Many nobles fled to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]], which welcomed the crown prince [[e:dae-gwang-hyeon|Dae Gwang-hyeon]].

bharatpur-state.t: The Jat kingdom of eastern Rajasthan whose mud-walled fortress of Lohagarh famously withstood a British siege in 1805.
bharatpur-state.o: [[e:jats|Jat]] peasant leaders around [[e:mathura|Mathura]] and [[e:agra|Agra]] rose against Mughal authority in the late 17th century. [[e:badan-singh|Badan Singh]], recognised as chief around 1722, consolidated the clans and fortified [[e:deeg|Deeg]] and Bharatpur. His son [[e:suraj-mal|Suraj Mal]] (ruled 1755–63) turned the chiefship into a major power, building the [[e:lohagarh-fort|Lohagarh]] fort and capturing Agra in 1761.
bharatpur-state.r: Bharatpur was a [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] [[e:jats|Jat]] monarchy with a strong military tradition and a wealthy farming base. Its forts at Bharatpur and [[e:deeg|Deeg]], with the Deeg water palaces, reflect [[e:suraj-mal|Suraj Mal's]] ambitions. In 1805 [[e:gerard-lake-1st-viscount-lake|Lord Lake]] failed to take [[e:lohagarh-fort|Lohagarh]] after four assaults; the fort finally fell to [[e:stapleton-cotton-1st-viscount-combermere|Lord Combermere]] in 1826, when the British intervened in a succession dispute and installed the young [[e:balwant-singh-of-bharatpur|Balwant Singh]]. The [[e:keoladeo-national-park|Keoladeo]] wetlands were kept as a royal duck-shooting reserve.
bharatpur-state.e: After independence Bharatpur joined the [[s:matsya-union|Matsya Union]] in March 1948, which merged into the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in 1949. [[e:keoladeo-national-park|Keoladeo]] is now a national park and [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]].

bourbon-spain.t: Spain under the Bourbon dynasty from Philip V to Isabella II, a time of centralising reform, Napoleonic invasion and the loss of most of its American empire.
bourbon-spain.o: [[e:charles-ii-of-spain|Charles II]], last of [[s:habsburg-spain|Habsburg Spain]], left the throne to [[e:philip-v-of-spain|Philip of Anjou]], grandson of [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]], who became Philip V in 1700. The [[e:war-of-the-spanish-succession|War of the Spanish Succession]] confirmed him as king but cost [[e:spain|Spain]] its European possessions at [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]] in 1713, while the [[e:nueva-planta-decrees|Nueva Planta decrees]] abolished the separate institutions of the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]].
bourbon-spain.r: The [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbons]] built a more centralised state on the French model, with intendants, new academies and royal factories. [[e:charles-iii-of-spain|Charles III]] (1759-1788) promoted roads, trade reform and enlightened ministers and expelled the [[e:jesuits|Jesuits]]. The monarchy was shattered by the 1808 French invasion; [[e:ferdinand-vii-of-spain|Ferdinand VII]] then restored absolutism, and the American colonies won independence in the 1810s and 1820s.
bourbon-spain.e: [[e:isabella-ii-of-spain|Isabella II]]'s reign was dominated by [[e:carlist-wars|Carlist Wars]], generals and court scandal. The [[e:glorious-revolution-spain|Glorious Revolution]] of September 1868 drove her into exile, opening the [[s:sexenio-democratico|Sexenio Democrático]].

broerec.t: Breton kingdom of the Vannes region, named the land of Waroch after a warlord who defied the Franks.
broerec.o: In the 6th century Breton rulers extended their power over the Vannetais, the former land of the [[s:ancient-veneti|Veneti]], which remained largely Gallo-Roman. [[e:gregory-of-tours|Gregory of Tours]] records the counts [[e:macliau|Macliau]] and his son [[e:waroch-ii|Waroch]] fighting for control of [[e:vannes|Vannes]].
broerec.r: [[e:waroch-ii|Waroch]] repeatedly raided Frankish territory around [[e:rennes|Rennes]] and [[e:nantes|Nantes]] and defeated or bought off Frankish armies sent by [[e:guntram|Guntram]] and [[e:chilperic-i|Chilperic I]] in the 570s and 580s. The region kept a strong Gallo-Roman element alongside the Breton settlers, and [[e:vannes|Vannes]] remained a bishopric.
broerec.e: Broërec remained the border zone between the [[e:bretons|Bretons]] and the [[s:franks|Franks]] until it was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-brittany|Kingdom of Brittany]] created by [[e:nominoe|Nominoe]], who was count of [[e:vannes|Vannes]] for [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]]. Its name survives in the Breton name of the Vannes region.

cr.a: Mikael Bodlore-Penlaez; derivative work by Pethrus

bishopric-of-dorpat.t: Prince-bishopric of south-eastern Estonia centred on Dorpat (Tartu), a prosperous Hanseatic frontier facing Pskov, until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1558.
bishopric-of-dorpat.o: [[e:hermann-of-buxhoeveden|Hermann of Buxhoeveden]], brother of [[e:albert-of-riga|Bishop Albert of Riga]], became [[e:bishop|bishop]] of the [[e:estonians|Estonians]] in 1220 and moved his see to [[e:tartu|Dorpat]] after its capture in 1224. The bishopric took over the former lands of [[s:ugandi|Ugandi]], [[s:vaiga|Vaiga]] and [[s:mohu|Mõhu]], and Hermann received them as a prince of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
bishopric-of-dorpat.r: The [[e:bishop|bishop]] ruled through a cathedral chapter and German [[e:vassal|vassals]], sharing power with the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]] and the diets of [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]]. [[e:tartu|Dorpat]], a Hanseatic member, grew rich from trade with [[e:pskov|Pskov]] and Novgorod and built a large Gothic cathedral. Estonian peasants worked the land under increasing [[e:serfdom|serfdom]].
bishopric-of-dorpat.e: At the start of the [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]] [[e:ivan-iv-of-russia|Ivan IV of Russia]] took [[e:tartu|Dorpat]] in 1558, and the last [[e:bishop|bishop]], [[e:hermann-wesel|Hermann Wesel]], was taken to [[e:russia|Russia]], where he died. The territory was later contested by Poland-[[e:lithuania|Lithuania]] and [[e:sweden|Sweden]], and passed to [[s:swedish-livonia|Swedish Livonia]] in the 1620s.

bavda-state.t: A Maratha jagir in the Western Ghats under Kolhapur, held by the hereditary Pant Amatya family.
bavda-state.o: Bavda (Gaganbawada) was held by the descendants of [[e:ramchandra-pant-amatya|Ramchandra Pant Amatya]], the minister who defended the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] kingdom during the war with [[e:aurangzeb|Aurangzeb]] in the 1690s. Around 1700 the family received this hill territory with the hereditary title of Pant Amatya, as feudatories of [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]].
bavda-state.r: The chiefs governed a hilly, forested territory on the [[e:western-ghats|Ghats]] overlooking the Konkan, under [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] overlordship and British supervision through the Kolhapur residency. Few further details of its rulers are widely recorded.
bavda-state.e: Bavda merged with [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1949 and became part of [[e:maharashtra|Maharashtra]] in 1960. Gaganbawada is a taluka of Kolhapur district.

belli.t: The Celtiberian people of Segeda, whose new city walls provoked the Roman war of 153 BCE and so moved the start of the Roman year to January.
belli.o: The Belli lived in the [[e:jalon|Jalón]] and [[e:huerva|Huerva]] valleys of modern [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] province from about the 4th century BCE, part of the wider Celtiberian world. Their towns included [[e:segeda|Segeda]] and [[e:contrebia-belaisca|Contrebia Belaisca]], the modern [[e:botorrita|Botorrita]].
belli.r: They lived in walled towns with councils of elders and magistrates. The [[e:botorrita|Botorrita]] bronzes, the longest texts in the Celtiberian language, come from [[e:contrebia-belaisca|Contrebia Belaisca]] and record local regulations, while a [[e:latin|Latin]] bronze from the same site records a Roman arbitration of 87 BCE. Their economy rested on farming, herding and metalworking.
belli.e: In 154 BCE [[e:segeda|Segeda]] enlarged its walls, which [[e:rome|Rome]] treated as a breach of treaty. To send an army quickly, Rome began the consular year on 1 January 153 BCE. Led by [[e:carus-of-segeda|Carus of Segeda]], the [[s:celtiberians|Celtiberians]] defeated the consul [[e:quintus-fulvius-nobilior|Nobilior]], but after [[e:numantia|Numantia]] fell in 133 BCE the Belli were absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]].

bauchi-emirate.t: A large emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate in north-central Nigeria, unusual in having been founded by a non-Fulani flag-bearer, Yakubu.
bauchi-emirate.o: [[e:yakubu-of-bauchi|Yakubu]], a Gerawa scholar and student of [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio]], was the only one of the original flag-bearers who was not a [[e:fula|Fulani]]. Receiving a flag around 1805, he campaigned among the many peoples of the [[e:jos-plateau|Jos plateau]] foothills and the upper [[e:gongola-river|Gongola]], and around 1809 founded the town of [[e:bauchi|Bauchi]] as his capital.
bauchi-emirate.r: [[e:yakubu-of-bauchi|Yakubu]] ruled for about forty years and built one of the larger [[e:emirate|emirates]] by conquering and raiding many small non-Muslim groups, whose captives supplied slaves for farms and trade. The emirate was governed by the emir with titled officials and sub-emirates on its frontiers, and owed allegiance and tribute to [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]]. Its southern borderlands remained contested hill country throughout the century.
bauchi-emirate.e: British forces occupied [[e:bauchi|Bauchi]] in 1902 and deposed the reigning emir, and the [[e:emirate|emirate]] became part of the [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]]. The [[e:emir|Emir]] of Bauchi continues as a traditional ruler in modern [[e:bauchi-state|Bauchi State]].

bulgaria.t: Present-day Bulgaria, a parliamentary republic since 1990 and member of NATO and the European Union.
bulgaria.o: After [[e:todor-zhivkov|Todor Zhivkov's]] fall in November 1989 ended the dominance of the [[s:peoples-republic-of-bulgaria|People's Republic of Bulgaria]]'s communist party, [[e:bulgarian-round-table|Round Table]] talks led to free elections in 1990. The country was renamed the Republic of Bulgaria in November 1990, and a democratic constitution was adopted in July 1991. The philosopher [[e:zhelyu-zhelev|Zhelyu Zhelev]] became the first directly elected president.
bulgaria.r: Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic with a single-chamber [[e:national-assembly-of-bulgaria|National Assembly]]. The transition was painful: a banking collapse and hyperinflation in 1996 to 1997 led to a currency board pegging the lev. The former tsar [[e:simeon-saxe-coburg-gotha|Simeon II]] became prime minister in 2001 as Simeon Saxe-Coburg-[[e:gotha|Gotha]]. Corruption and weak institutions remain central political issues.
bulgaria.e: Bulgaria joined [[e:nato|NATO]] in 2004 and the [[e:european-union|European Union]] in 2007. [[e:boyko-borisov|Boyko Borisov]] dominated politics from 2009 until mass protests in 2020, followed by repeated snap elections. The country fully joined the [[e:schengen-area|Schengen area]] in 2025 and adopted the euro in 2026.

bavarian-soviet-republic.t: Short-lived council republic in Munich in April 1919, crushed by government troops and Freikorps in a wave of violence.
bavarian-soviet-republic.o: After the murder of Bavarian premier [[e:kurt-eisner|Kurt Eisner]] in February 1919, the elected government of [[e:johannes-hoffmann|Johannes Hoffmann]] fled [[e:munich|Munich]] to [[e:bamberg|Bamberg]]. On 6-7 April 1919 a council republic was proclaimed by writers and anarchists, including [[e:ernst-toller|Ernst Toller]], [[e:erich-muhsam|Erich Mühsam]] and [[e:gustav-landauer|Gustav Landauer]].
bavarian-soviet-republic.r: The first council government was chaotic; within a week the Communists under [[e:eugen-levine|Eugen Leviné]] took over and formed a [[e:red-army|Red Army]]. They decreed the socialisation of banks and industry and seized hostages. Supplies to [[e:munich|Munich]] broke down. The killing of hostages at the Luitpold [[e:gymnasium|Gymnasium]] on 30 April inflamed opinion against the regime.
bavarian-soviet-republic.e: Government troops and [[e:freikorps|Freikorps]] units entered [[e:munich|Munich]] on 1-3 May 1919, killing several hundred people, including [[e:gustav-landauer|Landauer]]. [[e:eugen-levine|Leviné]] was executed. The episode pushed Bavarian politics sharply to the right.

beiyang-government.t: The internationally recognised government of the Republic of China based in Beijing, dominated first by Yuan Shikai and then by rival warlord cliques.
beiyang-government.o: [[e:yuan-shikai|Yuan Shikai]], commander of the [[e:beiyang-army|Beiyang Army]], the most modern Qing force, negotiated the abdication of the last emperor in 1912 and replaced [[e:sun-yat-sen|Sun Yat-sen]] as president of the new [[s:republic-of-china|Republic of China]], keeping the capital in [[e:beijing|Beijing]]. He crushed the Nationalists' [[e:second-revolution|Second Revolution]] of 1913 and governed increasingly as a dictator.
beiyang-government.r: After Yuan's failed attempt to restore the monarchy as the [[s:empire-of-china-1915-1916|Empire of China]] (1915-1916) and his death, control of [[e:beijing|Beijing]] passed between military cliques: the Anhui clique of [[e:duan-qirui|Duan Qirui]], the Zhili clique of [[e:cao-kun|Cao Kun]] and [[e:wu-peifu|Wu Peifu]], and the Fengtian clique of [[e:zhang-zuolin|Zhang Zuolin]]. Cabinets and presidents changed rapidly, while provinces ruled themselves. [[e:china|China]] joined the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] in 1917, and anger at the peace settlement sparked the May Fourth Movement in 1919.
beiyang-government.e: The [[s:nationalist-government|Nationalist government]]'s [[e:northern-expedition|Northern Expedition]] from 1926 defeated the northern warlords. [[e:zhang-zuolin|Zhang Zuolin]] abandoned [[e:beijing|Beijing]] in June 1928 and was killed by a Japanese bomb; Beijing was renamed Beiping and the capital moved to [[e:nanjing|Nanjing]].

blemmyes.t: Nomadic people of the Eastern Desert, ancestors of the Beja, who raided Roman Egypt and held Lower Nubia in late antiquity.
blemmyes.o: The Blemmyes lived in the desert hills between the [[e:nile|Nile]] and the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] and are generally identified as ancestors of the modern Beja. Greek geographers mention them from the 3rd century BCE, and from the 3rd century CE Roman sources record them raiding [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]] and the trade routes to the Red Sea ports.
blemmyes.r: They were organised in tribes under kings and phylarchs, and in the 5th century held parts of [[e:lower-nubia|Lower Nubia]], with [[e:kalabsha|Talmis]] (Kalabsha) as a centre. In 298 [[e:diocletian|Diocletian]] withdrew the frontier to [[e:philae|Philae]] and paid [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] to both the Blemmyes and the Nobadians. The Blemmyes worshipped [[e:isis|Isis]] and had the right to borrow her statue from Philae. Letters written in Greek, such as one from King [[e:phonen|Phonen]], survive at [[e:qasr-ibrim|Qasr Ibrim]].
blemmyes.e: In the 5th to 6th centuries the Christian kingdom of [[s:nobadia|Nobadia]] drove them from the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley; [[e:silko|King Silko]] recorded his victories at [[e:kalabsha|Kalabsha]]. The closure of the [[e:philae|Philae]] temple under Justinian around 537 ended their religious tie with [[e:egypt|Egypt]], and their descendants remained in the [[e:eastern-desert|Eastern Desert]].

beylik-of-titteri.t: The smallest of the three provinces of Ottoman Algiers, governed from Médéa by beys who controlled the highlands south of the capital.
beylik-of-titteri.o: The [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]] organised its territory in the mid-16th century into the provinces of the East, the West and Titteri, with the area around [[e:algiers|Algiers]] itself ruled directly. Titteri, created around 1548, covered the Tell [[e:atlas-mountains|Atlas]] and high plains south of Algiers, with [[e:medea|Médéa]] as its seat.
beylik-of-titteri.r: The bey, appointed by [[e:algiers|Algiers]], collected taxes from tribes and farmers, relying on [[e:janissaries|Janissary]] garrisons and allied makhzen tribes. Every few years he travelled to Algiers to deliver tribute in person. The province supplied grain, livestock and wool to the capital, and [[e:medea|Médéa]] was a market town with Andalusi and Ottoman influences.
beylik-of-titteri.e: After the French captured [[e:algiers|Algiers]] in 1830, the bey [[e:mustapha-boumezrag|Mustapha Boumezrag]] first submitted and then resisted. French troops occupied [[e:medea|Médéa]] in late 1830, and the [[e:beylik|beylik]] was dissolved into [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]].

bonampak.t: A small Maya city in the Lacandon forest whose murals give the most vivid surviving picture of a Classic Maya court, battle and ceremony.
bonampak.o: Bonampak, anciently Usiij Witz, was a minor centre near the Lacanjá river in [[e:chiapas|Chiapas]]. Its lords are attested in the [[e:late-classic-period|Late Classic]] from around 600 CE and were for long periods subordinate to their more powerful neighbour [[s:yaxchilan|Yaxchilan]].
bonampak.r: Structure 1 holds three painted rooms, created around 790 under the ruler [[e:yajaw-chan-muwaan|Yajaw Chan Muwaan]]. They show the presentation of an heir, a fierce battle, the judgement and torture of captives, and celebrations with dancers and musicians. The murals reveal costume, weapons, music and court hierarchy in rare detail, and show the close involvement of Yaxchilan's royal house.
bonampak.e: The murals were never finished, and Bonampak was abandoned soon after 800 CE. They were revealed to outsiders in 1946 by [[e:lacandon-maya|Lacandon Maya]] guides, transforming the image of the Maya as peaceful.

bishopric-of-osel-wiek.t: Prince-bishopric of western Estonia and its islands, ruled from Hapsal and Arensburg until its bishop sold it to Denmark in 1559-1560.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek.o: After the conquest of [[s:saaremaa|Saaremaa]] in 1227 and of [[s:laanemaa|Läänemaa]], a bishopric for the islands and the western coast was founded in 1228. Its lands were shared with the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], which took parts of Saaremaa and the island of [[e:muhu|Muhu]], while the [[e:bishop|bishop]] held most of Läänemaa and western Saaremaa.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] resided first at [[e:lihula|Lihula]], then from the 13th century at [[e:haapsalu|Hapsal]] (Haapsalu), and also built the castle of [[e:kuressaare|Arensburg]] (Kuressaare) on [[s:saaremaa|Saaremaa]]. They governed through German [[e:vassal|vassals]], a cathedral chapter and the diets of [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]]. Repeated Estonian revolts, including the uprising of 1343, shook the islands.
bishopric-of-osel-wiek.e: Facing the [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]], [[e:johann-von-munchhausen|Bishop Johann von Münchhausen]] sold the bishopric to [[e:frederick-ii-of-denmark|Frederick II of Denmark]] in 1559, and the king passed it to his brother [[e:magnus-duke-of-holstein|Magnus of Holstein]], who arrived in 1560. It became [[s:danish-osel|Danish Ösel]], and the mainland part fell to [[e:sweden|Sweden]].

berbice.t: A Dutch plantation colony on the Berbice river in Guyana, remembered above all for the great slave uprising of 1763.
berbice.o: In 1627 the [[s:county-of-zeeland|Zeeland]] merchant [[e:abraham-van-peere|Abraham van Peere]] received a charter from the [[e:dutch-west-india-company|Dutch West India Company]] to settle the Berbice river. The colony began as a trading post at [[e:fort-nassau-berbice|Fort Nassau]] upriver and was run as a private patroonship by the van Peere family.
berbice.r: Berbice developed [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and [[e:cotton|cotton]] plantations worked by enslaved Africans. After a French raid in 1712, the colony was ransomed and from 1720 run by the [[e:society-of-berbice|Society of Berbice]], a company of investors. In 1763 enslaved people led by [[e:cuffy|Coffy]] rose up, controlled most of the colony for nearly a year and were suppressed only with outside troops. [[e:new-amsterdam|New Amsterdam]] later became the capital.
berbice.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] occupied Berbice from 1796 and gained it formally in 1814. In 1831 it was merged with [[s:demerara-essequibo|Demerara-Essequibo]] to form [[s:british-guiana|British Guiana]]. [[e:cuffy|Coffy]] is Guyana's national hero, and 23 February, the start of the uprising, is the country's Republic Day.

bono-state.t: Early Akan kingdom at the forest edge in central Ghana, a gold-trading partner of Mande merchants and forerunner of later Akan states.
bono-state.o: Bono, with its capital at [[e:bono-manso|Bono Manso]] near modern Techiman, is regarded by [[e:akan|Akan]] tradition as one of the earliest Akan kingdoms. It grew where the savanna meets the forest, close to gold-bearing land and to the [[e:mande-peoples|Mande]] trading town of [[e:begho|Begho]]. Tradition dates its founding as early as the 13th century, though its chronology is uncertain.
bono-state.r: Bono's kings controlled gold mining and the trade in gold and kola northward to [[e:mande-peoples|Mande]] and [[e:hausa|Hausa]] traders, receiving cloth, salt and brass. [[e:akan|Akan]] institutions often credited to Bono include the use of gold weights, stools as symbols of office and matrilineal succession. Tradition names [[e:ameyaw-kwaakye|Ameyaw Kwaakye]] as a king under whom gold mining expanded.
bono-state.e: In 1723 the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]] under [[e:opoku-ware-i|Opoku Ware]] conquered [[e:bono-manso|Bono Manso]] and destroyed the town. Its people and royal stools were absorbed into the [[e:ashanti-empire|Ashanti]] system, and the Techiman traditional state claims succession from Bono.

bone-sultanate.t: The most powerful Bugis kingdom of South Sulawesi, whose prince Arung Palakka allied with the Dutch to break the power of Gowa in 1669.
bone-sultanate.o: Bone arose in the 14th century around [[e:watampone|Watampone]] on the [[e:gulf-of-bone|Gulf of Bone]]. Its chronicles tell of a tomanurung, a heavenly figure, who agreed to rule with the consent of the local community leaders. By the 16th century it was a rival of Gowa, and in 1582 it formed the [[e:tellumpoccoe|Tellumpoccoe]] alliance with Wajo and [[s:soppeng-kingdom|Soppeng]].
bone-sultanate.r: Bone was ruled by an arumpone, whose power was balanced by a council of seven lords. Gowa conquered it and imposed [[e:islam|Islam]] in 1611. The exiled prince [[e:arung-palakka|Arung Palakka]] joined the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]], defeated Gowa in 1666 to 1669, and made Bone the leading state of South [[e:sulawesi|Sulawesi]].
bone-sultanate.e: Bone resisted the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] in the 19th century, and in 1905 they conquered it, exiling its ruler [[e:la-pawawoi-karaeng-sigeri|La Pawawoi Karaeng Sigeri]]. The kingdom was restored under Dutch supervision in 1931 under [[e:la-mappanyukki|La Mappanyukki]] and merged into [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]] after independence. It is now [[e:bone-regency|Bone Regency]].

banu-kab-sheikhdom.t: An Arab tribal sheikhdom of the Khuzestan marshes that built canals and a navy and challenged Persians, Ottomans and the East India Company.
banu-kab-sheikhdom.o: The [[e:banu-kab|Banu Ka'b]], an Arab tribe from southern [[e:iraq|Iraq]], moved into the marshes of the lower [[e:karun-river|Karun]] in [[e:khuzestan|Khuzestan]] in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, as the [[s:mushasha|Musha'sha]] weakened. They settled at Qubban and later at [[e:shadegan|Fallahiyeh]] (modern Shadegan), which became the seat of their sheikhs.
banu-kab-sheikhdom.r: Under Sheikh Salman ibn [[e:sultan|Sultan]] (c. 1737 to 1768) the sheikhdom reached its height. He dug canals and built dams for [[e:rice|rice]] and date cultivation, assembled a fleet of armed boats, and resisted campaigns by [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan]] of the [[s:zand-empire|Zand Empire]] and the Ottoman pasha of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]]. In 1765 his ships seized vessels of the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]], provoking a British expedition. The [[e:banu-kab|Ka'b]] were Shia and Arabic-speaking.
banu-kab-sheikhdom.e: After Salman's death the sheikhdom fragmented. Its Muhaysin branch developed [[e:khorramshahr|Mohammerah]], and after an Ottoman sack of Mohammerah in 1837 leadership passed to what became the [[s:sheikhdom-of-mohammerah|Sheikhdom of Mohammerah]].

british-ceylon.t: The British Crown Colony of Ceylon, which unified the island under one administration and built a plantation economy of coffee, tea and rubber.
british-ceylon.o: British forces from the [[s:madras-presidency|Madras Presidency]] took the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] coastal provinces of [[s:dutch-ceylon|Dutch Ceylon]] in 1795 to 1796, and they became a [[e:crown-colony|Crown Colony]] in 1802. In 1815 the British, exploiting discontent among Kandyan chiefs, took over the [[s:kingdom-of-kandy|Kingdom of Kandy]], bringing the whole island under one rule for the first time.
british-ceylon.r: The [[e:colebrooke-cameron-commission|Colebrooke-Cameron]] reforms of 1833 centralised administration. [[e:coffee-economy|Coffee]] plantations spread in the hills until blight in the 1870s, after which [[e:tea|tea]], [[e:rubber|rubber]] and coconut dominated, worked by Tamil labourers from [[e:india|India]]. English education created a new elite, and a Buddhist revival led by [[e:anagarika-dharmapala|Anagarika Dharmapala]] grew. The [[e:donoughmore-constitution|Donoughmore Constitution]] of 1931 introduced universal suffrage.
british-ceylon.e: [[e:ceylon|Ceylon]] contributed to the Allied effort in the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]], and the [[e:soulbury-constitution|Soulbury Constitution]] prepared self-government. It gained independence peacefully in 1948 as the [[s:dominion-of-ceylon|Dominion of Ceylon]], with [[e:d-s-senanayake|D. S. Senanayake]] as first prime minister.

boeotian-league.t: Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
boeotian-league.o: The cities of [[e:boeotia|Boeotia]] shared a dialect, cults and a sense of kinship, and by the late 6th century BCE [[s:thebes|Thebes]] was gathering them into a federation, an effort [[s:plataea|Plataea]] resisted by allying with [[s:athens|Athens]]. After Boeotians fought on the Persian side in 479 BCE the league lapsed, and it was refounded after the defeat of [[e:athens|Athens]] at [[e:battle-of-coronea-447-bc|Coronea]] in 447 BCE.
boeotian-league.r: The [[e:hellenica-oxyrhynchia|Hellenica Oxyrhynchia]] describes its 5th-century constitution: [[e:boeotia|Boeotia]] was divided into eleven districts, each supplying a boeotarch, sixty federal councillors, soldiers and taxes in proportion, with [[s:thebes|Thebes]] holding four shares. Member cities kept local councils of propertied citizens. The federal coinage carried the Boeotian shield.
boeotian-league.e: The [[e:peace-of-antalcidas|King's Peace]] dissolved it in 386 BCE, but [[e:pelopidas|Pelopidas]] and [[e:epaminondas|Epaminondas]] revived it after 379 BCE and defeated [[s:sparta|Sparta]] at [[e:battle-of-leuctra|Leuctra]]. Alexander destroyed [[s:thebes|Thebes]] in 335 BCE; a Hellenistic league continued until [[e:rome|Rome]] dissolved it in 171 BCE.

barawa.t: A small Somali port city known for its Islamic scholarship and its own Bantu language, Chimiini, spoken by the Bravanese.
barawa.o: Barawa, or Brava, developed as a coastal trading town on the southern [[e:somalis|Somali]] coast in the early second millennium, settled by Somali Tunni clans together with Arab and Swahili-speaking merchants. Arab geographers mention it from around the 12th century, and its people developed the distinct Chimiini dialect of [[e:swahili|Swahili]].
barawa.r: The town was governed by its leading families and religious notables rather than a strong monarchy. It traded hides, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and grain from the [[e:shebelle-river|Shabelle]] and [[e:jubba-river|Jubba]] valleys, and was famous as a centre of Islamic learning, later linked with the [[e:qadiriyya|Qadiriyya]] brotherhood. It resisted the Portuguese, who sacked it in 1506, and was for long tributary to the [[s:ajuran-sultanate|Ajuran Sultanate]].
barawa.e: After Ajuran's decline Barawa came under Omani influence and in 1871 under the [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Sultanate of Zanzibar]]. Zanzibar leased the [[e:benadir|Benadir]] ports to [[e:italy|Italy]], and Barawa became part of [[s:italian-somaliland|Italian Somaliland]]. Its Bravanese community survives, though much reduced by the civil war after 1991.

barony-of-passavant.t: Frankish barony in the Mani held by the marshals of Achaea, whose castle of Passava watched over the unruly Maniots.
barony-of-passavant.o: Around 1220 [[e:john-of-neuilly|John of Neuilly]], hereditary marshal of the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]], received a fief at the entrance to the [[e:mani|Mani]] peninsula and built a castle there called Passavant, now Passava, near [[e:gytheio|Gytheio]]. Its purpose was to control the independent-minded population of the Mani and the route into [[e:laconia|Laconia]].
barony-of-passavant.r: The barony was small but held by one of the great officers of the principality, the marshal, who commanded the army. Its lords ruled from the castle over Greek villages, alongside the castle of [[e:grand-magne|Grand Magne]] built by [[e:william-ii-of-villehardouin|William II of Villehardouin]] further south.
barony-of-passavant.e: After [[e:william-ii-of-villehardouin|William II]] was captured at [[e:battle-of-pelagonia|Pelagonia]] in 1259, he ceded [[e:mystras|Mistras]], [[e:monemvasia|Monemvasia]] and [[e:grand-magne|Grand Magne]] to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], and Passavant was lost to the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] soon after, around 1263. The Neuilly heiress [[e:margaret-of-passavant|Margaret of Passavant]] later claimed [[e:akova|Akova]].

cr.a: Eric Gaba (Sting - fr:Sting); derivative work by Constantine

banate-of-leitha.t: State proclaimed by Hungarian irregulars in 1921 to stop the transfer of Burgenland to Austria, whose resistance led to the plebiscite that kept Sopron Hungarian.
banate-of-leitha.o: The peace treaties of [[e:treaty-of-saint-germain-en-laye-1919|Saint-Germain]] and [[e:treaty-of-trianon|Trianon]] assigned German-speaking western [[e:hungary|Hungary]], later called [[e:burgenland|Burgenland]], to [[e:austria|Austria]]. When the handover began in August 1921, Hungarian irregulars of the [[e:ragged-guard|Ragged Guard]] attacked Austrian gendarmes. On 4 October 1921 their commander, [[e:pal-pronay|Pál Prónay]], proclaimed the independent Banate of [[e:leitha|Leitha]] at [[e:oberwart|Oberwart]].
banate-of-leitha.r: The banate was a military occupation run by the irregulars, with a provisional administration and its own stamps; the Hungarian government officially disowned it while using it as a bargaining chip. Its population was mostly German-speaking, with Croatian and Hungarian minorities.
banate-of-leitha.e: Under Italian mediation the [[e:venice-protocol|Venice Protocol]] of October 1921 agreed a plebiscite in [[e:sopron|Sopron]], and the irregulars withdrew in November. [[e:burgenland|Burgenland]] passed to [[e:austria|Austria]], while Sopron voted in December 1921 to stay in [[e:hungary|Hungary]].

british-new-guinea.t: A British protectorate and then colony in southeastern New Guinea, administered for the Australian colonies and handed to Australia as Papua.
british-new-guinea.o: Fearing German expansion, [[s:colony-of-queensland|Queensland]] tried to annex eastern [[e:new-guinea|New Guinea]] in 1883, but [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] disallowed the move. In November 1884 [[e:james-elphinstone-erskine|Commodore James Erskine]] proclaimed a British [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the southeast at [[e:port-moresby|Port Moresby]], days after [[e:germany|Germany]] had raised its flag over the north, which became [[s:german-new-guinea|German New Guinea]]. In 1888 the territory was annexed as a crown colony.
british-new-guinea.r: The colony was funded largely by [[s:colony-of-queensland|Queensland]], [[s:colony-of-new-south-wales|New South Wales]] and [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]]. Administrator [[e:william-macgregor|William MacGregor]], from 1888 to 1898, explored the interior, set up government stations, appointed village constables and restricted land sales to Europeans. [[e:london-missionary-society|London Missionary Society]] workers, including [[e:james-chalmers-missionary|James Chalmers]], who was killed in 1901, were influential along the coast. Small gold rushes on [[e:misima|Misima]] and [[e:woodlark-island|Woodlark Island]] drew prospectors.
british-new-guinea.e: After federation, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] transferred the colony to the [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Commonwealth of Australia]], under the [[e:papua-act-1905|Papua Act]] of 1905, which took effect in 1906, when it was renamed the [[s:territory-of-papua|Territory of Papua]]. [[e:william-macgregor|MacGregor]]'s network of government stations and village constables remained the basis of Australian administration.
british-new-guinea.la: English, Motu, Papuan and Austronesian languages

banovina-of-croatia.t: Autonomous Croatian province created in 1939 in a late attempt to settle the Serb-Croat conflict within the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.
banovina-of-croatia.o: The [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]] had been divided in 1929 into banovinas that ignored historic borders. With war looming, the regent Prince Paul sought agreement with the [[e:croatian-peasant-party|Croatian Peasant Party]], and the [[e:cvetkovic-macek-agreement|Cvetković-Maček Agreement]] of 26 August 1939 merged the [[e:sava|Sava]] and Littoral banovinas with parts of [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]], [[e:herzegovina|Herzegovina]], [[e:syrmia|Srem]] and the [[e:dubrovnik|Dubrovnik]] area into one Banovina of [[e:croatia|Croatia]].
banovina-of-croatia.r: The banovina had autonomy over internal administration, education, justice and the economy under a ban, [[e:ivan-subasic|Ivan Šubašić]], while [[e:vladko-macek|Vladko Maček]] became deputy prime minister of [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]]. A [[e:croatian-parliament|Croatian Sabor]] was planned but never elected. [[e:serbs|Serbs]] in the banovina feared Croatian domination, while the separatist [[e:ustase|Ustaše]] rejected any settlement within Yugoslavia.
banovina-of-croatia.e: After the [[e:axis-powers|Axis]] invasion of April 1941, the [[e:ustase|Ustaše]] proclaimed the [[s:independent-state-of-croatia|Independent State of Croatia]] on 10 April, ending the banovina. Its borders influenced later debates about [[e:croatia|Croatia's]] territory, including the partition of [[e:bosnia|Bosnia]] discussed in the 1990s.
banovina-of-croatia.re: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam

british-honduras.t: Britain's only colony on the Central American mainland, a mahogany and chicle territory claimed by Guatemala that became independent Belize in 1981.
british-honduras.o: In 1862 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] formally declared the [[s:belize-settlement|Belize Settlement]] a colony, under the name British [[s:republic-of-honduras|Honduras]], subordinate to the governor of [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]]. Treaties with [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] in 1859 and with [[s:mexico|Mexico]] in 1893 fixed its borders, though [[e:guatemala|Guatemala]] later claimed the whole territory, arguing that [[e:britain|Britain]] had not kept a promise to build a road.
british-honduras.r: The settlers' assembly gave up its powers in 1871, making British [[s:republic-of-honduras|Honduras]] a crown colony, and in 1884 it received its own governor. Mahogany, logwood and later chicle for chewing gum were the main exports, controlled by a few British firms, notably the [[e:belize-estate-and-produce-company|Belize Estate and Produce Company]]. The population mixed [[e:criollo-people|Creoles]], [[e:garifuna|Garifuna]], Maya and Mestizo refugees from the [[e:caste-war-of-yucatan|Caste War]]. A hurricane devastated [[e:belize-city|Belize City]] in 1931.
british-honduras.e: Currency devaluation in 1949 sparked the nationalist [[e:peoples-united-party|People's United Party]], led by [[e:george-cadle-price|George Price]]. Self-government came in 1964, and the colony was renamed [[s:belize|Belize]] in 1973. After Hurricane Hattie, the capital moved to [[e:belmopan|Belmopan]] in 1970, and Belize became independent on 21 September 1981, with British troops guarding it against [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]].

beylik-of-shahrisabz.t: A Kenagas Uzbek beylik around Shahrisabz that defied the emirs of Bukhara until Russia conquered it in 1870.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.o: [[e:shahrisabz|Shahrisabz]], the old city of Kesh and birthplace of [[e:timur|Timur]], was the stronghold of the Kenagas [[e:uzbeks|Uzbek]] tribe, which long resisted the [[s:emirate-of-bukhara|Manghit Emirate]] of [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]]. In the mid-19th century the Kenagas [[e:bek|beks]] under [[e:jura-beg|Jura Beg]] and [[e:baba-beg|Baba Beg]] established effective independence.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.r: The [[e:bek|beks]] ruled a fertile oasis on the [[e:kashkadarya|Qashqadarya]] with the neighbouring town of [[e:kitob|Kitab]], fortifying it against [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]]. They exploited the [[e:emirate|emirate]]'s conflicts with [[e:russia|Russia]] and [[e:kokand|Kokand]], at times accepting nominal Bukharan overlordship. Little is recorded of their internal government.
beylik-of-shahrisabz.e: In 1870 a Russian force under General Abramov stormed [[e:shahrisabz|Shahrisabz]] and handed it to the [[s:emirate-of-bukhara|Emirate of Bukhara]], then a Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. [[e:jura-beg|Jura Beg]] and [[e:baba-beg|Baba Beg]] fled to [[e:kokand|Kokand]].

brigantes.t: The largest British confederation, ruling much of northern England under Queen Cartimandua until Rome conquered it after a civil war in the 70s.
brigantes.o: The Brigantes were a grouping of many communities across the [[e:pennines|Pennines]] and northern [[e:england|England]], from the [[e:river-mersey|Mersey]] and [[e:humber|Humber]] to the [[e:river-tyne|Tyne]]. Their name is linked to the goddess [[e:brigantia|Brigantia]]. By the late 40s they were ruled by Queen [[e:cartimandua|Cartimandua]], who had made a treaty with [[e:rome|Rome]] and governed as a client ruler.
brigantes.r: The confederation was loosely held, combining upland pastoralists and lowland farmers, and had no coinage of its own. Its political centre may have been at [[e:stanwick-iron-age-fortifications|Stanwick]] in [[e:north-yorkshire|North Yorkshire]], where vast earthwork enclosures were built in the 1st century. [[e:cartimandua|Cartimandua]] handed the fugitive [[e:caratacus|Caratacus]] to the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] in 51, and later her divorce from her consort [[e:venutius|Venutius]] split the Brigantes into rival factions.
brigantes.e: In 69 [[e:venutius|Venutius]] drove [[e:cartimandua|Cartimandua]] out, and Roman troops could only rescue her. [[e:quintus-petillius-cerialis|Petillius Cerialis]] then conquered the Brigantes from 71, with the legion based at [[e:york|York]]. The southern territory became a civitas centred on [[e:isurium-brigantum|Isurium Brigantum]], Aldborough, in [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]].

bastuli.t: A mixed Iberian and Phoenician people of the coast between Gibraltar and Almería, known to Greek writers as the Blastophoenicians.
bastuli.o: The Bastuli lived along the southern coast of [[e:iberia|Iberia]], roughly from the [[e:strait-of-gibraltar|Strait of Gibraltar]] to [[e:almeria|Almería]], from the mid-first millennium BCE. Ancient writers called them Bastuli-Poeni or Blastophoenicians, reflecting a population mixing native people with Phoenician and Punic settlers of towns such as [[s:malaka|Malaka]], [[s:sexi|Sexi]] and [[s:abdera-800|Abdera]].
bastuli.r: They lived from farming, fishing and fish salting, and their region minted coins in a distinctive Libyphoenician script. Little is known about their government, and it is debated whether they formed a people at all or were a label for the coastal Punicised communities.
bastuli.e: After the Roman conquest of the south in 206 BCE they came under [[s:hispania-ulterior|Hispania Ulterior]] and took part in the revolt of 197 BCE. Later they were absorbed into [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]].

bodeok.t: A short-lived puppet kingdom set up by Silla to house Goguryeo refugees under a Goguryeo prince after the fall of Pyongyang.
bodeok.o: After [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]] fell in 668, [[s:silla|Silla]] backed resistance to [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]]. In 670 it recognised [[e:anseung|Anseung]], a Goguryeo royal, as king of Goguryeo and settled him and his followers at [[e:iksan|Geummajeo]], modern Iksan, in former [[s:baekje|Baekje]] territory. In 674 Silla renamed him king of Bodeok.
bodeok.r: Bodeok served Silla's purposes during the war against [[s:later-tang|Tang]], giving [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]] refugees a figurehead and troops a base. [[e:anseung|Anseung]] married into the [[s:silla|Silla]] royal house, and the kingdom sent envoys to [[e:japan|Japan]]. Its autonomy was limited and it remained under close Silla control.
bodeok.e: In 683 [[e:anseung|Anseung]] was summoned to [[e:gyeongju|Gyeongju]], given the [[s:silla|Silla]] royal surname Kim and settled there. When his kinsman Daemun rebelled in 684, Silla crushed the revolt, abolished the kingdom and dispersed its people.

british-java.t: Five-year British rule of Java during the Napoleonic Wars, remembered for Raffles, land-tax reform and the sack of Yogyakarta.
british-java.o: After [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] annexed the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] targeted its colonies. In August 1811 a force from [[e:india|India]] under [[e:gilbert-elliot-1st-earl-of-minto|Lord Minto]] and General [[e:samuel-auchmuty|Samuel Auchmuty]] landed near [[e:batavia|Batavia]] and defeated the Franco-[[e:dutch|Dutch]] army of Governor-General [[e:jan-willem-janssens|Jan Willem Janssens]], who capitulated in September. [[e:stamford-raffles|Thomas Stamford Raffles]] was appointed lieutenant-governor.
british-java.r: [[e:stamford-raffles|Raffles]] replaced forced deliveries with a land rent assessed on villages, reduced the powers of Javanese regents, and in 1812 stormed the kraton of the [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta Sultanate]], creating [[s:pakualaman|Pakualaman]]. He also attacked the [[s:palembang-sultanate|Palembang Sultanate]]. British officials surveyed [[e:borobudur|Borobudur]] and Prambanan, and Raffles wrote his History of [[e:java|Java]].
british-java.e: The [[e:anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1814|Anglo-Dutch Convention of 1814]] returned [[e:java|Java]] to the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], and the British handed over in August 1816, when the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]] was restored. Some of the land-rent reforms survived, and [[e:stamford-raffles|Raffles]] went on to found [[s:singapore|Singapore]].

bahurutshe-chiefdom.t: The senior house of the Tswana, whose stone-walled capital Kaditshwene impressed early 19th-century visitors as one of the largest towns in southern Africa.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.o: The [[e:bahurutshe|Bahurutshe]] trace their descent from the founding [[e:tswana-people|Tswana]] lineage, from which the [[e:bakwena|Bakwena]] and other groups later branched. By the 16th century they were settled in the [[e:marico-river|Marico]] district of the western highveld, where they built aggregated towns with stone-walled [[e:cattle|cattle]] enclosures.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled large towns divided into wards, each under a headman, with public assemblies (kgotla) for justice and debate. The economy combined [[e:cattle|cattle]] herding, cereal farming and skilled metalworking in iron and [[e:copper|copper]]. When the missionary [[e:john-campbell-missionary|John Campbell]] visited [[e:kaditshwene|Kaditshwene]] in 1820 he estimated its population at 16,000 and admired its metal crafts and trade.
bahurutshe-chiefdom.e: [[e:kaditshwene|Kaditshwene]] was destroyed in the wars of the early 1820s, and the [[e:bahurutshe|Hurutshe]] later suffered under [[e:ndebele-kingdom|Mzilikazi's Ndebele]]. Reassembled under Moilwa in the [[e:marico-river|Marico]] valley, they came under the rule of the [[s:south-african-republic|Transvaal]] [[e:boers|Boer]] republic after 1852, though Hurutshe communities persist around [[e:zeerust|Zeerust]] and in [[e:botswana|Botswana]].

balasinor-state.t: A Babi Pathan Nawabi state of central Gujarat, now best known for the dinosaur fossils found on its former lands.
balasinor-state.o: Balasinor was founded around 1758 by a member of the Babi family, the Pathan dynasty that also held [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh State]] and [[s:radhanpur-state|Radhanpur State]]. It survived the [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] period by paying tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda State]].
balasinor-state.r: The Nawabs governed a small agricultural territory as part of the [[e:rewa-kantha-agency|Rewa Kantha Agency]]. Little is recorded about its internal politics. In 1981 large deposits of dinosaur bones and eggs were found at nearby [[e:raiyoli|Raiyoli]], now a fossil park promoted by members of the former ruling family.
balasinor-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Balasinor was merged into [[e:bombay-state|Bombay State]] in 1948 and has been part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] since 1960; it lies in [[e:mahisagar-district|Mahisagar district]].

bhadrawah-state.t: A small hill state in a high valley off the Chenab, contested by Chamba and Jammu before it became part of Jammu and Kashmir.
bhadrawah-state.o: [[e:bhadarwah|Bhadrawah]] was ruled by local [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] chiefs; tradition dates the state to around 1400, but its early history is poorly recorded.
bhadrawah-state.r: Set in a green upland valley, [[e:bhadarwah|Bhadrawah]] was for long periods a tributary or dependency of [[s:chamba-state|Chamba State]]. Its people spoke Bhadarwahi, and its Vasuki Nag temple is an important local shrine. Little detail of its government survives.
bhadrawah-state.e: [[e:bhadarwah|Bhadrawah]] passed to [[e:gulab-singh|Gulab Singh of Jammu]] and became part of [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir (princely state)]] in 1846. It is now a town in [[e:doda-district|Doda district]].

baro-bhuyans.t: A confederacy of Bengali landholders led by Isa Khan that resisted the Mughal conquest of Bengal for a generation.
baro-bhuyans.o: When the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] defeated [[e:daud-khan-karrani|Daud Khan Karrani]] in 1576 and ended Afghan rule in [[e:bengal|Bengal]], many landholders in the eastern river delta refused to submit. Known as the Baro-[[e:bhuyan|Bhuyans]], the twelve landlords, they gathered around [[e:isa-khan|Isa Khan]], a chief of Afghan and [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] descent based at [[e:sonargaon|Sonargaon]].
baro-bhuyans.r: The [[e:bhuyan|Bhuyans]] were Muslim and [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] zamindars who controlled the waterways of Bhati, the low delta, with fleets of war boats and fortified river posts. They kept their own revenues and alliances, cooperating against Mughal armies. [[e:isa-khan|Isa Khan]] defeated a Mughal fleet in 1584 and fought [[e:man-singh-i|Man Singh]], the Mughal governor.
baro-bhuyans.e: After [[e:isa-khan|Isa Khan's]] death in 1599 his son [[e:musa-khan-of-bengal|Musa Khan]] led the resistance. The Mughal governor [[e:islam|Islam]] Khan moved the capital to [[e:dhaka|Dhaka]] and defeated Musa Khan by 1611, absorbing eastern [[e:bengal|Bengal]] into the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]].

barwani-state.t: A Sisodia Rajput state on the Narmada in Nimar, one of the salute states of the Central India Agency.
barwani-state.o: The rulers of Barwani claimed descent from the [[e:sisodia|Sisodia]] house of [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]] and held lands in the [[e:narmada-river|Narmada]] valley for centuries. The register dates the state to 1650, when the capital was established at Barwani. Its territory had shrunk under [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] pressure by the 18th century.
barwani-state.r: The Ranas ruled the south bank of the [[e:narmada-river|Narmada]] and the [[e:satpura-range|Satpura]] hills, home to many [[e:bhils|Bhils]]. Under British paramountcy it was an eleven-gun salute state in the [[e:bhopawar-agency|Bhopawar Agency]], with an economy based on [[e:cotton|cotton]] and grain. Little is recorded of its rulers beyond these lists.
barwani-state.e: Barwani joined [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and [[e:madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] in 1956. It is now a district headquarters.

bida-emirate.t: The Fulani emirate that ruled the Nupe from Bida, a centre of crafts and slave raiding on the middle Niger until the Royal Niger Company's victory in 1897.
bida-emirate.o: In the early 19th century the [[e:fula|Fulani]] cleric [[e:mallam-dendo|Mallam Dendo]] gained influence in the [[s:nupe-kingdom|Nupe Kingdom]] by exploiting civil wars among its princes, and his sons took control of the country. After further conflicts, [[e:usman-zaki|Usman Zaki]] and his brother [[e:masaba|Masaba]] emerged as rulers, and around 1856 [[e:bida|Bida]] was founded as the capital of an [[e:emirate|emirate]] owing allegiance to the [[s:gwandu-emirate|Gwandu Emirate]].
bida-emirate.r: [[e:masaba|Masaba]], who ruled from 1859 to 1873, built a strong state with a large army and a network of fiefs held by royal princes. [[e:nupe-kingdom|Nupe]] raided its neighbours heavily for slaves, who worked on royal estates around [[e:bida|Bida]]. The city was famous for its glass [[e:bead|beads]], brass and [[e:silver|silver]] work and woven cloth, and it traded along the [[e:niger-river|Niger]] with European merchants.
bida-emirate.e: In January 1897 the [[s:royal-niger-company-territories|Royal Niger Company]] defeated [[e:emir|Emir]] Abubakar's army outside [[e:bida|Bida]]. British forces occupied the [[e:emirate|emirate]] in 1901 within [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Northern Nigeria]], and the [[e:etsu-nupe|Etsu Nupe]] still reigns at Bida.

bangwato-kingdom.t: The largest Tswana chiefdom, ruled from Shoshong and later Palapye, whose king Khama III helped keep Botswana out of Company rule.
bangwato-kingdom.o: The [[e:bamangwato|Bangwato]] branched off from the [[e:bakwena|Bakwena]] in the 18th century and settled in what is now central [[e:botswana|Botswana]]. After the disruptions of the 1820s they grew under [[e:sekgoma-i|Sekgoma I]], with [[e:shoshong|Shoshong]] as their capital, absorbing many refugees and subject groups.
bangwato-kingdom.r: Chiefs ruled through the kgotla and ward headmen, with [[e:cattle|cattle]] as the basis of wealth. [[e:shoshong|Shoshong]] became a key stop on the missionary and trade road to the north. [[e:khama-iii|Khama III]], a Christian, became chief in 1875, banned alcohol trading, moved the capital to [[e:palapye|Palapye]] in 1889 and promoted the [[e:london-missionary-society|London Missionary Society]] church.
bangwato-kingdom.e: The [[e:bamangwato|Bangwato]] joined the [[s:bechuanaland-protectorate|Bechuanaland Protectorate]] in 1885. In 1895 [[e:khama-iii|Khama]] travelled to [[e:london|London]] with other chiefs to resist transfer to the [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company]]. His grandson [[e:seretse-khama|Seretse Khama]] became [[e:botswana|Botswana's]] first president in 1966.

beja-state.t: A tiny Rajput hill state near Kasauli, among the smallest of the Simla Hill States.
beja-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins.
beja-state.r: Beja consisted of a few villages in the hills south-west of [[e:shimla|Shimla]]. It was occupied by the [[e:gurkhas|Gurkhas]] in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Its history is poorly recorded.
beja-state.e: Beja merged into [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948 and is now part of Solan district.

banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.t: The last Almoravid family, which crossed from Majorca to wage a fifty-year war against the Almohads across Ifriqiya and the central Maghreb.
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.o: The Banu Ghaniya, descendants of an Almoravid princess, held the [[e:balearic-islands|Balearic Islands]] as [[s:banu-ghaniya-majorca|Banu Ghaniya Majorca]] after the fall of the [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]]. In 1184 [[e:ali-ibn-ghaniya|Ali ibn Ghaniya]] landed at [[e:bejaia|Bejaia]], seized the city from the [[s:almohad-caliphate|Almohad Caliphate]] and opened a war to restore Almoravid rule, recognising the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] in [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]].
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.r: There was no fixed capital. The Banu Ghaniya fought as a roaming power, allied with Arab tribes such as the [[e:banu-sulaym|Banu Sulaym]] and, for a time, with [[e:sharaf-al-din-qaraqush|Qaraqush]]. Under Ali's brother [[e:yahya-ibn-ghaniya|Yahya ibn Ghaniya]] they took [[e:tunis|Tunis]] and [[e:mahdia|Mahdia]] around 1203, devastating towns and countryside across [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]] and [[s:tripolitania|Tripolitania]].
banu-ghaniya-of-ifriqiya.e: The [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Nasir retook [[e:mahdia|Mahdia]] and [[e:tunis|Tunis]] in 1205 to 1206 and installed a [[e:hafsid-dynasty|Hafsid]] governor, whose successors kept up the fight. Yahya was driven into the desert and died in the 1230s, ending the movement. The chaos helped the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsid Sultanate]] emerge.

bastarnae.t: Probably Germanic people of the lower Danube and Carpathians who fought for Macedon against Rome and later joined the Goths.
bastarnae.o: The Bastarnae appeared north of the lower [[e:danube|Danube]] around 200 BCE, the first Germanic-speaking people known to Greek and Roman writers, though some ancient authors thought them [[e:celts|Celts]]. One branch, the Peucini, lived on the island of [[e:peuce|Peuce]] in the Danube delta.
bastarnae.r: They were a warlike confederation of tribes, valued as [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]]. Philip V and [[e:perseus-of-macedon|Perseus of Macedon]] recruited them against [[e:rome|Rome]], and the [[e:zarubintsy-culture|Zarubintsy]] and [[e:poienesti-lukashevka-culture|Poienești-Lukashevka]] archaeological cultures are often linked to them. In 62 BCE they defeated [[e:gaius-antonius-hybrida|Gaius Antonius Hybrida]] near [[s:histria|Histria]]. In 29 BCE [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Marcus Licinius Crassus]] defeated them and killed their king [[e:deldo|Deldo]] in single combat.
bastarnae.e: Under the empire they remained a frontier people, joining the [[e:goths|Goths]] and [[s:carpi|Carpi]] in 3rd-century raids. Around 280 the emperor [[e:probus-emperor|Probus]] settled a large number of Bastarnae in [[e:thrace|Thrace]], after which they disappear as a distinct people.

bajana-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state on the edge of the Little Rann of Kutch, held by a family of Jat Maliks.
bajana-state.o: Bajana lay on the southern edge of the [[e:little-rann-of-kutch|Little Rann of Kutch]] in the [[e:jhalawad|Jhalawad]] region of [[e:kathiawar|Kathiawar]]. Its rulers were Muslim [[e:jats|Jats]], who held the estate from around 1700. Its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
bajana-state.r: The ruler governed a dry territory of grazing land and salt flats bordering the [[e:rann-of-kutch|Rann]]. After 1807 Bajana came under British supervision in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]] as a minor non-salute state. Few further details are recorded.
bajana-state.e: Bajana merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960. Its territory borders the [[e:indian-wild-ass-sanctuary|Wild Ass Sanctuary of the Little Rann]].

belarusian-peoples-republic.t: The first Belarusian attempt at independence, proclaimed under German occupation in 1918, whose Rada still survives in exile.
belarusian-peoples-republic.o: After the [[e:russian-revolution|Russian Revolution]] Belarusian activists formed a [[e:rada-of-the-belarusian-democratic-republic|Rada]] in [[e:minsk|Minsk]]. While German troops occupied the city, the [[e:radaa|Rada]] issued a series of charters, and on 25 March 1918 the Third Constituent Charter declared the Belarusian People's Republic independent of [[e:russia|Russia]]. [[e:jan-sierada|Jan Sierada]] became the first chairman of the Rada.
belarusian-peoples-republic.r: The republic never controlled much territory or had an army, as real power lay with the German military. Its government, led by figures such as [[e:raman-skirmunt|Raman Skirmunt]] and later [[e:anton-lutskevich|Anton Lutskevich]], organised schools in the Belarusian language and sought recognition abroad. It issued passports and sent missions to neighbouring states.
belarusian-peoples-republic.e: When the Germans withdrew in December 1918 the Bolsheviks took [[e:minsk|Minsk]] and set up the [[s:socialist-soviet-republic-of-byelorussia|Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia]]. The [[e:rada-of-the-belarusian-democratic-republic|Rada]] went into exile, where it has continued under successive leaders, making it the world's oldest government in exile. 25 March is marked by Belarusian opposition as Freedom Day.

byblos.t: Byblos, an ancient Phoenician port on the Lebanese coast that shipped cedar to Egypt for over two thousand years and gave the Greeks their word for papyrus.
byblos.o: Gubla, as its people called it, is among the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world. By c. 2600 BCE it had become a walled city whose harbour supplied cedar and resin from the [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]] mountains to the [[e:pharaoh|pharaohs]] of the [[s:old-kingdom-of-egypt|Old Kingdom of Egypt]], receiving gold, linen and [[e:papyrus|papyrus]] in return.
byblos.r: Kings ruled under the protection of the city's goddess, the [[e:baalat-gebal|Baalat Gebal]], whose temple received Egyptian offerings. In the 14th century BCE its king [[e:rib-hadda|Rib-Hadda]] sent dozens of the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]] begging [[e:egypt|Egypt]] for help. The sarcophagus of King [[e:ahiram|Ahiram]] bears one of the earliest inscriptions in the Phoenician alphabet, which Byblos helped to shape.
byblos.e: Byblos lost commercial leadership to [[s:tyre|Tyre]] and [[s:sidon|Sidon]] in the [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] and paid tribute to the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]], the [[s:chaldean-empire|Chaldean Empire]] and the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] in turn. It submitted peacefully to Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] in 332 BCE, ending its independent kingship. The town of Jbeil still occupies the site.
